paragraphs: This paper analyzes a perceptron's classification ability when inputs have finite precision. Its positive result rests on a specific probabilistic setting: there are n uniformly distributed pattern vectors, each represented by cn bits, with c greater than one. Under those conditions, the perceptron can realize every possible binary labeling of the patterns with high probability.

The storage result compares the resulting network with keeping the full input patterns. The network needs a proportion O(log n/n) of that storage, which shrinks as n increases. Thus, in the stated setting, representing a classification through the network can require a progressively smaller fraction of the memory needed to retain all patterns explicitly.

The authors also report O(n²) arithmetic operations for the perceptron algorithm with high probability, alongside an O(n^3.5) worst-case bound for methods such as linear programming. Those bounds use different probability qualifications, which matters when interpreting the comparison. The paper further identifies mathematical connections to VLSI circuit testing and random matrix theory.
summary.tldr: Under a uniform random finite-precision input model, a perceptron can realize all binary labelings with high probability while using compact storage.

title: Complexity of Finite Precision Neural Network Classifier

abstract: If neurons sum up their inputs in a non-linear way, as some simula(cid:173) tions suggest, how is this distributed fine-grained non-linearity ex(cid:173) ploited during learning? How are all the small sigmoids in synapse, spine and dendritic tree lined up in the right areas of their respective input spaces? In this report, I show how an abstract atemporal highly nested tree structure with a quadratic transfer function associated with each branchpoint, can self organise using only a single global reinforcement scalar, to perform binary classification tasks. The pro(cid:173) cedure works well, solving the 6-multiplexer and a difficult phoneme classification task as well as back-propagation does, and faster. Furthermore, it does not calculate an error gradient, but uses a statist(cid:173) ical scheme to build moving models of the reinforcement signal.

paragraphs: The paper asks how learning could organize nonlinear computations distributed throughout a neuron's dendritic structure. Its model is an abstract, deeply nested tree with a quadratic transfer function at each branch point. The tree is atemporal, so the study concerns how this nested structure computes a classification without modeling its evolution through biological time.

Learning uses a single global reinforcement value to organize the tree for binary classification. The procedure does not calculate an error gradient. Instead, it maintains statistical, moving models of the reinforcement signal. This addresses how many internal nonlinear components can be trained when the available feedback is a shared scalar evaluation of performance.

The author reports success on the 6-multiplexer and a difficult phoneme classification task, with performance matching backpropagation and faster learning. These results support the proposed statistical procedure as a way to train the artificial dendritic structure. The broader significance is that the model coordinates distributed nonlinear processing using a global reinforcement signal, demonstrating an alternative route to learning in the studied architecture.
summary.tldr: Nested artificial dendritic trees learn binary classification from one global reinforcement signal without calculating error gradients.

abstract: A large class of motor control tasks requires that on each cycle the con(cid:173) troller is told its current state and must choose an action to achieve a specified, state-dependent, goal behaviour. This paper argues that the optimization of learning rate, the number of experimental control deci(cid:173) sions before adequate performance is obtained, and robustness is of prime importance-if necessary at the expense of computation per control cy(cid:173) cle and memory requirement. This is motivated by the observation that a robot which requires two thousand learning steps to achieve adequate performance, or a robot which occasionally gets stuck while learning, will always be undesirable, whereas moderate computational expense can be accommodated by increasingly powerful computer hardware. It is not un(cid:173) reasonable to assume the existence of inexpensive 100 Mflop controllers within a few years and so even processes with control cycles in the low tens of milliseconds will have millions of machine instructions in which to make their decisions. This paper outlines a learning control scheme which aims to make effective use of such computational power. 1 MEMORY BASED LEARNING Memory-based learning is an approach applicable to both classification and func(cid:173) tion learning in which all experiences presented to the learning box are explic(cid:173) itly remembered. The memory, Mem, is a set of input-output pairs, Mem = {(Xl, YI), (X21 Y2), ... , (Xb Yk)}. When a prediction is required of the output of a novel input Xquery, the memory is searched to obtain experiences with inputs close to Xquery. These local neighbours are used to determine a locally consistent output for the query. Three memory-based techniques, Nearest Neighbour, Kernel Regression, and Local Weighted Regression, are shown in the accompanying figure.

paragraphs: This paper outlines an adaptive control scheme for tasks in which a controller repeatedly receives its current state and chooses an action toward a state-dependent goal. Its central priority is learning adequate behavior with few experimental control decisions while remaining robust. The authors argue that extra computation and memory can be acceptable costs for achieving those priorities.

The scheme is framed around learning forward models and introduces memory-based learning as a way to use past experience. Input–output pairs are explicitly stored. When a new prediction is needed, the system retrieves experiences with nearby inputs and uses them to estimate a locally consistent output. The supplied text discusses nearest-neighbor, kernel-regression, and locally weighted regression techniques.

The important tradeoff is between the expense of computation during a control cycle and the expense of learning through actions. The paper motivates spending available processing capacity to reduce undesirable learning behavior, including excessive trial decisions or becoming stuck. It presents this as a design direction for effective control, rather than reporting a measured performance improvement in the supplied passage.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes prioritizing robust, experience-efficient adaptive control by spending more computation and memory on learned forward models.

title: Fast, Robust Adaptive Control by Learning only Forward Models

abstract: We have designed, fabricated, and tested an analog VLSI chip which computes radial basis functions in parallel. We have de(cid:173) veloped a synapse circuit that approximates a quadratic function. We aggregate these circuits to form radial basis functions. These radial basis functions are then averaged together using a follower aggregator.
originalAbstract: We have designed, fabricated, and tested an analog VLSI chip which computes radial basis functions in parallel. We have de(cid:173) veloped a synapse circuit that approximates a quadratic function. We aggregate these circuits to form radial basis functions. These radial basis functions are then averaged together using a follower aggregator.

paragraphs: This paper presents an analog chip that computes radial basis functions in parallel. The contribution includes designing, fabricating, and testing the device, taking the computation into a physical circuit implementation. Parallel computation is part of the design: the chip supports multiple basis function calculations rather than describing only a single isolated computational element.

The basic building block is a synapse circuit that approximates a quadratic function. The authors combine these circuits to construct radial basis functions. This gives the implementation a clear progression from a simpler circuit response to a larger computational operation. The quadratic behavior is explicitly an approximation, so it is the circuit's usable response that underpins the construction.

The resulting radial basis function outputs are averaged using a follower aggregator. The overall design therefore connects three stages: quadratic approximation, assembly into basis functions, and aggregation of their outputs. Its significance is the demonstrated hardware realization of that sequence. The stated outcome is a fabricated and tested analog implementation, with the abstract emphasizing its circuit organization and parallel operation.
summary.tldr: The authors built and tested an analog chip that computes radial basis functions in parallel using quadratic-approximating circuits.

title: An Analog VLSI Chip for Radial Basis Functions

abstract: This workshop explored machine learning approaches to 3 topics: (1) finding structure in music (analysis, continuation, and comple(cid:173) tion of an unfinished piece), (2) modeling perception of time (ex(cid:173) traction of musical meter, explanation of human data on timing), and (3) interpolation in timbre space. In recent years, NIPS has heard neural networks generate tunes and harmonize chorales. With a large amount of music becoming available in computer readable form, real data can be used to train connectionist models. At the beginning of this workshop, Andreas Weigend focused on architectures to capture structure on multiple time scales. J. S. Bach's last (unfinished) fugue from Die Kunst der Fuge served as an example (Dirst & Weigend, 1994).1 The prediction approach to continuation and completion, as well as to modeling expectations, can be charac(cid:173) terized by the question "What's next?". Moving to time as the primary medium of musical communication, the inquiry in music perception and cognition shifted to the question "When next?" . In other words, so far we have considered patterns in time. They assume prior iden(cid:173) tification and subsequent processing of events. Bob Port, coming from the speech community, considered patterns of time, discussing timing in linguistic polyrhythms (e.g., hot cup of tea). He also drew parallels between timing in Japanese language and timing in music, supporting the hypothesis that perceptional rhythms entrain attentional rhythms. As a mechanism for entrainment, Devin McAuley presented adaptive oscillators: the oscillators adapt their frequencies such that their "firing" coincides with the beat of the music (McAuley, 1994). As the beat can be viewed as entrainment of an individual oscillator, the meter can be viewed as entrainment of multiple oscillators. paragraphs: This workshop report surveys machine learning approaches to musical structure, time perception, and interpolation in timbre space. One theme is learning from music available in computer-readable form. Models of structure across multiple time scales are discussed in connection with analyzing music and continuing or completing an unfinished composition.

A central distinction separates predicting the next musical event from understanding when events occur. Continuation and completion concern the sequence of events and the expectations it creates. Timing research instead examines the temporal patterns themselves. The workshop connects this question to speech rhythms and to the hypothesis that perceived rhythms can bring attentional rhythms into alignment.

Adaptive oscillators provide a proposed mechanism for that alignment. Their frequencies change so that their activity coincides with a musical beat; coordinating multiple oscillators offers an account of meter. The report also describes an analogy with pendulum clocks synchronizing through a shared support. These discussions connect sequence learning with dynamical explanations of timing, presenting several research directions rather than one unified experimental result.
summary.tldr: A workshop connects neural approaches to musical structure with oscillator-based accounts of beat, meter, and timing perception.

title: Connectionism for Music and Audition

We then show how the same principles may be used to select data for two alternative, statistically-based learning architectures: mixtures of Gaussians and locally weighted regression. title: Active Learning with Statistical Models

abstract: The observed distribution of natural images is far from uniform. On the contrary, real images have complex and important struc(cid:173) ture that can be exploited for image processing, recognition and analysis. There have been many proposed approaches to the prin(cid:173) cipled statistical modeling of images, but each has been limited in either the complexity of the models or the complexity of the im(cid:173) ages. We present a non-parametric multi-scale statistical model for images that can be used for recognition, image de-noising, and in a "generative mode" to synthesize high quality textures.

On the contrary, real images have complex and important struc(cid:173) ture that can be exploited for image processing, recognition and analysis. There have been many proposed approaches to the prin(cid:173) cipled statistical modeling of images, but each has been limited in either the complexity of the models or the complexity of the im(cid:173) ages. We present a non-parametric multi-scale statistical model for images that can be used for recognition, image de-noising, and in a "generative mode" to synthesize high quality textures.

paragraphs: Natural images occupy a structured part of the space of possible images. Their visual organization means that some arrangements occur much more often than others. The paper starts from the idea that capturing this uneven distribution can support several tasks, including recognizing images and removing noise from them.

The authors introduce a statistical image model described as non-parametric and multi-scale. The multi-scale aspect makes structure at different image scales part of the modeling approach. The motivation is to address a tension in earlier statistical methods, which the abstract describes as restricted either in the complexity of their models or in the complexity of the images they could handle.

The proposed model can be used for recognition, denoising, and generating textures. These uses connect understanding observed images with producing new image content through the same statistical framework. The abstract specifically reports synthesis of high-quality textures. Its broader contribution is a model intended to capture useful natural-image structure across several image-processing purposes, rather than serving only one task.
summary.tldr: A non-parametric image model captures structure across scales for recognition, denoising, and texture synthesis.

title: A Non-Parametric Multi-Scale Statistical Model for Natural Images

abstract: We introduce two new techniques for density estimation. Our approach poses the problem as a supervised learning task which can be performed using Neural Networks. We introduce a stochastic method for learning the cumulative distribution and an analogous deterministic technique. We demonstrate convergence of our methods both theoretically and experimentally, and provide comparisons with the Parzen estimate. Our theoretical results demonstrate better convergence properties than the Parzen estimate.
originalAbstract: We introduce two new techniques for density estimation. Our approach poses the problem as a supervised learning task which can be performed using Neural Networks. We introduce a stochastic method for learning the cumulative distribution and an analogous deterministic technique. We demonstrate convergence of our methods both theoretically and experimentally, and provide comparisons with the Parzen estimate. Our theoretical results demonstrate better convergence properties than the Parzen estimate.

paragraphs: The paper introduces two techniques for estimating a probability density by reformulating the problem as supervised learning. This allows neural networks to perform the learning task. The key change is how the estimation problem is posed, giving a supervised-learning procedure a role in recovering the distribution represented by the observations.

One technique uses a stochastic method to learn the cumulative distribution, and the other is an analogous deterministic technique. The cumulative distribution describes accumulated probability, providing the quantity around which the proposed learning approach is constructed. Presenting both versions gives two related ways to pursue the same density-estimation objective.

The authors demonstrate convergence theoretically and experimentally, and compare their methods with the Parzen estimate. Their theoretical results establish better convergence properties than that reference method. This supports the mathematical promise of the reformulation alongside experimental evidence of convergence. The stated advantage concerns convergence properties; it does not establish that every finite dataset or implementation will yield better estimates or lower computational cost.
summary.tldr: Two neural-network density-estimation techniques recast the task as supervised learning and have better theoretical convergence properties than the Parzen estimate.

title: Neural Networks for Density Estimation

abstract: We explore the statistical properties of natural sound stimuli preprocessed with a bank of linear filters. The responses of such filters exhibit a striking form of statistical dependency, in which the response variance of each filter grows with the response amplitude of filters tuned for nearby frequencies. These dependencies may be substantially reduced using an operation known as divisive normalization, in which the response of each filter is divided by a weighted sum of the rectified responses of other filters. The weights may be chosen to maximize the independence of the normalized responses for an ensemble of natural sounds. We demonstrate that the resulting model accounts for nonlinearities in the response characteristics of the auditory nerve, by comparing model simulations to electrophysiological recordings. In previous work (NIPS, 1998) we demonstrated that an analogous model derived from the statistics of natural images accounts for non-linear properties of neurons in primary visual cortex. Thus, divisive normalization appears to be a generic mechanism for eliminating a type of statistical dependency that is prevalent in natural signals of different modalities.

paragraphs: The authors examine natural sounds after processing them with a bank of linear filters. They find a particular dependency: a filter's response variance grows with the response amplitude of filters tuned to nearby frequencies. Thus, the strength of activity in one frequency region carries information about how variable nearby filter responses will be.

They reduce these dependencies using divisive normalization. Each filter response is divided by a weighted sum of rectified responses from other filters, making its output depend on the surrounding activity. The weights can be selected to maximize independence across normalized responses for a collection of natural sounds, tying the transformation to measured signal statistics.

Comparisons between simulations and electrophysiological recordings show that the resulting model accounts for nonlinear response characteristics of the auditory nerve. The authors connect this finding to analogous earlier work on natural images and visual cortex. Together, the results suggest that divisive normalization may be a general mechanism for reducing a recurring kind of statistical dependency across sensory modalities.
summary.tldr: Divisive normalization reduces dependencies in natural-sound filter responses and accounts for observed nonlinearities in auditory-nerve responses.

title: Natural Sound Statistics and Divisive Normalization in the Auditory System

abstract: We investigate the generalization performance of some learning prob- lems in Hilbert functional Spaces. We introduce a notion of convergence of the estimated functional predictor to the best underlying predictor, and obtain an estimate on the rate of the convergence. This estimate allows us to derive generalization bounds on some learning formulations.
originalAbstract: We investigate the generalization performance of some learning prob- lems in Hilbert functional Spaces. We introduce a notion of convergence of the estimated functional predictor to the best underlying predictor, and obtain an estimate on the rate of the convergence. This estimate allows us to derive generalization bounds on some learning formulations.

paragraphs: The paper examines generalization for certain learning problems whose predictors belong to Hilbert spaces of functions. Its central comparison is between a predictor estimated through learning and the best underlying predictor. This frames the analysis around how closely the learned function approaches that target, rather than only how well it fits the observations used to estimate it.

The authors introduce a notion of convergence for this comparison and obtain an estimate of its rate. Defining convergence specifies what it means for the estimated predictor to approach the target. Estimating the rate adds a quantitative account of that approach, providing more information than a statement that convergence occurs.

They then use the rate estimate to derive generalization bounds for some learning formulations. The contribution is this chain from a definition of predictor convergence to quantitative guarantees about generalization. Its stated scope is particular learning problems and formulations in Hilbert functional spaces; the abstract does not assert that the same bound covers every method in such spaces.
summary.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for some Hilbert-space learning formulations by estimating convergence rates toward the best underlying predictor.

title: Generalization Performance of Some Learning Problems in Hilbert Functional Spaces

abstract: A key issue in supervised protein classiﬁcation is the representation of in- put sequences of amino acids. Recent work using string kernels for pro- tein data has achieved state-of-the-art classiﬁcation performance. How- ever, such representations are based only on labeled data — examples with known 3D structures, organized into structural classes — while in practice, unlabeled data is far more plentiful. In this work, we de- velop simple and scalable cluster kernel techniques for incorporating un- labeled data into the representation of protein sequences. We show that our methods greatly improve the classiﬁcation performance of string ker- nels and outperform standard approaches for using unlabeled data, such as adding close homologs of the positive examples to the training data. We achieve equal or superior performance to previously presented cluster kernel methods while achieving far greater computational efﬁciency.

In this work, we de- velop simple and scalable cluster kernel techniques for incorporating un- labeled data into the representation of protein sequences. We show that our methods greatly improve the classiﬁcation performance of string ker- nels and outperform standard approaches for using unlabeled data, such as adding close homologs of the positive examples to the training data. We achieve equal or superior performance to previously presented cluster kernel methods while achieving far greater computational efﬁciency.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent amino-acid sequences for protein classification when unlabeled sequences are much more plentiful than labeled examples. Here, labeled proteins have known three-dimensional structures and belong to structural classes. The authors build on strong classification results from string kernels while seeking to use the additional unlabeled data.

They develop simple, scalable cluster-kernel techniques that incorporate unlabeled sequences into the representation. This places the extra data inside the way proteins are compared for classification. The approach makes the abundance of unlabeled sequences useful for a supervised task whose structural labels are relatively scarce.

The reported methods substantially improve string-kernel classification performance and outperform standard ways of using unlabeled data, including adding close homologs of positive examples to training. They also match or exceed previously presented cluster-kernel methods while requiring much less computation. The results support both parts of the contribution: unlabeled data improves the representation, and the proposed techniques provide that benefit with greater computational efficiency than earlier cluster-kernel approaches.
summary.tldr: Scalable cluster kernels use unlabeled protein sequences to improve classification while greatly reducing computation relative to earlier cluster-kernel methods.

title: Semi-supervised Protein Classification Using Cluster Kernels

abstract: A balanced network leads to contradictory constraints on memory models, as exemplified in previous work on accommodation of synfire chains. Here we show that these constraints can be overcome by introducing a 'shadow' inhibitory pattern for each excitatory pattern of the model. This is interpreted as a double- balance principle, whereby there exists both global balance between average excitatory and inhibitory currents and local balance between the currents carrying coherent activity at any given time frame. This principle can be applied to networks with Hebbian cell assemblies, leading to a high capacity of the associative memory. The number of possible patterns is limited by a combinatorial constraint that turns out to be P=0.06N within the specific model that we employ. This limit is reached by the Hebbian cell assembly network. To the best of our knowledge this is the first time that such high memory capacities are demonstrated in the asynchronous state of models of spiking neurons.

paragraphs: Balanced spiking networks impose constraints that can conflict with storing memory patterns. This paper proposes resolving those constraints by pairing each excitatory pattern with a corresponding inhibitory shadow pattern. The pairing is intended to preserve useful organized activity while maintaining the balance required by the network.

The authors call this double balance. Global balance concerns average excitatory and inhibitory currents, while local balance concerns currents carrying coherent activity within a given time frame. Applying both forms of balance to networks with Hebbian cell assemblies produces an associative-memory model with high capacity in an asynchronous state.

Within the specific model studied, a combinatorial constraint limits the number of patterns to P = 0.06N, and the Hebbian cell-assembly network reaches that limit. The result shows that the proposed inhibitory pairing can reconcile balance with substantial memory storage in this model. The capacity expression is explicitly model-specific, and the authors qualify their historical claim as the first such high asynchronous spiking-network capacity demonstration to their knowledge.
summary.tldr: Pairing excitatory memories with inhibitory shadow patterns enables a doubly balanced spiking network to reach its model-specific memory-capacity limit.

title: The Doubly Balanced Network of Spiking Neurons: A Memory Model with High Capacity

abstract: This paper presents an energy normalization transform as a method to reduce system errors in the LF-ASD brain-computer interface. The energy normalization transform has two major benefits to the system performance. First, it can increase class separation between the active and idle EEG data. Second, it can desensitize the system to the signal amplitude variability. For four subjects in the study, the benefits resulted in the performance improvement of the LF-ASD in the range from 7.7% to 18.9%, while for the fifth subject, who had the highest non-normalized accuracy of 90.5%, the performance did not change notably with normalization.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates an energy-normalization transform for reducing errors in the LF-ASD brain-computer interface. The system distinguishes active EEG data from idle EEG data, making the separation between these classes important to its performance. The proposed transform changes how signal energy enters that distinction.

The authors identify two potential benefits. Normalization can make active and idle data more separable, and it can reduce sensitivity to variations in signal amplitude. These address different aspects of the classification problem: how distinct the target classes appear and how much changing signal magnitude affects the system. The transform is evaluated through its effect on the interface's performance.

Four subjects show reported performance improvements ranging from 7.7% to 18.9%. A fifth subject, whose accuracy before normalization was already the highest at 90.5%, shows no notable change. The results support normalization as a useful modification for several participants in the study, while also showing that its benefit was not uniform across all five subjects.
summary.tldr: Energy normalization improved LF-ASD brain-computer interface performance for four of five subjects, with little change for the strongest initial performer.

title: Impact of an Energy Normalization Transform on the Performance of the LF-ASD Brain Computer Interface

abstract: Dominant sets are a new graph-theoretic concept that has proven to be relevant in pairwise data clustering problems, such as image seg- mentation. They generalize the notion of a maximal clique to edge- weighted graphs and have intriguing, non-trivial connections to continu- ous quadratic optimization and spectral-based grouping. We address the problem of grouping out-of-sample examples after the clustering process has taken place. This may serve either to drastically reduce the compu- tational burden associated to the processing of very large data sets, or to efficiently deal with dynamic situations whereby data sets need to be updated continually. We show that the very notion of a dominant set of- fers a simple and efficient way of doing this. Numerical experiments on various grouping problems show the effectiveness of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to group new examples after an initial clustering has already been computed. Its starting point is dominant-set clustering, which uses pairwise relationships represented by a weighted graph. Dominant sets extend the idea of maximal cliques to weighted edges and connect this graph-based view with continuous quadratic optimization and spectral grouping.

The authors show that the dominant-set concept itself supplies a simple, efficient way to handle examples outside the original sample. This makes extending a clustering a distinct operation from forming the initial groups. The approach addresses both large datasets, where processing everything together can be expensive, and changing datasets, where new observations keep arriving.

Numerical experiments across several grouping problems support the method's effectiveness. Its practical significance is the ability to reuse an existing clustering when additional examples need assignments. That capability may substantially reduce computational work for large collections or support continual updates. These are potential benefits of the extension procedure, while the reported experimental finding is effectiveness on the grouping problems studied.
summary.tldr: The paper extends dominant-set clustering to new examples efficiently, supporting large datasets and continual updates.

title: Efficient Out-of-Sample Extension of Dominant-Set Clusters

abstract: We considered a gamma distribution of interspike intervals as a statisti- cal model for neuronal spike generation. The model parameters consist of a time-dependent ﬁring rate and a shape parameter that characterizes spiking irregularities of individual neurons. Because the environment changes with time, observed data are generated from the time-dependent ﬁring rate, which is an unknown function. A statistical model with an unknown function is called a semiparametric model, which is one of the unsolved problem in statistics and is generally very difﬁcult to solve. We used a novel method of estimating functions in information geometry to estimate the shape parameter without estimating the unknown function. We analytically obtained an optimal estimating function for the shape parameter independent of the functional form of the ﬁring rate. This estimation is efﬁcient without Fisher information loss and better than maximum likelihood estimation.

paragraphs: This paper models the intervals between neuronal spikes with a gamma distribution. The model separates a time-dependent firing rate from a shape parameter describing irregularity. The estimation problem is difficult because the firing rate changes with the environment and its time dependence is an unknown function.

The authors aim to estimate the irregularity parameter without first estimating that entire function. They use estimating functions from information geometry and analytically derive an optimal estimating function for the shape parameter. Its form does not depend on the functional form of the changing firing rate, addressing the nuisance function within this semiparametric model.

The abstract reports efficient estimation without loss of Fisher information and an advantage over maximum-likelihood estimation. These claims concern the gamma interspike-interval model under study. The significance is that a changing activity level need not be reconstructed explicitly to estimate the parameter of interest. The method offers a mathematically derived way to characterize spiking irregularity while leaving the unknown firing-rate function unestimated.
summary.tldr: An information-geometric estimator measures spiking irregularity in a gamma interval model without estimating the unknown time-varying firing rate.

title: Unbiased Estimator of Shape Parameter for Spiking Irregularities under Changing Environments

abstract: Based on a large scale spiking neuron model of the input layers 4C and of macaque, we identify neural mechanisms for the observed contrast dependent receptive field size of V1 cells. We observe a rich variety of mechanisms for the phenomenon and analyze them based on the relative gain of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs. We observe an average growth in the spatial extent of excitation and inhibition for low contrast, as predicted from phenomenological models. However, contrary to phenomenological models, our simulation results suggest this is neither sufficient nor necessary to explain the phenomenon.
originalAbstract: Based on a large scale spiking neuron model of the input layers 4C and of macaque, we identify neural mechanisms for the observed contrast dependent receptive field size of V1 cells. We observe a rich variety of mechanisms for the phenomenon and analyze them based on the relative gain of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs. We observe an average growth in the spatial extent of excitation and inhibition for low contrast, as predicted from phenomenological models. However, contrary to phenomenological models, our simulation results suggest this is neither sufficient nor necessary to explain the phenomenon.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why the receptive-field size of cells in primary visual cortex changes with contrast. A receptive field describes the spatial region influencing a cell's response. The authors examine this phenomenon using a large-scale spiking-neuron model of macaque V1 input layers, seeking mechanisms within the modeled neural interactions.

The simulations reveal a variety of mechanisms, which the authors analyze through the relative gains of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs. This directs attention to the balance of influences that promote or suppress a response. The model also shows that excitation and inhibition extend over larger spatial regions on average at low contrast, matching a prediction of phenomenological models.

However, the simulations suggest that this spatial expansion is neither sufficient nor necessary to explain the receptive-field effect. Observing expansion alone therefore does not establish the explanation, and the phenomenon need not require it within the model. The findings favor examining the interaction of excitation and inhibition rather than treating their spatial extent as a complete account.
summary.tldr: A spiking-neuron model suggests multiple mechanisms for contrast-dependent receptive fields, beyond expansion of excitation and inhibition alone.

title: Neural mechanisms of contrast dependent receptive field size in V1

abstract: Current road-traffic optimisation practice around the world is a combination of hand tuned policies with a small degree of automatic adaption. Even state-ofthe-art research controllers need good models of the road traffic, which cannot be obtained directly from existing sensors. We use a policy-gradient reinforcement learning approach to directly optimise the traffic signals, mapping currently deployed sensor observations to control signals. Our trained controllers are (theoretically) compatible with the traffic system used in Sydney and many other cities around the world. We apply two policy-gradient methods: (1) the recent natural actor-critic algorithm, and (2) a vanilla policy-gradient algorithm for comparison. Along the way we extend natural-actor critic approaches to work for distributed and online infinite-horizon problems.

paragraphs: Traffic-signal control often relies on hand-tuned policies with limited automatic adjustment. More sophisticated controllers can require detailed traffic models that existing sensors do not directly provide. This paper investigates learning signal-control policies directly from the observations available through deployed sensors, using policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

The learned policy maps sensor observations to traffic-control signals. The authors apply natural actor-critic learning and include a conventional policy-gradient method for comparison. This places the optimization at the level of the control policy itself, addressing the difficulty of obtaining the traffic model required by other approaches.

The work also extends natural actor-critic methods to distributed, online problems with an infinite time horizon. Those extensions accommodate learning and control that continue over time across distributed components. The trained controllers are described as theoretically compatible with the traffic system used in Sydney and many other cities. This is a compatibility claim about the proposed approach; the abstract does not report a real-world deployment or a quantified traffic improvement.
summary.tldr: Policy-gradient learning maps existing traffic-sensor observations directly to signals and extends natural actor-critic methods for ongoing distributed control.

title: Natural Actor-Critic for Road Traffic Optimisation

abstract: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is a popular method for extracting independent features from visual data. However, as a fundamentally linear technique, there is always nonlinear residual redundancy that is not captured by ICA. Hence there have been many attempts to try to create a hierarchical version of ICA, but so far none of the approaches have a natural way to apply them more than once. Here we show that there is a relatively simple technique that transforms the absolute values of the outputs of a previous application of ICA into a normal distribution, to which ICA maybe applied again. This results in a recursive ICA algorithm that may be applied any number of times in order to extract higher order structure from previous layers.

However, as a fundamentally linear technique, there is always nonlinear residual redundancy that is not captured by ICA. Hence there have been many attempts to try to create a hierarchical version of ICA, but so far none of the approaches have a natural way to apply them more than once. Here we show that there is a relatively simple technique that transforms the absolute values of the outputs of a previous application of ICA into a normal distribution, to which ICA maybe applied again. paragraphs: Independent component analysis extracts independent features from visual data, but its linear structure leaves nonlinear redundancy unaddressed. This paper asks how ICA can be applied repeatedly to capture structure beyond a single layer. The authors identify repeatability as a problem for earlier attempts to build hierarchical versions of ICA.

Their solution inserts a transformation between successive applications. It takes the absolute values of the outputs from one ICA stage and transforms them into a normal distribution. ICA can then be applied again to the transformed representation. This creates a repeatable sequence in which each stage supplies suitable input for the next.

The resulting recursive algorithm can be applied any number of times to extract higher-order structure from preceding layers. Its main contribution is therefore a simple mechanism for continuing the hierarchy, addressing the lack of a natural repeated application in prior approaches. The abstract establishes the recursive construction and its intended role in capturing residual structure, without claiming that every additional layer necessarily improves a particular task.
summary.tldr: Transforming the magnitudes of ICA outputs into a normal distribution enables repeated ICA layers that extract higher-order structure.

title: Recursive ICA

abstract: The ill-posed nature of the MEG/EEG source localization problem requires the incorporation of prior assumptions when choosing an appropriate solution out of an infinite set of candidates. Bayesian methods are useful in this capacity because they allow these assumptions to be explicitly quantified. Recently, a number of empirical Bayesian approaches have been proposed that attempt a form of model selection by using the data to guide the search for an appropriate prior. While seemingly quite different in many respects, we apply a unifying framework based on automatic relevance determination (ARD) that elucidates various attributes of these methods and suggests directions for improvement. We also derive theoretical properties of this methodology related to convergence, local minima, and localization bias and explore connections with established algorithms.

paragraphs: Locating the sources of MEG or EEG measurements is an ill-posed problem: infinitely many candidate solutions can fit the task, so selecting one requires prior assumptions. Bayesian methods make those assumptions explicit through a prior. The paper examines empirical Bayesian approaches, which use the observed data to help choose an appropriate prior as part of model selection.

Although these approaches can appear quite different, the authors analyze them through a common framework based on automatic relevance determination, or ARD. This shared perspective makes their attributes easier to compare and suggests directions for improving them. The contribution is therefore partly explanatory: it organizes multiple approaches around a common underlying methodology.

The paper also derives theoretical properties concerning convergence, local minima, and localization bias, and explores connections with established algorithms. These topics address how the methods behave during optimization and how their solutions relate to source location. Together, the analysis clarifies the consequences of using data to guide prior selection in a problem where prior assumptions are unavoidable.
summary.tldr: An ARD-based framework unifies empirical Bayesian source-localization methods and analyzes their convergence, local minima, and localization bias.

title: Analysis of Empirical Bayesian Methods for Neuroelectromagnetic Source Localization

abstract: Web servers on the Internet need to maintain high reliability, but the cause of intermittent failures of web transactions is non-obvious. We use Bayesian inference to diagnose problems with web services. This diagnosis problem is far larger than any previously attempted: it requires inference of 10^4 possible faults from 10^5 observations. Further, such inference must be performed in less than a second. Inference can be done at this speed by combining a variational approximation, a mean-field approximation, and the use of stochastic gradient descent to optimize a variational cost function. We use this fast inference to diagnose a time series of anomalous HTTP requests taken from a real web service. The inference is fast enough to analyze network logs with billions of entries in a matter of hours.

paragraphs: Intermittent web failures can be difficult to diagnose because observed request problems do not directly identify their causes. This paper uses Bayesian inference to reason about possible faults from observations. Its target problem involves 10,000 possible faults and 100,000 observations, with inference required to finish in less than a second.

The authors meet that computational requirement by combining a variational approximation, a mean-field approximation, and stochastic gradient descent on a variational cost function. These components make the inference problem tractable enough for the required speed. The contribution centers on bringing probabilistic diagnosis to a scale and latency requirement that would otherwise make it difficult to use.

The method is applied to a time series of anomalous HTTP requests from a real web service. The reported inference speed is sufficient to analyze logs containing billions of entries within hours. This connects the subsecond inference requirement to a larger operational workload: fast individual diagnostic computations make it possible to process an extensive history of service observations.
summary.tldr: Combined variational and mean-field approximations enable subsecond Bayesian fault inference for large-scale web-service diagnosis.

title: Fast Variational Inference for Large-scale Internet Diagnosis

abstract: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) have been extensively studied and used in the context of planning and decision-making, and many methods exist to find the optimal policy for problems modelled as MDPs. Although finding the optimal policy is sufficient in many domains, in certain applications such as decision support systems where the policy is executed by a human (rather than a machine), finding all possible near-optimal policies might be useful as it provides more flexibility to the person executing the policy. In this paper we introduce the new concept of non-deterministic MDP policies, and address the question of finding near-optimal non-deterministic policies. We propose two solutions to this problem, one based on a Mixed Integer Program and the other one based on a search algorithm. We include experimental results obtained from applying this framework to optimize treatment choices in the context of a medical decision support system.
originalAbstract: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) have been extensively studied and used in the context of planning and decision-making, and many methods exist to find the optimal policy for problems modelled as MDPs. Although finding the optimal policy is sufficient in many domains, in certain applications such as decision support systems where the policy is executed by a human (rather than a machine), finding all possible near-optimal policies might be useful as it provides more flexibility to the person executing the policy. In this paper we introduce the new concept of non-deterministic MDP policies, and address the question of finding near-optimal non-deterministic policies. We propose two solutions to this problem, one based on a Mixed Integer Program and the other one based on a search algorithm. We include experimental results obtained from applying this framework to optimize treatment choices in the context of a medical decision support system.

paragraphs: An optimal policy for a Markov decision process supplies a prescription for decision-making. That can be sufficient when a machine executes the policy, but human decision support may benefit from offering flexibility among good choices. This paper asks how to represent and find near-optimal policies that leave room for the person making the decisions.

The authors introduce non-deterministic MDP policies to address this goal. The motivation is to make multiple acceptable choices available while retaining a near-optimality requirement. This changes the planning question from merely finding an optimal prescription to identifying a more flexible policy whose permitted choices remain tied to the quality of the resulting decisions.

Two computational solutions are proposed: one based on mixed-integer programming and another on search. The paper includes experiments applying the framework to treatment-choice optimization in a medical decision support system. Its contribution is a formal and algorithmic approach to flexibility in sequential decisions, illustrated through that application rather than a claim that the framework establishes clinical benefits.
summary.tldr: Non-deterministic MDP policies offer flexibility among near-optimal choices, with proposed mixed-integer-programming and search methods.

title: MDPs with Non-Deterministic Policies

abstract: We study the behavior of block (cid:96)1/(cid:96)2 regularization for multivariate regression, where a K-dimensional response vector is regressed upon a ﬁxed set of p co- variates. The problem of support union recovery is to recover the subset of covariates that are active in at least one of the regression problems. Study- ing this problem under high-dimensional scaling (where the problem parame- ters as well as sample size n tend to inﬁnity simultaneously), our main result is to show that exact recovery is possible once the order parameter given by θ(cid:96)1/(cid:96)2(n, p, s) : = n/[2ψ(B∗) log(p − s)] exceeds a critical threshold. Here n is the sample size, p is the ambient dimension of the regression model, s is the size of the union of supports, and ψ(B∗) is a sparsity-overlap function that measures a combination of the sparsities and overlaps of the K-regression coefﬁcient vectors that constitute the model. This sparsity-overlap function reveals that block (cid:96)1/(cid:96)2 regularization for multivariate regression never harms performance relative to a naive (cid:96)1-approach, and can yield substantial improvements in sample complexity (up to a factor of K) when the regression vectors are suitably orthogonal rela- tive to the design. We complement our theoretical results with simulations that demonstrate the sharpness of the result, even for relatively small problems.

paragraphs: When several responses are regressed on the same candidate variables, one goal is to identify every variable used by at least one response. The paper studies this support-union problem using block l1/l2 regularization. Its analysis considers a high-dimensional regime in which sample size and problem dimensions grow together.

The main result identifies a threshold above which exact recovery is possible. The controlling quantity is the sample size divided by twice a sparsity-overlap function times log(p − s), where p counts candidate variables and s counts active variables in the union. The sparsity-overlap function captures how the regression coefficient vectors’ sparsity patterns and overlap interact.

Within the analysis, block regularization is no worse than a naive l1 approach and can substantially reduce the required sample size. Improvements can reach a factor of K, the number of responses, when the coefficient vectors have suitable orthogonality relative to the design. Simulations support the sharpness of the theoretical threshold even for relatively small problems, linking the asymptotic analysis to finite examples.
summary.tldr: A recovery threshold explains when joint sparse regression identifies all active variables and when sharing across responses reduces sample requirements.

title: High-dimensional support union recovery in multivariate regression

abstract: We consider the problem of variable group selection for least squares regression, namely, that of selecting groups of variables for best regression performance, leveraging and adhering to a natural grouping structure within the explanatory variables. We show that this problem can be efficiently addressed by using a certain greedy style algorithm. More precisely, we propose the Group Orthogonal Matching Pursuit algorithm (Group-OMP), which extends the standard OMP procedure (also referred to as ``forward greedy feature selection algorithm for least squares regression) to perform stage-wise group variable selection. We prove that under certain conditions Group-OMP can identify the correct (groups of) variables. We also provide an upperbound on the $l_\infty$ norm of the difference between the estimated regression coefficients and the true coefficients. Experimental results on simulated and real world datasets indicate that Group-OMP compares favorably to Group Lasso, OMP and Lasso, both in terms of variable selection and prediction accuracy.

We show that this problem can be efficiently addressed by using a certain greedy style algorithm. More precisely, we propose the Group Orthogonal Matching Pursuit algorithm (Group-OMP), which extends the standard OMP procedure (also referred to as ``forward greedy feature selection algorithm for least squares regression) to perform stage-wise group variable selection. We prove that under certain conditions Group-OMP can identify the correct (groups of) variables. We also provide an upperbound on the $l_\infty$ norm of the difference between the estimated regression coefficients and the true coefficients. Experimental results on simulated and real world datasets indicate that Group-OMP compares favorably to Group Lasso, OMP and Lasso, both in terms of variable selection and prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: In some regression problems, explanatory variables come in natural groups. Selecting variables one at a time can fail to respect that organization. This paper studies how to choose groups for least-squares regression and proposes Group Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, or Group-OMP, as an efficient greedy method that incorporates the grouping directly into selection.

Group-OMP extends ordinary Orthogonal Matching Pursuit from stage-wise selection of individual variables to stage-wise selection of groups. The authors prove that the procedure can recover the correct variable groups under certain conditions. They also bound the infinity-norm difference between estimated and true regression coefficients, which controls the largest absolute error among the coefficients.

Experiments on simulated and real datasets compare Group-OMP with Group Lasso, ordinary OMP, and Lasso. The reported results are favorable for both variable selection and prediction accuracy. The paper therefore connects a simple group-aware selection procedure with conditional recovery guarantees and empirical evidence. Its theoretical claim is specifically that correct recovery holds under the stated conditions, while its experimental findings describe performance on the datasets evaluated.
summary.tldr: Group-OMP greedily selects variable groups, with conditional recovery guarantees, coefficient-error bounds, and favorable reported regression results.

title: Grouped Orthogonal Matching Pursuit for Variable Selection and Prediction

abstract: Extensive games are often used to model the interactions of multiple agents within an environment. Much recent work has focused on increasing the size of an extensive game that can be feasibly solved. Despite these improvements, many interesting games are still too large for such techniques. A common approach for computing strategies in these large games is to first employ an abstraction technique to reduce the original game to an abstract game that is of a manageable size. This abstract game is then solved and the resulting strategy is used in the original game. Most top programs in recent AAAI Computer Poker Competitions use this approach. The trend in this competition has been that strategies found in larger abstract games tend to beat strategies found in smaller abstract games. These larger abstract games have more expressive strategy spaces and therefore contain better strategies. In this paper we present a new method for computing strategies in large games. This method allows us to compute more expressive strategies without increasing the size of abstract games that we are required to solve. We demonstrate the power of the approach experimentally in both small and large games, while also providing a theoretical justification for the resulting improvement.

Larger abstract games offer more expressive strategy spaces, but require solving larger problems. Strategy grafting introduces a way to compute more expressive strategies without increasing the size of the abstract games that must be solved.

Its significance is the separation between strategy expressiveness and the size of an individual abstraction that needs solving. This offers a way to improve strategies for large games while continuing to work with abstract games of manageable size.
summary.tldr: Strategy grafting computes more expressive game strategies without requiring larger abstract games to be solved.

title: Strategy Grafting in Extensive Games

abstract: Independent Components Analysis (ICA) and its variants have been successfully used for unsupervised feature learning. However, standard ICA requires an orthonoramlity constraint to be enforced, which makes it difﬁcult to learn overcomplete features. In addition, ICA is sensitive to whitening. These properties make it challenging to scale ICA to high dimensional data. In this paper, we propose a robust soft reconstruction cost for ICA that allows us to learn highly overcomplete sparse features even on unwhitened data. Our formulation reveals formal connections between ICA and sparse autoencoders, which have previously been observed only empirically. Our algorithm can be used in conjunction with off-the-shelf fast unconstrained optimizers. We show that the soft reconstruction cost can also be used to prevent replicated features in tiled convolutional neural networks. Using our method to learn highly overcomplete sparse features and tiled convolutional neural networks, we obtain competitive performances on a wide variety of object recognition tasks. We achieve state-of-the-art test accuracies on the STL-10 and Hollywood2 datasets.

These representations contain more features than input dimensions. Sensitivity to whitening creates another obstacle to using ICA with high-dimensional data. This paper changes the formulation to address both issues.

The proposed method introduces a robust, soft reconstruction cost. It allows highly overcomplete sparse features to be learned even when the data have not been whitened, and it works with existing fast unconstrained optimizers. The formulation also establishes formal connections between ICA and sparse autoencoders, giving mathematical support to a relationship previously observed empirically.

title: ICA with Reconstruction Cost for Efficient Overcomplete Feature Learning

abstract: This work introduces Divide-Factor-Combine (DFC), a parallel divide-and-conquer framework for noisy matrix factorization. DFC divides a large-scale matrix factorization task into smaller subproblems, solves each subproblem in parallel using an arbitrary base matrix factorization algorithm, and combines the subproblem solutions using techniques from randomized matrix approximation. Our experiments with collaborative filtering, video background modeling, and simulated data demonstrate the near-linear to super-linear speed-ups attainable with this approach. Moreover, our analysis shows that DFC enjoys high-probability recovery guarantees comparable to those of its base algorithm.

Our experiments with collaborative filtering, video background modeling, and simulated data demonstrate the near-linear to super-linear speed-ups attainable with this approach. paragraphs: Factoring a large noisy matrix can demand substantial computation. Divide-Factor-Combine, or DFC, addresses that cost by organizing the work into smaller pieces. The framework first divides a matrix-factorization task into subproblems, then solves those subproblems in parallel, and finally combines their solutions into an answer for the original task.

DFC can use an arbitrary matrix-factorization algorithm as its base solver. Its main contribution is therefore a way to organize and combine computation rather than a single replacement factorization routine. The combination stage uses techniques from randomized matrix approximation, providing a principled bridge between solutions obtained separately and the larger matrix they collectively describe.

Experiments involving collaborative filtering, video background modeling, and simulated data demonstrate speedups ranging from near-linear to super-linear. These are attainable results in the reported experiments, rather than a universal speedup guarantee. Separately, the analysis establishes high-probability recovery guarantees comparable to those of the underlying solver. Together, these findings indicate that dividing the work can yield substantial computational gains while retaining comparable theoretical recovery assurance.
summary.tldr: DFC parallelizes noisy matrix factorization through smaller subproblems while retaining recovery guarantees comparable to its base solver.

title: Divide-and-Conquer Matrix Factorization

abstract: In many practical machine learning problems, the acquisition of labeled data is often expensive and/or time consuming. This motivates us to study a problem as follows: given a label budget, how to select data points to label such that the learning performance is optimized. We propose a selective labeling method by analyzing the generalization error of Laplacian regularized Least Squares (LapRLS). In particular, we derive a deterministic generalization error bound for LapRLS trained on subsampled data, and propose to select a subset of data points to label by minimizing this upper bound. Since the minimization is a combinational problem, we relax it into continuous domain and solve it by projected gradient descent. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: When labels are expensive or slow to obtain, choosing which examples to label becomes part of the learning problem. This paper asks how to use a fixed labeling budget effectively. It develops a selection method specifically through an analysis of Laplacian-regularized least squares, abbreviated LapRLS.

The authors derive a deterministic upper bound on the generalization error of LapRLS trained using a subset of the data. They use this bound as the selection objective: choose examples whose labeling would minimize the bound. This links the choice of training examples to a theoretical measure of the learner's possible error.

Selecting a subset is a combinatorial optimization problem, so the authors relax it into a continuous problem and solve that relaxation using projected gradient descent. Benchmark experiments report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical bound motivates the selection rule, while the experiments provide evidence that optimizing this surrogate can lead to useful choices of labeled examples.
summary.tldr: A selective-labeling method allocates a fixed label budget by minimizing a relaxed upper bound on LapRLS generalization error.

title: Selective Labeling via Error Bound Minimization

abstract: This paper proposes a novel image representation called a Graphical Gaussian Vector, which is a counterpart of the codebook and local feature matching approaches. In our method, we model the distribution of local features as a Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF) which can efficiently represent the spatial relationship among local features. We consider the parameter of GMRF as a feature vector of the image. Using concepts of information geometry, proper parameters and a metric from the GMRF can be obtained. Finally we define a new image feature by embedding the metric into the parameters, which can be directly applied to scalable linear classifiers. Our method obtains superior performance over the state-of-the-art methods in the standard object recognition datasets and comparable performance in the scene dataset. As the proposed method simply calculates the local auto-correlations of local features, it is able to achieve both high classification accuracy and high efficiency.

It models their distribution with a Gaussian Markov Random Field, then uses the model’s parameters to describe the image. The resulting Graphical Gaussian Vector offers an alternative to representations built around codebooks or direct matching of local features.

The authors use information geometry to select suitable parameters and a metric for the probabilistic model. They then incorporate that metric into the parameter-based feature representation. This produces a vector that can be used directly by scalable linear classifiers, connecting a structured model of local relationships to a comparatively simple classification stage.

The reported evaluations show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods on standard object-recognition datasets and comparable performance on a scene dataset. The method computes local autocorrelations of features, which the authors identify as supporting both efficiency and classification accuracy. The findings suggest that spatial statistical relationships can provide useful image information without requiring a costly final classifier.
summary.tldr: Graphical Gaussian Vectors encode spatial feature relationships in an image vector suitable for efficient linear classification.

title: Graphical Gaussian Vector for Image Categorization

abstract: We investigate two new optimization problems — minimizing a submodular function subject to a submodular lower bound constraint (submodular cover) and maximizing a submodular function subject to a submodular upper bound constraint (submodular knapsack). We are motivated by a number of real-world applications in machine learning including sensor placement and data subset selection, which require maximizing a certain submodular function (like coverage or diversity) while simultaneously minimizing another (like cooperative cost). These problems are often posed as minimizing the difference between submodular functions [9, 23] which is in the worst case inapproximable. We show, however, that by phrasing these problems as constrained optimization, which is more natural for many applications, we achieve a number of bounded approximation guarantees. We also show that both these problems are closely related and, an approximation algorithm solving one can be used to obtain an approximation guarantee for the other. We provide hardness results for both problems thus showing that our approximation factors are tight up to log-factors. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the performance and good scalability properties of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Applications such as sensor placement and data subset selection can require balancing coverage or diversity against cooperative cost. This paper studies formulations where both quantities are submodular. One minimizes a submodular objective while requiring another submodular quantity to exceed a threshold; the other maximizes an objective under a submodular upper-bound constraint.

The distinction between these constrained formulations and subtracting one submodular function from another matters theoretically. The difference formulation can be inapproximable in the worst case. For the constrained problems, the authors obtain bounded approximation guarantees, providing explicit control over how the algorithmic solution relates to the optimum.

The paper also shows a close relationship between the two problems: an approximation algorithm for one can yield an approximation guarantee for the other. Hardness results establish that the approximation factors are tight up to logarithmic factors. Empirical results demonstrate performance and good scalability. Together, the results make constrained formulations useful both for expressing application requirements and for obtaining meaningful algorithmic guarantees.
summary.tldr: Submodular cover and knapsack formulations yield bounded approximation guarantees, linked algorithms, and hardness results tight up to logarithmic factors.

title: Submodular Optimization with Submodular Cover and Submodular Knapsack Constraints

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of 3D human pose estimation in the wild. A significant challenge is the lack of training data, i.e., 2D images of humans annotated with 3D poses. Such data is necessary to train state-of-the-art CNN architectures. Here, we propose a solution to generate a large set of photorealistic synthetic images of humans with 3D pose annotations. We introduce an image-based synthesis engine that artificially augments a dataset of real images with 2D human pose annotations using 3D Motion Capture (MoCap) data. Given a candidate 3D pose our algorithm selects for each joint an image whose 2D pose locally matches the projected 3D pose. The selected images are then combined to generate a new synthetic image by stitching local image patches in a kinematically constrained manner. The resulting images are used to train an end-to-end CNN for full-body 3D pose estimation. We cluster the training data into a large number of pose classes and tackle pose estimation as a K-way classification problem. Such an approach is viable only with large training sets such as ours. Our method outperforms the state of the art in terms of 3D pose estimation in controlled environments (Human3.6M) and shows promising results for in-the-wild images (LSP). This demonstrates that CNNs trained on artificial images generalize well to real images.

These findings support the reported transfer from artificial training images to real photographs. The distinction between the stronger controlled-setting result and the promising in-the-wild result is important to the scope of the evidence.
summary.tldr: Motion-capture-guided patch synthesis creates annotated training images that improve CNN-based three-dimensional human pose estimation.

title: MoCap-guided Data Augmentation for 3D Pose Estimation in the Wild

abstract: Tensor factorization is a powerful tool to analyse multi-way data. Recently proposed nonlinear factorization methods, although capable of capturing complex relationships, are computationally quite expensive and may suffer a severe learning bias in case of extreme data sparsity. Therefore, we propose a distributed, flexible nonlinear tensor factorization model, which avoids the expensive computations and structural restrictions of the Kronecker-product in the existing TGP formulations, allowing an arbitrary subset of tensor entries to be selected for training. Meanwhile, we derive a tractable and tight variational evidence lower bound (ELBO) that enables highly decoupled, parallel computations and high-quality inference. Based on the new bound, we develop a distributed, key-value-free inference algorithm in the MapReduce framework, which can fully exploit the memory cache mechanism in fast MapReduce systems such as Spark. Experiments demonstrate the advantages of our method over several state-of-the-art approaches, in terms of both predictive performance and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization analyzes data organized along multiple dimensions. Nonlinear versions can capture complex relationships, but existing approaches can be expensive and develop substantial learning bias when observations are extremely sparse. This paper proposes a flexible nonlinear model designed to support efficient distributed inference and more freedom in selecting training observations.

The model avoids the costly Kronecker-product computations and structural restrictions found in existing tensor Gaussian process formulations. In particular, it allows an arbitrary subset of tensor entries to be used for training. The authors derive a tractable, tight variational evidence lower bound, an optimization objective that enables approximate inference while separating much of the computation.

That separation supports a distributed inference algorithm within MapReduce. The algorithm avoids key-value operations and can exploit memory caching in systems such as Spark. Experiments report advantages over several state-of-the-art approaches in both prediction and computational efficiency. The contribution connects modeling flexibility with an inference objective and execution strategy intended to make that flexibility practical at scale.
summary.tldr: A flexible nonlinear tensor model enables arbitrary training subsets and distributed inference, improving prediction and efficiency in experiments.

title: Distributed Flexible Nonlinear Tensor Factorization

abstract: We study the cost sharing problem for cooperative games in situations where the cost function C is not available via oracle queries, but must instead be learned from samples drawn from a distribution, represented as tuples (S, C(S)), for different subsets S of players. We formalize this approach, which we call statistical cost sharing, and consider the computation of the core and the Shapley value. Expanding on the work by Balcan et al, we give precise sample complexity bounds for computing cost shares that satisfy the core property with high probability for any function with a non-empty core. For the Shapley value, which has never been studied in this setting, we show that for submodular cost functions with curvature bounded curvature kappa it can be approximated from samples from the uniform distribution to a sqrt{1 - kappa} factor, and that the bound is tight. We then define statistical analogues of the Shapley axioms, and derive a notion of statistical Shapley value and that these can be approximated arbitrarily well from samples from any distribution and for any function.

paragraphs: Cost sharing asks how to divide a cooperative group's cost among its members. This paper studies the setting where an algorithm cannot query the cost of any chosen group. Instead, it observes sampled groups together with their costs and must derive allocations from that data.

For the core, a cooperative stability concept, the authors give precise sample-complexity bounds for computing cost shares satisfying the core property with high probability when the cost function has a nonempty core. For the ordinary Shapley value, they prove a tight approximation factor of square root of one minus kappa under uniform sampling and submodular costs with bounded curvature kappa.

The paper then introduces statistical versions of the Shapley axioms and derives a corresponding statistical Shapley value. This new quantity can be approximated arbitrarily well from samples drawn from any distribution for any cost function. That broader result concerns the newly defined statistical value; it does not remove the conditions attached to approximating the ordinary Shapley value.
summary.tldr: Statistical cost sharing derives allocation guarantees from sampled group costs and introduces a broadly learnable statistical Shapley value.

title: Statistical Cost Sharing

abstract: Inferring topological and geometrical information from data can offer an alternative perspective in machine learning problems. Methods from topological data analysis, e.g., persistent homology, enable us to obtain such information, typically in the form of summary representations of topological features. However, such topological signatures often come with an unusual structure (e.g., multisets of intervals) that is highly impractical for most machine learning techniques. While many strategies have been proposed to map these topological signatures into machine learning compatible representations, they suffer from being agnostic to the target learning task. In contrast, we propose a technique that enables us to input topological signatures to deep neural networks and learn a task-optimal representation during training. Our approach is realized as a novel input layer with favorable theoretical properties. Classification experiments on 2D object shapes and social network graphs demonstrate the versatility of the approach and, in case of the latter, we even outperform the state-of-the-art by a large margin.
