paragraphs: Topological data analysis summarizes aspects of the shape and structure of data. Methods such as persistent homology produce signatures that can complement other information used in machine learning. However, these summaries may take unusual forms, including collections of intervals, that ordinary learning methods cannot readily accept as inputs.

Existing conversion strategies make these signatures easier to use but typically do not adapt the representation to the prediction task. The paper introduces a neural-network input layer that accepts topological signatures and learns their representation during training. This lets the task influence which aspects of the signature become useful features, rather than fixing that conversion independently of learning.

The authors establish favorable theoretical properties for the layer and evaluate it on classification of two-dimensional object shapes and social network graphs. These experiments demonstrate use across different kinds of structured data. For the social network graph task, they report a large improvement over the state of the art. The main contribution is a trainable connection between topological summaries and deep learning.
summary.tldr: A trainable input layer lets deep networks adapt topological signatures to their task, with strong reported graph-classification results.

title: Deep Learning with Topological Signatures

abstract: This paper investigates connections between discrete and continuous approaches for decomposable submodular function minimization. We provide improved running time estimates for the state-of-the-art continuous algorithms for the problem using combinatorial arguments. We also provide a systematic experimental comparison of the two types of methods, based on a clear distinction between level-0 and level-1 algorithms.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates connections between discrete and continuous approaches for decomposable submodular function minimization. We provide improved running time estimates for the state-of-the-art continuous algorithms for the problem using combinatorial arguments. We also provide a systematic experimental comparison of the two types of methods, based on a clear distinction between level-0 and level-1 algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how discrete and continuous methods relate when minimizing decomposable submodular functions. Both families address the same optimization problem, but their connection is the central subject of the work. The authors examine that connection through theoretical running-time analysis and a systematic comparison of algorithm behavior in experiments.

The theoretical contribution uses combinatorial arguments to obtain improved running-time estimates for leading continuous algorithms. This matters because it shows that reasoning associated with discrete structure can sharpen our understanding of continuous approaches. The stated improvement concerns the estimates for these algorithms, so the contribution is a better analysis of their computational requirements rather than an asserted new solver.

The experimental contribution compares the two families while explicitly distinguishing level-0 from level-1 algorithms. That distinction provides an organizing basis for the comparison, alongside the theoretical connection. Together, the contributions make the relationship between discrete and continuous methods more concrete: discrete arguments improve continuous-method analysis, and experiments systematically examine the alternatives within a shared classification.
summary.tldr: Combinatorial analysis sharpens running-time estimates for continuous submodular minimization methods, alongside a systematic comparison with discrete approaches.

title: Decomposable Submodular Function Minimization: Discrete and Continuous

abstract: We study the least squares regression problem $\min_{\Theta \in \RR^{p_1 \times \cdots \times p_D}} \| \cA(\Theta) - b \|_2^2$, where $\Theta$ is a low-rank tensor, defined as $\Theta = \sum_{r=1}^{R} \theta_1^{(r)} \circ \cdots \circ \theta_D^{(r)}$, for vectors $\theta_d^{(r)} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_d}$ for all $r \in [R]$ and $d \in [D]$. %$R$ is small compared with $p_1,\ldots,p_D$, Here, $\circ$ denotes the outer product of vectors, and $\cA(\Theta)$ is a linear function on $\Theta$. This problem is motivated by the fact that the number of parameters in $\Theta$ is only $R \cdot \sum_{d=1}^D p_D$, which is significantly smaller than the $\prod_{d=1}^{D} p_d$ number of parameters in ordinary least squares regression. We consider the above CP decomposition model of tensors $\Theta$, as well as the Tucker decomposition. For both models we show how to apply data dimensionality reduction techniques based on {\it sparse} random projections $\Phi \in \RR^{m \times n}$, with $m \ll n$, to reduce the problem to a much smaller problem $\min_{\Theta} \|\Phi \cA(\Theta) - \Phi b\|_2^2$, for which $\|\Phi \cA(\Theta) - \Phi b\|_2^2 = (1 \pm \varepsilon) \| \cA(\Theta) - b \|_2^2$ holds simultaneously for all $\Theta$. We obtain a significantly smaller dimension and sparsity in the randomized linear mapping $\Phi$ than is possible for ordinary least squares regression. Finally, we give a number of numerical simulations supporting our theory.

We obtain a significantly smaller dimension and sparsity in the randomized linear mapping $\Phi$ than is possible for ordinary least squares regression. Finally, we give a number of numerical simulations supporting our theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies least-squares regression when the unknown parameter is a low-rank tensor, a multidimensional array represented through smaller components. Such a representation can require far fewer parameters than treating every array entry independently. The authors consider both CP and Tucker decompositions and ask how this structure can also reduce the size of the regression computation.

Their approach applies a sparse random projection to both the model predictions and the observed response vector. This produces a smaller least-squares problem. The theoretical guarantee preserves squared residuals within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± ε simultaneously for every tensor in the considered model class, so preservation is not restricted to a single chosen candidate.

By exploiting low-rank tensor structure, the authors obtain smaller projection dimensions and greater sparsity than are possible for ordinary least-squares regression. Numerical simulations support the theory. The contribution connects compact parameter structure with compact data processing: the regression problem can be reduced while retaining a uniform approximation to its objective across candidate tensors.
summary.tldr: Sparse random projections shrink low-rank tensor regression while uniformly preserving its least-squares objective approximately.

title: Near Optimal Sketching of Low-Rank Tensor Regression

abstract: We review the current state of automatic differentiation (AD) for array programming in machine learning (ML), including the different approaches such as operator overloading (OO) and source transformation (ST) used for AD, graph-based intermediate representations for programs, and source languages. Based on these insights, we introduce a new graph-based intermediate representation (IR) which specifically aims to efficiently support fully-general AD for array programming. Unlike existing dataflow programming representations in ML frameworks, our IR naturally supports function calls, higher-order functions and recursion, making ML models easier to implement. The ability to represent closures allows us to perform AD using ST without a tape, making the resulting derivative (adjoint) program amenable to ahead-of-time optimization using tools from functional language compilers, and enabling higher-order derivatives. Lastly, we introduce a proof of concept compiler toolchain called Myia which uses a subset of Python as a front end.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation supplies the derivatives needed to train many machine learning models. This paper reviews how differentiation tools support programs that operate on arrays, including operator overloading, source transformation, and graph representations of programs. It uses that review to motivate a representation designed around the requirements of general differentiation.

The proposed graph representation supports function calls, functions that take or return other functions, and recursion. These features let model implementations retain richer programming structure. It also represents closures, which combine a function with its surrounding context. That capability enables source transformation to construct derivative programs without a tape for recording execution.

The resulting derivative program can be optimized ahead of execution using techniques from functional language compilers, and the approach supports higher-order derivatives. The authors introduce Myia, a proof-of-concept compiler with a restricted Python front end. The contribution connects programming-language design with differentiation: the structure used to represent a model also determines which derivative computations and compiler optimizations are readily available.
summary.tldr: A new program representation supports richer automatic differentiation and ahead-of-time optimization, demonstrated through the Myia compiler prototype.

title: Automatic differentiation in ML: Where we are and where we should be going

abstract: Beam search is widely used for approximate decoding in structured prediction problems. Models often use a beam at test time but ignore its existence at train time, and therefore do not explicitly learn how to use the beam. We develop an unifying meta-algorithm for learning beam search policies using imitation learning. In our setting, the beam is part of the model and not just an artifact of approximate decoding. Our meta-algorithm captures existing learning algorithms and suggests new ones. It also lets us show novel no-regret guarantees for learning beam search policies.
originalAbstract: Beam search is widely used for approximate decoding in structured prediction problems. We develop an unifying meta-algorithm for learning beam search policies using imitation learning. In our setting, the beam is part of the model and not just an artifact of approximate decoding. Our meta-algorithm captures existing learning algorithms and suggests new ones. It also lets us show novel no-regret guarantees for learning beam search policies.

paragraphs: Beam search is a common way to approximately decode structured predictions by maintaining several candidate solutions during search. Many models use this procedure when making predictions but are trained without explicitly accounting for it. The paper focuses on that mismatch: a model that will rely on a beam should also learn how to use it.

The authors develop a general framework for learning beam-search policies through imitation learning. Within this formulation, the beam is part of the model itself. Training therefore addresses behavior within the search procedure, making the way candidates are handled a component of what is learned.

The resulting meta-algorithm encompasses existing learning algorithms and suggests additional ones. It also supports new no-regret guarantees for learning beam-search policies. These are theoretical contributions about learning within the framework, rather than claims that approximate decoding always finds the best structured output. The paper's significance is to unify beam-aware training approaches and provide a basis for designing and analyzing further policies.
summary.tldr: An imitation-learning framework makes beam search part of the learned model and provides new no-regret guarantees.

title: Learning Beam Search Policies via Imitation Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks, trained with large amount of labeled data, can fail to generalize well when tested with examples from a target domain whose distribution differs from the training data distribution, referred as the source domain. It can be expensive or even infeasible to obtain required amount of labeled data in all possible domains. Unsupervised domain adaptation sets out to address this problem, aiming to learn a good predictive model for the target domain using labeled examples from the source domain but only unlabeled examples from the target domain. Domain alignment approaches this problem by matching the source and target feature distributions, and has been used as a key component in many state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods. However, matching the marginal feature distributions does not guarantee that the corresponding class conditional distributions will be aligned across the two domains. We propose co-regularized domain alignment for unsupervised domain adaptation, which constructs multiple diverse feature spaces and aligns source and target distributions in each of them individually, while encouraging that alignments agree with each other with regard to the class predictions on the unlabeled target examples. The proposed method is generic and can be used to improve any domain adaptation method which uses domain alignment. We instantiate it in the context of a recent state-of-the-art method and observe that it provides significant performance improvements on several domain adaptation benchmarks.

paragraphs: A model trained on labeled examples from one domain can perform poorly when its inputs come from another distribution. Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses this situation using labeled source examples and unlabeled target examples. One common approach makes the two domains' feature distributions resemble each other, but this overall match does not guarantee that examples belonging to corresponding classes are aligned.

The paper proposes constructing several diverse feature spaces and aligning source and target distributions separately within each one. It then encourages these different alignments to agree on the class predictions they assign to unlabeled target examples. Agreement therefore constrains the alignment process through its predictive consequences, alongside the matching of feature distributions.

The method is presented as a generic addition to approaches that already use domain alignment. The authors apply it to a recent state-of-the-art method and report significant improvements on several adaptation benchmarks. These results support the usefulness of combining diverse alignments with prediction agreement; the abstract does not claim that agreement guarantees correct class alignment in every setting.
summary.tldr: Aligning domains in multiple feature spaces while encouraging prediction agreement improves the tested unsupervised adaptation method.

title: Co-regularized Alignment for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Instrumental variable (IV) regression is a strategy for learning causal relationships in observational data. If measurements of input X and output Y are confounded, the causal relationship can nonetheless be identified if an instrumental variable Z is available that influences X directly, but is conditionally independent of Y given X and the unmeasured confounder. The classic two-stage least squares algorithm (2SLS) simplifies the estimation problem by modeling all relationships as linear functions. We propose kernel instrumental variable regression (KIV), a nonparametric generalization of 2SLS, modeling relations among X, Y, and Z as nonlinear functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove the consistency of KIV under mild assumptions, and derive conditions under which convergence occurs at the minimax optimal rate for unconfounded, single-stage RKHS regression. In doing so, we obtain an efficient ratio between training sample sizes used in the algorithm's first and second stages. In experiments, KIV outperforms state of the art alternatives for nonparametric IV regression.

paragraphs: Kernel instrumental variable regression addresses causal estimation when input and output measurements are confounded. The abstract describes identification using an instrument that directly influences the input and is conditionally independent of the output given the input and unmeasured confounder. This instrumental-variable structure supplies a route to estimating causal relationships from observational data.

Classic two-stage least squares simplifies the problem by using linear relationships. The proposed KIV method generalizes that approach to nonlinear functions represented in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. It retains the instrumental-variable estimation strategy while allowing richer relationships among the instrument, input, and output.

The authors prove consistency under mild assumptions and derive conditions for matching the minimax-optimal convergence rate of unconfounded, single-stage kernel regression. Their analysis also yields an efficient allocation of training samples between the two stages. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art alternatives for nonparametric instrumental-variable regression. The rate comparison is conditional on the derived requirements, while the experimental results support the practical value of the nonlinear formulation.
summary.tldr: KIV extends two-stage instrumental-variable regression to nonlinear kernel models, with consistency and conditional optimal-rate guarantees.

title: Kernel Instrumental Variable Regression

abstract: State-of-the-art implementations of boosting, such as XGBoost and LightGBM, can process large training sets extremely fast. However, this performance requires that the memory size is sufficient to hold a 2-3 multiple of the training set size. This paper presents an alternative approach to implementing the boosted trees, which achieves a significant speedup over XGBoost and LightGBM, especially when the memory size is small. This is achieved using a combination of three techniques: early stopping, effective sample size, and stratified sampling. Our experiments demonstrate a 10-100 speedup over XGBoost when the training data is too large to fit in memory.

This is achieved using a combination of three techniques: early stopping, effective sample size, and stratified sampling. Our experiments demonstrate a 10-100 speedup over XGBoost when the training data is too large to fit in memory.

paragraphs: Fast boosted-tree implementations can demand substantially more memory than the training data alone occupies. The paper describes XGBoost and LightGBM as requiring memory sufficient for roughly two to three times the training-set size to achieve their high performance. It addresses the practical problem that their speed can become harder to obtain when memory is limited.

The proposed alternative combines early stopping, effective sample size, and stratified sampling. These three techniques form an implementation strategy for boosted trees that aims to reduce the computational burden under constrained memory. Their combination is the main methodological contribution stated in the abstract, linking decisions about sampling and stopping to the efficiency of training.

The authors report significant speedups over both XGBoost and LightGBM, particularly with small memory budgets. When the training data itself does not fit in memory, their experiments show a 10–100-fold speedup over XGBoost. That condition matters: the numerical gain is specifically reported for data exceeding available memory. The findings highlight memory capacity as a central consideration when evaluating the practical speed of boosting systems.
summary.tldr: A boosted-tree implementation combining stopping and sampling techniques reports 10–100-fold speedups over XGBoost when training data exceeds memory.

title: Faster Boosting with Smaller Memory

abstract: Bayesian methods promise to fix many shortcomings of deep learning, but they are impractical and rarely match the performance of standard methods, let alone improve them. In this paper, we demonstrate practical training of deep networks with natural-gradient variational inference. By applying techniques such as batch normalisation, data augmentation, and distributed training, we achieve similar performance in about the same number of epochs as the Adam optimiser, even on large datasets such as ImageNet. Importantly, the benefits of Bayesian principles are preserved: predictive probabilities are well-calibrated, uncertainties on out-of-distribution data are improved, and continual-learning performance is boosted. This work enables practical deep learning while preserving benefits of Bayesian principles. A PyTorch implementation is available as a plug-and-play optimiser.

This work enables practical deep learning while preserving benefits of Bayesian principles. A PyTorch implementation is available as a plug-and-play optimiser.

paragraphs: Bayesian approaches promise useful uncertainty estimates for deep learning, but making them practical and competitive with standard training has been difficult. This paper demonstrates deep-network training using natural-gradient variational inference. The aim is to preserve benefits associated with Bayesian learning while bringing its training performance closer to widely used optimization methods.

The authors incorporate techniques such as batch normalization, data augmentation, and distributed training. With these techniques, they report performance similar to Adam in approximately the same number of training epochs, including on ImageNet. The stated comparison concerns performance and epoch counts, showing that the Bayesian training approach can work at a substantial data scale.

The experiments also retain benefits beyond the main predictive performance measure. Predictive probabilities are well calibrated, uncertainty on out-of-distribution data improves, and continual-learning performance increases. These results matter because competitiveness alone would leave open whether the Bayesian formulation still provides its intended advantages. A plug-and-play PyTorch optimizer makes the demonstrated approach available in a familiar training form.
summary.tldr: Natural-gradient variational inference achieves Adam-like performance and epoch counts while retaining calibration, uncertainty, and continual-learning benefits.

title: Practical Deep Learning with Bayesian Principles

abstract: We propose a new complexity measure for Markov decision processes (MDPs), the maximum expected hitting cost (MEHC). This measure tightens the closely related notion of diameter [JOA10] by accounting for the reward structure. We show that this parameter replaces diameter in the upper bound on the optimal value span of an extended MDP, thus refining the associated upper bounds on the regret of several UCRL2-like algorithms. Furthermore, we show that potential-based reward shaping [NHR99] can induce equivalent reward functions with varying informativeness, as measured by MEHC. By analyzing the change in the maximum expected hitting cost, this work presents a formal understanding of the effect of potential-based reward shaping on regret (and sample complexity) in the undiscounted average reward setting. We further establish that shaping can reduce or increase MEHC by at most a factor of two in a large class of MDPs with finite MEHC and unsaturated optimal average rewards.

paragraphs: The paper introduces maximum expected hitting cost, or MEHC, as a measure of difficulty for Markov decision processes. It refines the related diameter measure by incorporating reward structure. This matters because the rewards available while moving through a decision process can affect how informative the learning problem is.

The authors show that MEHC can replace diameter in an upper bound on the optimal value span of an extended decision process. This replacement tightens associated regret bounds for several algorithms resembling UCRL2. The result improves theoretical descriptions of learning difficulty by accounting for rewards alongside the process’s state-transition structure.

The paper also examines potential-based reward shaping, which can produce equivalent reward functions with different informativeness as measured by MEHC. Its analysis formalizes effects on regret and sample complexity in the undiscounted average-reward setting. For a large class of processes with finite MEHC and unsaturated optimal average rewards, shaping changes MEHC by at most a factor of two in either direction. That bound is conditional on the stated class.
summary.tldr: MEHC incorporates rewards into decision-process complexity, refining regret bounds and quantifying how reward shaping can change learning difficulty.

title: Maximum Expected Hitting Cost of a Markov Decision Process and Informativeness of Rewards

abstract: We study the adaptive influence maximization problem with myopic feedback under the independent cascade model: one sequentially selects k nodes as seeds one by one from a social network, and each selected seed returns the immediate neighbors it activates as the feedback available for by later selections, and the goal is to maximize the expected number of total activated nodes, referred as the influence spread. We show that the adaptivity gap, the ratio between the optimal adaptive influence spread and the optimal non-adaptive influence spread, is at most 4 and at least e/(e-1), and the approximation ratios with respect to the optimal adaptive influence spread of both the non-adaptive greedy and adaptive greedy algorithms are at least \frac{1}{4}(1 - \frac{1}{e}) and at most \frac{e^2 + 1}{(e + 1)^2} < 1 - \frac{1}{e}. Moreover, the approximation ratio of the non-adaptive greedy algorithm is no worse than that of the adaptive greedy algorithm, when considering all graphs. Our result confirms a long-standing open conjecture of Golovin and Krause (2011) on the constant approximation ratio of adaptive greedy with myopic feedback, and it also suggests that adaptive greedy may not bring much benefit under myopic feedback.

We show that the adaptivity gap, the ratio between the optimal adaptive influence spread and the optimal non-adaptive influence spread, is at most 4 and at least e/(e-1), and the approximation ratios with respect to the optimal adaptive influence spread of both the non-adaptive greedy and adaptive greedy algorithms are at least \frac{1}{4}(1 - \frac{1}{e}) and at most \frac{e^2 + 1}{(e + 1)^2} < 1 - \frac{1}{e}. paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose influential starting points in a social network when decisions happen sequentially. After selecting a node, the decision maker sees only which immediate neighbors it activates. Later choices can use this feedback, but they cannot observe the full cascade through the network. The objective is to maximize expected total activation under the independent cascade model.

The authors bound the advantage of adapting decisions to this limited feedback. The largest possible ratio between optimal adaptive and optimal fixed selections lies between e/(e−1) and 4. They also establish constant approximation guarantees for both adaptive and non-adaptive greedy selection, measured against the optimal adaptive strategy.

A notable worst-case result is that non-adaptive greedy has an approximation ratio no worse than adaptive greedy when considering all graphs. This does not say adaptation never helps on a particular network. It establishes the conjectured constant guarantee for adaptive greedy while suggesting that immediate-neighbor feedback may offer relatively limited benefits to that algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the value of adapting influence-maximization decisions when feedback reveals only a seed’s immediate activations.

title: Adaptive Influence Maximization with Myopic Feedback

abstract: Embodied agents operating in human spaces must be able to master how their environment works: what objects can the agent use, and how can it use them? We introduce a reinforcement learning approach for exploration for interaction, whereby an embodied agent autonomously discovers the affordance landscape of a new unmapped 3D environment (such as an unfamiliar kitchen). Given an egocentric RGB-D camera and a high-level action space, the agent is rewarded for maximizing successful interactions while simultaneously training an image-based affordance segmentation model. The former yields a policy for acting efficiently in new environments to prepare for downstream interaction tasks, while the latter yields a convolutional neural network that maps image regions to the likelihood they permit each action, densifying the rewards for exploration. We demonstrate our idea with AI2-iTHOR. The results show agents can learn how to use new home environments intelligently and that it prepares them to rapidly address various downstream tasks like "find a knife and put it in the drawer." Project page: http://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/interaction-exploration/

paragraphs: An agent entering an unfamiliar home needs to discover what it can do with the objects around it. The paper treats this as exploration for interaction: learning which parts of a new three-dimensional environment support particular actions. Its agent receives an egocentric RGB-D view and operates through a high-level action space.

Two learning processes develop together. A reinforcement-learning policy is rewarded for successful interactions, while an image-based affordance model learns to associate image regions with the likelihood that each action will work there. The policy helps gather interaction experience, and the affordance predictions provide denser rewards for further exploration. Exploration thus builds both practical behavior and a visual account of usable objects and regions.

Experiments in AI2-iTHOR show that agents can learn how to interact intelligently with new home environments. This preparation helps them quickly address later tasks involving finding and placing objects. The stated benefit is that exploratory experience becomes useful groundwork for downstream interaction goals, connecting discovery of an environment’s possibilities with subsequent task execution.
summary.tldr: An agent jointly learns exploratory behavior and visual action possibilities, preparing it to perform later tasks in unfamiliar home environments.

title: Learning Affordance Landscapes for Interaction Exploration in 3D Environments

abstract: Vanilla convolutions in modern deep networks are known to operate locally and at fixed scale (e.g., the widely-adopted 3*3 kernels in image-oriented tasks). This causes low efficacy in connecting two distant locations in the network. In this work, we propose a novel convolutional operator dubbed as fast Fourier convolution (FFC), which has the main hallmarks of non-local receptive fields and cross-scale fusion within the convolutional unit. According to spectral convolution theorem in Fourier theory, point-wise update in the spectral domain globally affects all input features involved in Fourier transform, which sheds light on neural architectural design with non-local receptive field. Our proposed FFC is inspired to capsulate three different kinds of computations in a single operation unit: a local branch that conducts ordinary small-kernel convolution, a semi-global branch that processes spectrally stacked image patches, and a global branch that manipulates image-level spectrum. All branches complementarily address different scales. A multi-branch aggregation step is included in FFC for cross-scale fusion. FFC is a generic operator that can directly replace vanilla convolutions in a large body of existing networks, without any adjustments and with comparable complexity metrics (e.g., FLOPs). We experimentally evaluate FFC in three major vision benchmarks (ImageNet for image recognition, Kinetics for video action recognition, MSCOCO for human keypoint detection). It consistently elevates accuracies in all above tasks by significant margins.

paragraphs: Ordinary small convolution kernels process nearby features at a fixed scale, making direct communication between distant image locations difficult. Fast Fourier Convolution introduces an operator that combines local processing with broader interactions inside a single unit. Its motivation comes from Fourier theory: a pointwise change in the spectral domain can affect all features participating in the transform.

The authors present FFC as a replacement for ordinary convolutions in many existing networks, with comparable computational complexity measures such as FLOPs. Evaluations span image recognition on ImageNet, video action recognition on Kinetics, and human keypoint detection on MSCOCO. Significant accuracy improvements across all three tasks support the usefulness of combining spectral interactions with conventional local computation.
summary.tldr: Fast Fourier Convolution combines local and spectral processing to connect distant features and improve accuracy across several vision tasks.

title: Fast Fourier Convolution

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the best-fitting single neuron as measured by the expected square loss $\E_{(x,y)\sim \mathcal{D}}[(\sigma(w^\top x)-y)^2]$ over some unknown joint distribution $\mathcal{D}$ by using gradient descent to minimize the empirical risk induced by a set of i.i.d. samples $S\sim \mathcal{D}^n$. The activation function $\sigma$ is an arbitrary Lipschitz and non-decreasing function, making the optimization problem nonconvex and nonsmooth in general, and covers typical neural network activation functions and inverse link functions in the generalized linear model setting. In the agnostic PAC learning setting, where no assumption on the relationship between the labels $y$ and the input $x$ is made, if the optimal population risk is $\mathsf{OPT}$, we show that gradient descent achieves population risk $O(\mathsf{OPT})+\eps$ in polynomial time and sample complexity when $\sigma$ is strictly increasing. For the ReLU activation, our population risk guarantee is $O(\mathsf{OPT}^{1/2})+\eps$. When labels take the form $y = \sigma(v^\top x) + \xi$ for zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise $\xi$, we show that the population risk guarantees for gradient descent improve to $\mathsf{OPT} + \eps$. Our sample complexity and runtime guarantees are (almost) dimension independent, and when $\sigma$ is strictly increasing, require no distributional assumptions beyond boundedness. For ReLU, we show the same results under a nondegeneracy assumption for the marginal distribution of the input.

When labels take the form $y = \sigma(v^\top x) + \xi$ for zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise $\xi$, we show that the population risk guarantees for gradient descent improve to $\mathsf{OPT} + \eps$. For ReLU, we show the same results under a nondegeneracy assumption for the marginal distribution of the input.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether gradient descent can learn a good single neuron when labels need not follow a neuron model. It minimizes squared error on independent, identically distributed samples and studies error on the underlying population. The activation is Lipschitz and non-decreasing, but the resulting optimization can still be nonconvex and nonsmooth.

Writing OPT for the smallest achievable population error, the authors prove a bound of O(OPT) plus an arbitrarily small tolerance for strictly increasing activations. For ReLU, the bound is O(sqrt(OPT)) plus that tolerance. These guarantees come with polynomial runtime and sample requirements that are almost independent of dimension. The strictly increasing case requires only boundedness as a distributional condition; ReLU additionally requires a nondegeneracy assumption on inputs.

Stronger structure in the labels yields a stronger result. When labels come from a neuron plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise, the guarantee improves to OPT plus the tolerance. The paper therefore distinguishes what gradient descent can achieve with unrestricted label relationships from what becomes possible under a specified noise model.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent learns a near-best single neuron under stated activation and input assumptions, with sharper guarantees for labels generated by a noisy neuron.

title: Agnostic Learning of a Single Neuron with Gradient Descent

abstract: Visual and audio modalities are highly correlated, yet they contain different information. Their strong correlation makes it possible to predict the semantics of one from the other with good accuracy. Their intrinsic differences make cross-modal prediction a potentially more rewarding pretext task for self-supervised learning of video and audio representations compared to within-modality learning. Based on this intuition, we propose Cross-Modal Deep Clustering (XDC), a novel self-supervised method that leverages unsupervised clustering in one modality (e.g., audio) as a supervisory signal for the other modality (e.g., video). This cross-modal supervision helps XDC utilize the semantic correlation and the differences between the two modalities. Our experiments show that XDC outperforms single-modality clustering and other multi-modal variants. XDC achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among self-supervised methods on multiple video and audio benchmarks. Most importantly, our video model pretrained on large-scale unlabeled data significantly outperforms the same model pretrained with full-supervision on ImageNet and Kinetics for action recognition on HMDB51 and UCF101. To the best of our knowledge, XDC is the first self-supervised learning method that outperforms large-scale fully-supervised pretraining for action recognition on the same architecture.

Cross-Modal Deep Clustering, or XDC, uses that combination to learn representations without manual labels. The method clusters examples in one modality and uses those group assignments as training supervision for the other modality, allowing audio and vision to guide each other's learning.

The motivation is that predicting information across modalities may be more rewarding than learning entirely within one modality. Shared meaning makes the prediction possible, while differences between sound and images make it useful. Experiments find that XDC outperforms single-modality clustering and other multimodal variants, and achieves leading self-supervised accuracy on multiple audio and video benchmarks.

The strongest reported comparison concerns action recognition. On HMDB51 and UCF101, a video model pretrained with XDC on large-scale unlabeled data significantly outperforms the same architecture pretrained with full supervision on ImageNet and Kinetics. This provides evidence that cross-modal supervision can produce highly effective transferable representations, with the comparison tied to the evaluated architecture, datasets, and tasks.
summary.tldr: XDC trains audio and video representations using each modality's clusters to supervise the other, yielding strong self-supervised action-recognition results.

title: Self-Supervised Learning by Cross-Modal Audio-Video Clustering

abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) distances such as Wasserstein have been used in several areas such as GANs and domain adaptation. OT, however, is very sensitive to outliers (samples with large noise) in the data since in its objective function, every sample, including outliers, is weighed similarly due to the marginal constraints. To remedy this issue, robust formulations of OT with unbalanced marginal constraints have previously been proposed. However, employing these methods in deep learning problems such as GANs and domain adaptation is challenging due to the instability of their dual optimization solvers. In this paper, we resolve these issues by deriving a computationally-efficient dual form of the robust OT optimization that is amenable to modern deep learning applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our formulation in two applications of GANs and domain adaptation. Our approach can train state-of-the-art GAN models on noisy datasets corrupted with outlier distributions. In particular, the proposed optimization method computes weights for training samples reflecting how difficult it is for those samples to be generated in the model. In domain adaptation, our robust OT formulation leads to improved accuracy compared to the standard adversarial adaptation methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/yogeshbalaji/robustOT.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions and is used in generative modeling and domain adaptation. Standard formulations are sensitive to outliers because marginal constraints give noisy samples similar standing to other observations. Robust formulations relax those constraints, but the abstract identifies instability in their dual optimization solvers as an obstacle to deep-learning applications.

The authors derive a computationally efficient dual form of robust optimal transport that is suitable for these applications. This reformulation addresses how the robust objective is optimized. In generative modeling, the optimization also assigns training-sample weights that reflect how difficult those samples are for the model to generate.

Experiments demonstrate the method in GAN training and domain adaptation. The approach can train state-of-the-art GAN models on datasets contaminated by outlier distributions, and it improves adaptation accuracy relative to standard adversarial adaptation methods. The findings support the usefulness of making robust transport computationally workable, connecting its treatment of noisy observations to concrete improvements in the evaluated learning tasks.
summary.tldr: An efficient dual formulation makes robust optimal transport practical for GAN training with outliers and improves evaluated domain-adaptation accuracy.

title: Robust Optimal Transport with Applications in Generative Modeling and Domain Adaptation

abstract: Prioritized Experience Replay (PER) is a deep reinforcement learning technique in which agents learn from transitions sampled with non-uniform probability proportionate to their temporal-difference error. We show that any loss function evaluated with non-uniformly sampled data can be transformed into another uniformly sampled loss function with the same expected gradient. Surprisingly, we find in some environments PER can be replaced entirely by this new loss function without impact to empirical performance. Furthermore, this relationship suggests a new branch of improvements to PER by correcting its uniformly sampled loss function equivalent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed modifications to PER and the equivalent loss function in several MuJoCo and Atari environments.

We show that any loss function evaluated with non-uniformly sampled data can be transformed into another uniformly sampled loss function with the same expected gradient. Surprisingly, we find in some environments PER can be replaced entirely by this new loss function without impact to empirical performance. Furthermore, this relationship suggests a new branch of improvements to PER by correcting its uniformly sampled loss function equivalent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed modifications to PER and the equivalent loss function in several MuJoCo and Atari environments.

paragraphs: Experience replay lets a reinforcement learning agent learn again from previously observed transitions. Prioritized Experience Replay changes how often transitions are selected, favoring those with larger temporal-difference errors. This paper examines the relationship between that sampling choice and the loss function used to learn from the selected data.

The main result shows that a loss evaluated under nonuniform sampling can be transformed into a different loss under uniform sampling with the same expected gradient. In other words, changing which examples appear more often can be represented through a change in the learning objective's gradient contributions. The equivalence concerns the average update, so it does not itself assert that individual sampled updates are identical.

In some tested environments, the transformed loss replaces prioritized replay without changing empirical performance. The authors also use the equivalence to identify improvements by correcting the uniformly sampled loss associated with prioritized replay. Experiments in several MuJoCo and Atari environments support those modifications. The contribution therefore provides both an explanation of replay prioritization and a route to improving it through loss design.
summary.tldr: Nonuniform replay sampling can be translated into a uniformly sampled loss with the same expected gradient, enabling alternative and improved replay methods.

title: An Equivalence between Loss Functions and Non-Uniform Sampling in Experience Replay

abstract: We introduce the use of empirical centralization to derive novel practical, probabilistic, sample-dependent bounds to the Supremum Deviation (SD) of empirical means of functions in a family from their expectations. Our bounds have optimal dependence on the maximum (i.e., wimpy) variance and the function ranges, and the same dependence on the number of samples as existing SD bounds. To compute the SD bounds in practice, we develop tightly-concentrated Monte Carlo estimators of the empirical Rademacher average of the empirically-centralized family, and we show novel concentration results for the empirical wimpy variance. Our experimental evaluation shows that our bounds greatly outperform non-centralized bounds and are extremely practical even at small sample sizes.

To compute the SD bounds in practice, we develop tightly-concentrated Monte Carlo estimators of the empirical Rademacher average of the empirically-centralized family, and we show novel concentration results for the empirical wimpy variance. Our experimental evaluation shows that our bounds greatly outperform non-centralized bounds and are extremely practical even at small sample sizes.

paragraphs: An empirical average can differ from the underlying expected value. When many functions are considered together, the supremum deviation measures the largest such discrepancy across the family. This paper develops probabilistic bounds on that quantity using empirical centralization, making the guarantees depend on the observed sample.

The bounds have optimal dependence on the largest variance among the functions and on their ranges, while retaining the sample-count dependence of existing bounds. To make the result computable, the authors develop tightly concentrated Monte Carlo estimators of the empirical Rademacher average for the centered family. They also prove concentration results for the empirical maximum variance.

These components connect the theoretical bound to quantities that can be estimated in practice. Experiments show substantially tighter results than non-centralized bounds and practical usefulness even with small samples. The improvement therefore concerns how variance, range, and observed data enter a uniform guarantee, without claiming a better dependence on sample count than the existing bounds used for comparison.
summary.tldr: Empirical centralization yields practical uniform convergence bounds with optimal variance and range dependence and improved empirical tightness.

title: Sharp uniform convergence bounds through empirical centralization

abstract: Recent literature has made much progress in understanding \emph{online LQR}: a modern learning-theoretic take on the classical control problem where a learner attempts to optimally control an unknown linear dynamical system with fully observed state, perturbed by i.i.d. Gaussian noise. \iftoggle{nips}{The}{It is now understood that the} optimal regret over time horizon $T$ against the optimal control law scales as $\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{T})$. In this paper, we show that the same regret rate (against a suitable benchmark) is attainable even in the considerably more general non-stochastic control model, where the system is driven by \emph{arbitrary adversarial} noise \citep{agarwal2019online}. We attain the optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret when the dynamics are unknown to the learner, and $\mathrm{poly}(\log T)$ regret when known, provided that the cost functions are strongly convex (as in LQR). Our algorithm is based on a novel variant of online Newton step \citep{hazan2007logarithmic}, which adapts to the geometry induced by adversarial disturbances, and our analysis hinges on generic regret bounds for certain structured losses in the OCO-with-memory framework \citep{anava2015online}.

paragraphs: Online control studies how a learner controls a dynamical system while learning about it. In online linear quadratic regulation, an unknown linear system has a fully observed state and independent Gaussian disturbances. This paper asks whether favorable regret rates remain possible when disturbances can instead be arbitrary and adversarial.

The authors show that, against a suitable benchmark, unknown dynamics still permit regret growing at a square-root rate in the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors. When the dynamics are known, they obtain regret polynomial in the logarithm of the horizon. These guarantees require strongly convex cost functions, as arise in linear quadratic regulation.

The algorithm uses a new variant of online Newton step that adapts to geometry induced by the disturbances. Its analysis develops regret bounds for structured losses in online convex optimization with memory. The result shows that replacing stochastic noise with adversarial disturbances need not worsen the leading time dependence of regret for unknown dynamics in the studied setting, despite the broader disturbance model.
summary.tldr: With strongly convex costs, adversarial-noise control achieves square-root regret for unknown dynamics and polylogarithmic regret for known dynamics.

title: Making Non-Stochastic Control (Almost) as Easy as Stochastic

abstract: We analyze the influence of adversarial training on the loss landscape of machine learning models. To this end, we first provide analytical studies of the properties of adversarial loss functions under different adversarial budgets. We then demonstrate that the adversarial loss landscape is less favorable to optimization, due to increased curvature and more scattered gradients. Our conclusions are validated by numerical analyses, which show that training under large adversarial budgets impede the escape from suboptimal random initialization, cause non-vanishing gradients and make the models' minima found sharper. Based on these observations, we show that a periodic adversarial scheduling (PAS) strategy can effectively overcome these challenges, yielding better results than vanilla adversarial training while being much less sensitive to the choice of learning rate.

To this end, we first provide analytical studies of the properties of adversarial loss functions under different adversarial budgets. We then demonstrate that the adversarial loss landscape is less favorable to optimization, due to increased curvature and more scattered gradients. Our conclusions are validated by numerical analyses, which show that training under large adversarial budgets impede the escape from suboptimal random initialization, cause non-vanishing gradients and make the models' minima found sharper. Based on these observations, we show that a periodic adversarial scheduling (PAS) strategy can effectively overcome these challenges, yielding better results than vanilla adversarial training while being much less sensitive to the choice of learning rate.

paragraphs: Adversarial training changes the optimization problem a model must solve. This paper examines how allowing adversarial perturbations of different sizes changes the loss landscape. Its central concern is why stronger adversarial training can become difficult to optimize, even before considering the quality of the resulting model.

Analytical studies show increased curvature and more scattered gradients in the adversarial loss landscape. Numerical analyses support this account: large adversarial budgets hinder escape from unfavorable random initializations, produce gradients that do not vanish, and lead to sharper minima. Together, these findings identify concrete optimization difficulties associated with the strength of the adversary.

The authors respond with periodic adversarial scheduling, or PAS, which schedules adversarial training periodically. They report that this strategy can overcome the identified challenges, improve results relative to vanilla adversarial training, and substantially reduce sensitivity to learning-rate choice. The contribution connects an analysis of training geometry with a practical scheduling intervention. Its findings support adjusting the adversarial training schedule as a way to improve the optimization process.
summary.tldr: The paper links adversarial training to harder loss landscapes and proposes periodic scheduling that improves optimization and reduces learning-rate sensitivity.

title: On the Loss Landscape of Adversarial Training: Identifying Challenges and How to Overcome Them

abstract: Out-of-distribution generalization is one of the key challenges when transferring a model from the lab to the real world. Existing efforts mostly focus on building invariant features among source and target domains. Based on invariant features, a high-performing classifier on source domains could hopefully behave equally well on a target domain. In other words, we hope the invariant features to be \emph{transferable}. However, in practice, there are no perfectly transferable features, and some algorithms seem to learn ``more transferable'' features than others. How can we understand and quantify such \emph{transferability}? In this paper, we formally define transferability that one can quantify and compute in domain generalization. We point out the difference and connection with common discrepancy measures between domains, such as total variation and Wasserstein distance. We then prove that our transferability can be estimated with enough samples and give a new upper bound for the target error based on our transferability. Empirically, we evaluate the transferability of the feature embeddings learned by existing algorithms for domain generalization. Surprisingly, we find that many algorithms are not quite learning transferable features, although few could still survive. In light of this, we propose a new algorithm for learning transferable features and test it over various benchmark datasets, including RotatedMNIST, PACS, Office-Home and WILDS-FMoW. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm achieves consistent improvement over many state-of-the-art algorithms, corroborating our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained on source domains will work on a different target domain. Many methods seek invariant features, hoping that a strong source classifier will also perform well elsewhere. This paper focuses on the next question: how to quantify whether learned features actually support that transfer.

The authors formally define a computable notion of transferability and explain its relationship to domain discrepancy measures such as total variation and Wasserstein distance. They prove that transferability can be estimated with enough samples and derive an upper bound on target error using it. This connects a measurable feature property with a theoretical statement about performance after transfer.

Guided by this finding, the authors introduce an algorithm designed to learn transferable features. Across RotatedMNIST, PACS, Office-Home, and WILDS-FMoW, it consistently improves over many state-of-the-art methods tested. The contribution combines a diagnostic definition, an error bound, and a learning approach informed by both.
summary.tldr: A formal measure of feature transferability supports target-error bounds and an algorithm that improves performance across several domain generalization benchmarks.

title: Quantifying and Improving Transferability in Domain Generalization

abstract: Achieving sample efficiency in online episodic reinforcement learning (RL) requires optimally balancing exploration and exploitation. When it comes to a finite-horizon episodic Markov decision process with $S$ states, $A$ actions and horizon length $H$, substantial progress has been achieved towards characterizing the minimax-optimal regret, which scales on the order of $\sqrt{H^2SAT}$ (modulo log factors) with $T$ the total number of samples. While several competing solution paradigms have been proposed to minimize regret, they are either memory-inefficient, or fall short of optimality unless the sample size exceeds an enormous threshold (e.g., $S^6A^4 \,\mathrm{poly}(H)$ for existing model-free methods).To overcome such a large sample size barrier to efficient RL, we design a novel model-free algorithm, with space complexity $O(SAH)$, that achieves near-optimal regret as soon as the sample size exceeds the order of $SA\,\mathrm{poly}(H)$. In terms of this sample size requirement (also referred to the initial burn-in cost), our method improves --- by at least a factor of $S^5A^3$ --- upon any prior memory-efficient algorithm that is asymptotically regret-optimal. Leveraging the recently introduced variance reduction strategy (also called {\em reference-advantage decomposition}), the proposed algorithm employs an {\em early-settled} reference update rule, with the aid of two Q-learning sequences with upper and lower confidence bounds. The design principle of our early-settled variance reduction method might be of independent interest to other RL settings that involve intricate exploration-exploitation trade-offs.

paragraphs: An online reinforcement learning agent must explore unfamiliar actions while using what it already knows. Regret measures the reward sacrificed during that learning process. For finite-horizon problems with S states, A actions, and episodes of length H, earlier memory-efficient methods could approach optimal regret only after a very large initial sample requirement.

The paper introduces a model-free algorithm that stores information using O(SAH) space and reaches near-optimal regret once the sample count exceeds an order of SA times a polynomial in H. Its initial sample requirement improves by at least a factor of S⁵A³ over prior memory-efficient algorithms that eventually attain optimal regret.

The mechanism combines variance reduction with an early-settled reference update rule. Two Q-learning sequences provide upper and lower confidence bounds to support that rule. The significance is that strong regret guarantees become available after substantially fewer samples while retaining economical memory use. The authors also suggest that this variance-reduction design might help other reinforcement learning settings with difficult exploration decisions.
summary.tldr: A memory-efficient model-free algorithm substantially reduces the initial sample requirement for near-optimal regret in finite-horizon reinforcement learning.

title: Breaking the Sample Complexity Barrier to Regret-Optimal Model-Free Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Feature selection, as a vital dimension reduction technique, reduces data dimension by identifying an essential subset of input features, which can facilitate interpretable insights into learning and inference processes. Algorithmic stability is a key characteristic of an algorithm regarding its sensitivity to perturbations of input samples. In this paper, we propose an innovative unsupervised feature selection algorithm attaining this stability with provable guarantees. The architecture of our algorithm consists of a feature scorer and a feature selector. The scorer trains a neural network (NN) to globally score all the features, and the selector adopts a dependent sub-NN to locally evaluate the representation abilities for selecting features. Further, we present algorithmic stability analysis and show that our algorithm has a performance guarantee via a generalization error bound. Extensive experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate superior generalization performance of our proposed algorithm to strong baseline methods. Also, the properties revealed by our theoretical analysis and the stability of our algorithm-selected features are empirically confirmed.

paragraphs: Feature selection reduces the number of inputs a learning system uses by retaining an informative subset. This can make the resulting analysis easier to interpret. The paper focuses on unsupervised selection and on whether selected features remain stable when the input samples change.

The proposed algorithm combines two linked components. A neural network scores all features globally, while a dependent subnetwork evaluates their ability to represent the data locally. Together, these components connect broad feature scoring with the more focused task of choosing a subset.

The authors analyze algorithmic stability, meaning sensitivity to changes in the sample used by the algorithm. They establish stability guarantees and a generalization error bound. This connects the selection procedure to a theoretical performance guarantee beyond its behavior on the observed samples.

Experiments on real-world datasets show better generalization than strong baseline methods. They also empirically support properties identified by the theory and the stability of the selected features. The contribution therefore combines a selection architecture with evidence about both its predictive usefulness and its consistency under sample perturbations.
summary.tldr: A paired neural scorer and selector provides unsupervised feature selection with stability guarantees and strong empirical generalization.

title: Algorithmic stability and generalization of an unsupervised feature selection algorithm

abstract: Despite Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable accuracy, whether the results are trustworthy is still unexplored. Previous studies suggest that many modern neural networks are over-confident on the predictions, however, surprisingly, we discover that GNNs are primarily in the opposite direction, i.e., GNNs are under-confident. Therefore, the confidence calibration for GNNs is highly desired. In this paper, we propose a novel trustworthy GNN model by designing a topology-aware post-hoc calibration function. Specifically, we first verify that the confidence distribution in a graph has homophily property, and this finding inspires us to design a calibration GNN model (CaGCN) to learn the calibration function. CaGCN is able to obtain a unique transformation from logits of GNNs to the calibrated confidence for each node, meanwhile, such transformation is able to preserve the order between classes, satisfying the accuracy-preserving property. Moreover, we apply the calibration GNN to self-training framework, showing that more trustworthy pseudo labels can be obtained with the calibrated confidence and further improve the performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model in terms of both calibration and accuracy.

paragraphs: Accurate predictions do not automatically come with reliable confidence scores. This paper finds that the graph neural networks studied are primarily underconfident, contrasting with the overconfidence reported for many other neural networks. It addresses how to adjust those scores so that they better reflect the reliability of node predictions.

The authors observe that confidence has a homophily pattern in graphs: connected nodes tend to exhibit similar confidence. They use this finding to build CaGCN, a graph neural network that performs calibration after prediction. It uses graph topology to learn a node-specific transformation from the original prediction scores to calibrated confidence.

The transformation preserves the ordering of classes, so calibration retains the original predicted class and its accuracy. The authors also incorporate CaGCN into self-training, where model predictions become training labels. Calibrated confidence produces more trustworthy pseudo labels and improves performance in that setting. Experiments support benefits for calibration and accuracy, with accuracy preservation applying to the calibration transformation itself and further accuracy gains arising through its use in self-training.
summary.tldr: CaGCN uses graph structure to calibrate node confidence while preserving class rankings and improving pseudo labels for self-training.

title: Be Confident! Towards Trustworthy Graph Neural Networks via Confidence Calibration

abstract: The goal of self-supervised visual representation learning is to learn strong, transferable image representations, with the majority of research focusing on object or scene level. On the other hand, representation learning at part level has received significantly less attention. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised approach to object part discovery and segmentation and make three contributions. First, we construct a proxy task through a set of objectives that encourages the model to learn a meaningful decomposition of the image into its parts. Secondly, prior work argues for reconstructing or clustering pre-computed features as a proxy to parts; we show empirically that this alone is unlikely to find meaningful parts; mainly because of their low resolution and the tendency of classification networks to spatially smear out information. We suggest that image reconstruction at the level of pixels can alleviate this problem, acting as a complementary cue. Lastly, we show that the standard evaluation based on keypoint regression does not correlate well with segmentation quality and thus introduce different metrics, NMI and ARI, that better characterize the decomposition of objects into parts. Our method yields semantic parts which are consistent across fine-grained but visually distinct categories, outperforming the state of the art on three benchmark datasets. Code is available at the project page: https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/unsup-parts/.

This paper proposes an unsupervised method for discovering and segmenting parts. It builds a proxy task with objectives designed to encourage a meaningful decomposition of each image into components.

The authors empirically challenge the idea that reconstructing or clustering precomputed features is sufficient for meaningful part discovery. abstract: Transformers have shown great power in time series forecasting due to their global-range modeling ability. However, their performance can degenerate terribly on non-stationary real-world data in which the joint distribution changes over time. Previous studies primarily adopt stationarization to attenuate the non-stationarity of original series for better predictability. But the stationarized series deprived of inherent non-stationarity can be less instructive for real-world bursty events forecasting. This problem, termed over-stationarization in this paper, leads Transformers to generate indistinguishable temporal attentions for different series and impedes the predictive capability of deep models. To tackle the dilemma between series predictability and model capability, we propose Non-stationary Transformers as a generic framework with two interdependent modules: Series Stationarization and De-stationary Attention. Concretely, Series Stationarization unifies the statistics of each input and converts the output with restored statistics for better predictability. To address the over-stationarization problem, De-stationary Attention is devised to recover the intrinsic non-stationary information into temporal dependencies by approximating distinguishable attentions learned from raw series. Our Non-stationary Transformers framework consistently boosts mainstream Transformers by a large margin, which reduces MSE by 49.43% on Transformer, 47.34% on Informer, and 46.89% on Reformer, making them the state-of-the-art in time series forecasting. Code is available at this repository: https://github.com/thuml/Nonstationary_Transformers.

paragraphs: Real-world time series can change their statistical behavior over time, making forecasting difficult. Normalizing a series can improve predictability, but it can also remove information needed to anticipate bursts and other changing behavior. The paper calls this over-stationarization and connects it to Transformers producing insufficiently distinct attention patterns for different series.

The proposed framework combines two interdependent modules. Series Stationarization standardizes input statistics and restores the corresponding statistics at the output. De-stationary Attention brings information about the original changing behavior back into the model's temporal dependencies. It does so by approximating distinguishable attention patterns associated with the raw series, aiming to retain useful information lost through normalization.

The authors report improvements across mainstream Transformer models, with mean squared error reductions of 49.43% for Transformer, 47.34% for Informer, and 46.89% for Reformer. These empirical results support treating normalization and attention jointly. The approach addresses both the difficulty of modeling changing distributions and the loss of predictive detail caused by making inputs statistically uniform.
summary.tldr: Non-stationary Transformers combine input normalization with attention that restores changing-series information, substantially improving reported forecasting errors.

title: Non-stationary Transformers: Exploring the Stationarity in Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Stereo matching is a classic challenging problem in computer vision, which has recently witnessed remarkable progress by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). This paradigm shift leads to two interesting and entangled questions that have not been addressed well. First, it is unclear whether stereo matching DNNs that are trained from scratch really learn to perform matching well. This paper studies this problem from the lens of white-box adversarial attacks. It presents a method of learning stereo-constrained photometrically-consistent attacks, which by design are weaker adversarial attacks, and yet can cause catastrophic performance drop for those DNNs. This observation suggests that they may not actually learn to perform matching well in the sense that they should otherwise achieve potentially even better after stereo-constrained perturbations are introduced. Second, stereo matching DNNs are typically trained under the simulation-to-real (Sim2Real) pipeline due to the data hungriness of DNNs. Thus, alleviating the impacts of the Sim2Real photometric gap in stereo matching DNNs becomes a pressing need. Towards joint adversarially robust and domain generalizable stereo matching, this paper proposes to learn DNN-contextualized binary-pattern-driven non-parametric cost-volumes. It leverages the perspective of learning the cost aggregation via DNNs, and presents a simple yet expressive design that is fully end-to-end trainable, without resorting to specific aggregation inductive biases. In experiments, the proposed method is tested in the SceneFlow dataset, the KITTI2015 dataset, and the Middlebury dataset. It significantly improves the adversarial robustness, while retaining accuracy performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. It also shows a better Sim2Real generalizability. Our code and pretrained models are released at \href{https://github.com/kelkelcheng/AdversariallyRobustStereo}{this Github Repo}.

paragraphs: Stereo matching finds correspondences between two views of a scene. This paper asks whether strong neural stereo systems actually learn reliable matching. It develops white-box attacks constrained to remain consistent across the stereo pair and photometrically consistent. Despite these restrictions, the attacks cause severe performance drops, suggesting weaknesses in the matching behavior learned by the tested networks.

The proposed response combines binary-pattern-based nonparametric matching cost volumes with neural contextualization and learned cost aggregation. The design is trainable end to end and does not require specific aggregation inductive biases. It addresses both adversarial vulnerability and the photometric gap between simulated training images and real images.

Experiments on SceneFlow, KITTI2015, and Middlebury show significantly improved adversarial robustness while maintaining accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The approach also improves simulation-to-real generalization. These findings support revisiting the construction of matching costs as part of neural stereo design, with benefits for both attack resistance and transfer across image domains.
summary.tldr: Combining nonparametric matching costs with neural aggregation improves stereo robustness and simulation-to-real generalization while retaining competitive accuracy.

title: Revisiting Non-Parametric Matching Cost Volumes for Robust and Generalizable Stereo Matching

abstract: We show that, for any sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon > 0$, when both players in a general-sum two-player (bimatrix) game employ optimistic mirror descent (OMD) with smooth regularization, learning rate $\eta = O(\epsilon^2)$ and $T = \Omega(poly(1/\epsilon))$ repetitions, either the dynamics reach an $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium (NE), or the average correlated distribution of play is an $\Omega(poly(\epsilon))$-strong coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE): any possible unilateral deviation does not only leave the player worse, but will decrease its utility by $\Omega(poly(\epsilon))$. As an immediate consequence, when the iterates of OMD are bounded away from being Nash equilibria in a bimatrix game, we guarantee convergence to an \emph{exact} CCE after only $O(1)$ iterations. Our results reveal that uncoupled no-regret learning algorithms can converge to CCE in general-sum games remarkably faster than to NE in, for example, zero-sum games. To establish this, we show that when OMD does not reach arbitrarily close to a NE, the (cumulative) regret of both players is not only negative, but decays linearly with time. Given that regret is the canonical measure of performance in online learning, our results suggest that cycling behavior of no-regret learning algorithms in games can be justified in terms of efficiency.

paragraphs: Learning dynamics in a game can keep cycling instead of settling at a Nash equilibrium. This paper shows that such behavior can still lead to a strong equilibrium guarantee for average play. It studies general-sum two-player games in which both players use optimistic mirror descent with smooth regularization.

For sufficiently small approximation tolerance, an appropriately small learning rate, and enough repetitions, the authors establish two possible outcomes. Either the dynamics reach an approximate Nash equilibrium, or the average joint distribution of play becomes a strong coarse correlated equilibrium. In the latter case, switching unilaterally to a fixed alternative action decreases a player’s expected utility by a quantitatively bounded amount.

If the iterates remain bounded away from Nash equilibria, the analysis also gives convergence to an exact coarse correlated equilibrium after a constant number of iterations. The proof shows that both players’ cumulative regret becomes negative and decreases linearly over time. Thus, continued cycling can accompany efficient equilibrium learning, with the guarantee applying to accumulated play rather than requiring the current strategies to settle.
summary.tldr: Under stated conditions, optimistic mirror descent reaches approximate Nash equilibrium or produces average play with a strong coarse correlated equilibrium guarantee.

title: Optimistic Mirror Descent Either Converges to Nash or to Strong Coarse Correlated Equilibria in Bimatrix Games

abstract: There has been significant progress in developing reinforcement learning (RL) training systems. Past works such as IMPALA, Apex, Seed RL, Sample Factory, and others, aim to improve the system's overall throughput. In this paper, we aim to address a common bottleneck in the RL training system, i.e., parallel environment execution, which is often the slowest part of the whole system but receives little attention. With a curated design for paralleling RL environments, we have improved the RL environment simulation speed across different hardware setups, ranging from a laptop and a modest workstation, to a high-end machine such as NVIDIA DGX-A100. On a high-end machine, EnvPool achieves one million frames per second for the environment execution on Atari environments and three million frames per second on MuJoCo environments. When running EnvPool on a laptop, the speed is 2.8x that of the Python subprocess. Moreover, great compatibility with existing RL training libraries has been demonstrated in the open-sourced community, including CleanRL, rl_games, DeepMind Acme, etc. Finally, EnvPool allows researchers to iterate their ideas at a much faster pace and has great potential to become the de facto RL environment execution engine. Example runs show that it only takes five minutes to train agents to play Atari Pong and MuJoCo Ant on a laptop. EnvPool is open-sourced at https://github.com/sail-sg/envpool.

EnvPool targets that bottleneck through an execution engine designed to run many environments in parallel.

The reported improvements span laptops, workstations, and high-end machines. On a high-end system, EnvPool reaches one million frames per second for Atari environment execution and three million for MuJoCo. This matters because a faster execution engine can become part of established training workflows. Example runs train agents to play Atari Pong and MuJoCo Ant in five minutes on a laptop, illustrating the potential for faster experimental iteration.
summary.tldr: EnvPool accelerates parallel reinforcement-learning environment execution across hardware scales and integrates with existing training libraries.

title: EnvPool: A Highly Parallel Reinforcement Learning Environment Execution Engine

abstract: We consider the projected gradient algorithm for the nonconvex best subset selection problem that minimizes a given empirical loss function under an $\ell_0$-norm constraint. Through decomposing the feasible set of the given sparsity constraint as a finite union of linear subspaces, we present two acceleration schemes with global convergence guarantees, one by same-space extrapolation and the other by subspace identification. The former fully utilizes the problem structure to greatly accelerate the optimization speed with only negligible additional cost. The latter leads to a two-stage meta-algorithm that first uses classical projected gradient iterations to identify the correct subspace containing an optimal solution, and then switches to a highly-efficient smooth optimization method in the identified subspace to attain superlinear convergence. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed accelerated algorithms are magnitudes faster than their non-accelerated counterparts as well as the state of the art.
