paragraphs: Best subset selection seeks a model that minimizes an empirical loss while using only a limited number of nonzero variables. This sparsity constraint makes the problem nonconvex. The paper studies how to accelerate projected gradient optimization by exploiting the structure of the feasible solutions: they form a finite collection of linear subspaces, each corresponding to a selection of variables.

The first acceleration scheme uses same-space extrapolation. It takes advantage of progress within a shared subspace to speed optimization while adding negligible computational cost. The second scheme identifies a subspace before changing optimization methods. It begins with ordinary projected gradient iterations, identifies the appropriate subspace containing an optimal solution, and then applies an efficient smooth optimizer within it.

The authors provide global convergence guarantees for both schemes and superlinear convergence for the second-stage approach. Their experiments report orders-of-magnitude speed improvements over unaccelerated methods and the state of the art. The central contribution is to use the geometry of sparse solutions to organize faster optimization.
summary.tldr: Two acceleration schemes exploit the subspace structure of sparse optimization to provide convergence guarantees and substantial empirical speedups.

title: Accelerated Projected Gradient Algorithms for Sparsity Constrained Optimization Problems

abstract: This paper deals with deep transductive learning, and proposes TransBoost as a procedure for fine-tuning any deep neural model to improve its performance on any (unlabeled) test set provided at training time. TransBoost is inspired by a large margin principle and is efficient and simple to use. Our method significantly improves the ImageNet classification performance on a wide range of architectures, such as ResNets, MobileNetV3-L, EfficientNetB0, ViT-S, and ConvNext-T, leading to state-of-the-art transductive performance.Additionally we show that TransBoost is effective on a wide variety of image classification datasets. The implementation of TransBoost is provided at: https://github.com/omerb01/TransBoost .

paragraphs: TransBoost addresses deep transductive learning, where the unlabeled test inputs are available during training. The method fine-tunes an existing deep neural model with the aim of improving performance on that supplied test set. Availability of those inputs is a central feature of the setting, even though their labels are not provided.

The procedure is inspired by a large-margin principle and is described as efficient and simple to use. It is proposed as a broadly applicable fine-tuning method rather than a change tied to one network architecture. The paper evaluates it across ResNets, MobileNetV3-L, EfficientNetB0, ViT-S, and ConvNext-T, covering a range of models within image classification.

The authors report significant ImageNet classification improvements across these architectures and state-of-the-art transductive performance. They also demonstrate effectiveness on other image-classification datasets. These findings support using the specific unlabeled test set to guide fine-tuning in the transductive setting, with the reported gains spanning multiple architectures and datasets.
summary.tldr: TransBoost uses an available unlabeled test set for transductive fine-tuning, improving image classification across multiple architectures and datasets.

title: TransBoost: Improving the Best ImageNet Performance using Deep Transduction

abstract: This paper tackles post-hoc interpretability for audio processing networks. Our goal is to interpret decisions of a trained network in terms of high-level audio objects that are also listenable for the end-user. To this end, we propose a novel interpreter design that incorporates non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). In particular, a regularized interpreter module is trained to take hidden layer representations of the targeted network as input and produce time activations of pre-learnt NMF components as intermediate outputs. Our methodology allows us to generate intuitive audio-based interpretations that explicitly enhance parts of the input signal most relevant for a network's decision. We demonstrate our method's applicability on popular benchmarks, including a real-world multi-label classification task.

In particular, a regularized interpreter module is trained to take hidden layer representations of the targeted network as input and produce time activations of pre-learnt NMF components as intermediate outputs. Our methodology allows us to generate intuitive audio-based interpretations that explicitly enhance parts of the input signal most relevant for a network's decision. paragraphs: The paper aims to explain the decisions of an already trained audio-processing network through sounds a person can listen to. Its target is an interpretation in terms of meaningful audio objects, connecting a network's internal representations to audible parts of the input. This makes the explanation available in the same medium as the original signal.

The proposed interpreter incorporates non-negative matrix factorization, or NMF. A regularized module receives hidden-layer representations from the network being explained and produces time activations for previously learned NMF components. These intermediate activations connect the network's internal information to components that vary over the duration of the audio.

The method then generates audio interpretations that emphasize the portions of the input most relevant to a decision. A listener can inspect those emphasized sounds to understand what the network relied on. The authors demonstrate applicability on popular benchmarks, including a real-world classification task where an example can carry multiple labels. The contribution is a concrete route from hidden representations to listenable explanations for existing audio networks.
summary.tldr: An NMF-based interpreter turns an audio network's hidden representations into listenable explanations emphasizing decision-relevant sounds.

title: Listen to Interpret: Post-hoc Interpretability for Audio Networks with NMF

abstract: With the popularity of automatic code generation tools, such as Copilot, the study of the potential hazards of these tools is gaining importance. In this work, we explore the social bias problem in pre-trained code generation models. We propose a new paradigm to construct code prompts and successfully uncover social biases in code generation models. To quantify the severity of social biases in generated code, we develop a dataset along with three metrics to evaluate the overall social bias and fine-grained unfairness across different demographics. Experimental results on three pre-trained code generation models (Codex, InCoder, and CodeGen) with varying sizes, reveal severe social biases. Moreover, we conduct analysis to provide useful insights for further choice of code generation models with low social bias.

paragraphs: Automatically generated code can carry social biases, making evaluation of these systems about more than whether a program works. This paper examines that problem in pretrained code-generation models. The authors introduce a way to construct code prompts that exposes biased behavior, turning a broad concern about generated software into something that can be systematically investigated.

To measure the issue, they develop a dataset and three metrics. These measures address both overall social bias and more detailed unfairness across demographic groups. Looking at both levels matters because a single overall assessment cannot describe all of the differences between groups that the evaluation is designed to capture.

Experiments cover Codex, InCoder, and CodeGen at varying model sizes and reveal severe social biases in the tested models. Further analysis provides insights intended to help choose models with lower social bias. The paper's contribution is an evaluation approach and evidence of the problem in these systems, supplying a basis for comparing generated code along a social dimension as well as its technical usefulness.
summary.tldr: A new prompt-construction approach, dataset, and three metrics expose severe social biases in three tested code-generation model families.

title: Uncovering and Quantifying Social Biases in Code Generation

abstract: Vision-based emergent communication (EC) aims to learn to communicate through sketches and demystify the evolution of human communication. Ironically, previous works neglect multi-round interaction, which is indispensable in human communication. To fill this gap, we first introduce a novel Interactive Sketch Question Answering (ISQA) task, where two collaborative players are interacting through sketches to answer a question about an image. To accomplish this task, we design a new and efficient interactive EC system, which can achieve an effective balance among three evaluation factors, including the question answering accuracy, drawing complexity and human interpretability. Our experimental results demonstrate that multi-round interactive mechanism facilitates tar- geted and efficient communication between intelligent agents. The code will be released.

paragraphs: Research on visual emergent communication studies how agents learn to convey information through sketches. This paper focuses on a feature that earlier work overlooked: communication can unfold through multiple rounds of interaction. It introduces Interactive Sketch Question Answering, a task in which two cooperating players exchange sketches to answer a question about an image.

The authors design an interactive communication system for this task and assess it along three dimensions: answer accuracy, drawing complexity, and human interpretability. Considering these together makes the task more demanding than simply producing a correct answer. The sketches also need to communicate efficiently and remain understandable to people.

The experiments show that multiple rounds of interaction facilitate targeted, efficient communication between the agents. The system achieves an effective balance among the three evaluation factors. The contribution is therefore both a task for studying interactive visual communication and a system demonstrating its usefulness. It supplies evidence that the opportunity to interact can shape how agents communicate relevant visual information.
summary.tldr: A sketch-based question-answering task shows that multiple interaction rounds help agents communicate accurately, efficiently, and interpretably.

title: Emergent Communication in Interactive Sketch Question Answering

abstract: Solving complicated AI tasks with different domains and modalities is a key step toward artificial general intelligence. While there are numerous AI models available for various domains and modalities, they cannot handle complicated AI tasks autonomously. Considering large language models (LLMs) have exhibited exceptional abilities in language understanding, generation, interaction, and reasoning, we advocate that LLMs could act as a controller to manage existing AI models to solve complicated AI tasks, with language serving as a generic interface to empower this. Based on this philosophy, we present HuggingGPT, an LLM-powered agent that leverages LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) to connect various AI models in machine learning communities (e.g., Hugging Face) to solve AI tasks. Specifically, we use ChatGPT to conduct task planning when receiving a user request, select models according to their function descriptions available in Hugging Face, execute each subtask with the selected AI model, and summarize the response according to the execution results. By leveraging the strong language capability of ChatGPT and abundant AI models in Hugging Face, HuggingGPT can tackle a wide range of sophisticated AI tasks spanning different modalities and domains and achieve impressive results in language, vision, speech, and other challenging tasks, which paves a new way towards the realization of artificial general intelligence.

While there are numerous AI models available for various domains and modalities, they cannot handle complicated AI tasks autonomously. Considering large language models (LLMs) have exhibited exceptional abilities in language understanding, generation, interaction, and reasoning, we advocate that LLMs could act as a controller to manage existing AI models to solve complicated AI tasks, with language serving as a generic interface to empower this. Based on this philosophy, we present HuggingGPT, an LLM-powered agent that leverages LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) to connect various AI models in machine learning communities (e.g., Hugging Face) to solve AI tasks. Specifically, we use ChatGPT to conduct task planning when receiving a user request, select models according to their function descriptions available in Hugging Face, execute each subtask with the selected AI model, and summarize the response according to the execution results. By leveraging the strong language capability of ChatGPT and abundant AI models in Hugging Face, HuggingGPT can tackle a wide range of sophisticated AI tasks spanning different modalities and domains and achieve impressive results in language, vision, speech, and other challenging tasks, which paves a new way towards the realization of artificial general intelligence.

paragraphs: Many specialized AI models can handle individual language, image, or speech tasks, but combining them into a solution requires coordination. HuggingGPT assigns that coordination role to a large language model. It uses language as the interface through which a controller interprets a request and chooses among models with different capabilities.

The system uses ChatGPT to plan the work, select models based on their function descriptions in Hugging Face, and arrange execution of the resulting subtasks. It then summarizes a response using the execution results. Model descriptions are therefore operational information: they help connect a user's request to the particular tools needed to carry it out.

The authors report that this combination can handle sophisticated tasks spanning multiple modalities and domains, including language, vision, and speech. The contribution is an agent architecture that connects language-based planning with a collection of specialized models. Its stated results support the usefulness of this orchestration approach, while the paper presents it as a direction toward broader AI capabilities rather than a demonstration that artificial general intelligence has been achieved.
summary.tldr: HuggingGPT uses ChatGPT to plan tasks, select specialized Hugging Face models, coordinate execution, and summarize results.

title: HuggingGPT: Solving AI Tasks with ChatGPT and its Friends in Hugging Face

abstract: It is a long-term vision for Autonomous Driving (AD) community that the perception models can learn from a large-scale point cloud dataset, to obtain unified representations that can achieve promising results on different tasks or benchmarks. Previous works mainly focus on the self-supervised pre-training pipeline, meaning that they perform the pre-training and fine-tuning on the same benchmark, which is difficult to attain the performance scalability and cross-dataset application for the pre-training checkpoint. In this paper, for the first time, we are committed to building a large-scale pre-training point-cloud dataset with diverse data distribution, and meanwhile learning generalizable representations from such a diverse pre-training dataset. We formulate the point-cloud pre-training task as a semi-supervised problem, which leverages the few-shot labeled and massive unlabeled point-cloud data to generate the unified backbone representations that can be directly applied to many baseline models and benchmarks, decoupling the AD-related pre-training process and downstream fine-tuning task. During the period of backbone pre-training, by enhancing the scene- and instance-level distribution diversity and exploiting the backbone's ability to learn from unknown instances, we achieve significant performance gains on a series of downstream perception benchmarks including Waymo, nuScenes, and KITTI, under different baseline models like PV-RCNN++, SECOND, CenterPoint.

That arrangement makes it difficult to establish whether a pretrained model provides broadly reusable knowledge.

The authors build a large pretraining dataset with diverse point-cloud distributions and treat learning as a semi-supervised problem. A small amount of labeled data accompanies a much larger unlabeled collection. During backbone training, the approach increases diversity at both the scene and individual-object levels and develops the model's ability to learn from unfamiliar instances.

The resulting backbone representations can support multiple downstream models and benchmarks, separating pretraining from a particular fine-tuning task. The authors report significant perception improvements on Waymo, nuScenes, and KITTI using models including PV-RCNN++, SECOND, and CenterPoint. These results support the usefulness of diverse pretraining for transfer across the evaluated settings, making reusable perception backbones the central contribution.
summary.tldr: AD-PT uses diverse, largely unlabeled point clouds to pretrain reusable perception backbones that improve multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks.

title: AD-PT: Autonomous Driving Pre-Training with Large-scale Point Cloud Dataset

abstract: We study collaborative normal mean estimation, where $m$ strategic agents collect i.i.d samples from a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ at a cost. They all wish to estimate the mean $\mu$. By sharing data with each other, agents can obtain better estimates while keeping the cost of data collection small. To facilitate this collaboration, we wish to design mechanisms that encourage agents to collect a sufficient amount of data and share it truthfully, so that they are all better off than working alone. In naive mechanisms, such as simply pooling and sharing all the data, an individual agent might find it beneficial to under-collect and/or fabricate data, which can lead to poor social outcomes. We design a novel mechanism that overcomes these challenges via two key techniques: first, when sharing the others' data with an agent, the mechanism corrupts this dataset proportional to how much the data reported by the agent differs from the others; second, we design minimax optimal estimators for the corrupted dataset. Our mechanism, which is Nash incentive compatible and individually rational, achieves a social penalty (sum of all agents' estimation errors and data collection costs) that is at most a factor 2 of the global minimum. When applied to high dimensional (non-Gaussian) distributions with bounded variance, this mechanism retains these three properties, but with slightly weaker results. Finally, in two special cases where we restrict the strategy space of the agents, we design mechanisms that essentially achieve the global minimum.

paragraphs: Agents estimating the same normal-distribution mean can reduce collection costs by sharing independent samples. But simple pooling creates incentives to contribute too little or fabricate observations. The paper designs a collaboration mechanism that accounts for these strategic choices while seeking accurate estimates at low collective cost.

When returning other participants’ data to an agent, the mechanism adds corruption in proportion to how much that agent’s report differs from the others. It pairs this rule with minimax-optimal estimators for the corrupted data. The value of the information an agent receives is therefore tied to its contribution, creating incentives within the collaboration.

The mechanism is Nash incentive compatible and individually rational, and its combined estimation-error and collection-cost penalty is at most twice the global minimum. An extension to high-dimensional, non-Gaussian distributions with bounded variance retains the three stated properties with weaker results. In two special cases with restricted agent strategies, alternative mechanisms essentially achieve the global minimum. The guarantees thus connect statistical estimation quality with participants’ incentives.
summary.tldr: The paper designs incentive-compatible data sharing for mean estimation with total error and collection cost within twice the global optimum.

title: Mechanism Design for Collaborative Normal Mean Estimation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as T0, FLAN, and OPT-IML excel in multi-tasking under a unified instruction-following paradigm, where they also exhibit remarkable generalization abilities to unseen tasks. Despite their impressive performance, these LLMs, with sizes ranging from several billion to hundreds of billions of parameters, demand substantial computational resources, making their training and inference expensive and inefficient. Furthermore, adapting these models to downstream applications, particularly complex tasks, is often unfeasible due to the extensive hardware requirements for finetuning, even when utilizing parameter-efficient approaches such as prompt tuning. Additionally, the most powerful multi-task LLMs, such as OPT-IML-175B and FLAN-PaLM-540B, are not publicly accessible, severely limiting their customization potential. To address these challenges, we introduce a pretrained small scorer, \textit{Cappy}, designed to enhance the performance and efficiency of multi-task LLMs. With merely 360 million parameters, Cappy functions either independently on classification tasks or serve as an auxiliary component for LLMs, boosting their performance. Moreover, Cappy enables efficiently integrating downstream supervision without requiring LLM finetuning nor the access to their parameters. Our experiments demonstrate that, when working independently on 11 language understanding tasks from PromptSource, Cappy outperforms LLMs that are several orders of magnitude larger. Besides, on 45 complex tasks from BIG-Bench, Cappy boosts the performance of the advanced multi-task LLM, FLAN-T5, by a large margin. Furthermore, Cappy is flexible to cooperate with other LLM adaptations, including finetuning and in-context learning, offering additional performance enhancement.

paragraphs: Large instruction-following language models can handle many tasks, but their computational demands make training, inference, and adaptation expensive. Cappy addresses these obstacles with a pretrained scorer containing 360 million parameters, designed to support task performance without requiring changes to a large model’s parameters.

summary.tldr: Cappy is a small pretrained scorer that performs classification and improves larger language models without requiring access to their parameters.

title: Cappy: Outperforming and Boosting Large Multi-Task LMs with a Small Scorer

abstract: Recalibrating probabilistic classifiers is vital for enhancing the reliability and accuracy of predictive models. Despite the development of numerous recalibration algorithms, there is still a lack of a comprehensive theory that integrates calibration and sharpness (which is essential for maintaining predictive power). In this paper, we introduce the concept of minimum-risk recalibration within the framework of mean-squared-error (MSE) decomposition, offering a principled approach for evaluating and recalibrating probabilistic classifiers. Using this framework, we analyze the uniform-mass binning (UMB) recalibration method and establish a finite-sample risk upper bound of order $\tilde{O}(B/n + 1/B^2)$ where $B$ is the number of bins and $n$ is the sample size. By balancing calibration and sharpness, we further determine that the optimal number of bins for UMB scales with $n^{1/3}$, resulting in a risk bound of approximately $O(n^{-2/3})$. Additionally, we tackle the challenge of label shift by proposing a two-stage approach that adjusts the recalibration function using limited labeled data from the target domain. Our results show that transferring a calibrated classifier requires significantly fewer target samples compared to recalibrating from scratch. We validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations, which confirm the tightness of the proposed bounds, the optimal number of bins, and the effectiveness of label shift adaptation.

paragraphs: Recalibrating a classifier should make its probabilities reliable while preserving their predictive usefulness. This paper brings calibration and sharpness into one framework based on decomposing mean-squared error. The resulting notion of minimum-risk recalibration evaluates the balance between these goals, rather than treating reliable probabilities and informative predictions as separate concerns.

The authors apply this framework to uniform-mass binning, which recalibrates predictions through bins. With B bins and n samples, they derive a finite-sample risk upper bound of order B/n plus 1/B², up to logarithmic factors. Balancing these terms gives an optimal bin count scaling as n to the one-third power and an approximately n to the minus two-thirds risk bound. This provides a principled connection between available data and binning resolution.

The paper also considers label shift and proposes a two-stage adjustment using limited labeled target-domain data. Its results show that transferring an already calibrated classifier requires significantly fewer target samples than recalibrating from scratch. Numerical simulations support the tightness of the bounds, the bin-count choice, and the effectiveness of the adaptation procedure.
summary.tldr: A minimum-risk framework balances calibration and sharpness, deriving binning guarantees and a sample-efficient approach to label-shift adaptation.

title: Minimum-Risk Recalibration of Classifiers

abstract: Anomaly detection aims at detecting unexpected behaviours in the data. Because anomaly detection is usually an unsupervised task, traditional anomaly detectors learn a decision boundary by employing heuristics based on intuitions, which are hard to verify in practice. This introduces some uncertainty, especially close to the decision boundary, that may reduce the user trust in the detector's predictions. A way to combat this is by allowing the detector to reject predictions with high uncertainty (Learning to Reject). This requires employing a confidence metric that captures the distance to the decision boundary and setting a rejection threshold to reject low-confidence predictions. However, selecting a proper metric and setting the rejection threshold without labels are challenging tasks. In this paper, we solve these challenges by setting a constant rejection threshold on the stability metric computed by ExCeeD. Our insight relies on a theoretical analysis of such a metric. Moreover, setting a constant threshold results in strong guarantees: we estimate the test rejection rate, and derive a theoretical upper bound for both the rejection rate and the expected prediction cost. Experimentally, we show that our method outperforms some metric-based methods.

paragraphs: Unsupervised anomaly detectors must distinguish ordinary data from unexpected behavior without labels that directly validate their decision boundaries. Their heuristic boundaries can therefore produce uncertain predictions, especially for nearby examples. Allowing a detector to reject uncertain cases offers one response, but choosing both a confidence measure and a rejection threshold without labels is difficult.

This paper uses a stability metric computed by ExCeeD and applies a constant rejection threshold to it. The choice is supported by a theoretical analysis of the metric. The method thus turns rejection into a rule grounded in the behavior of an existing stability measure, addressing both how to express confidence and how to decide which predictions to withhold.

The analysis estimates the test-time rejection rate and derives upper bounds for both that rate and expected prediction cost. These guarantees help characterize the consequences of permitting rejection, beyond simply improving confidence in retained predictions. Experiments show that the method outperforms some other metric-based approaches. The stated comparison is selective, while the theoretical contribution provides explicit control over aspects of rejection behavior.
summary.tldr: A constant threshold on ExCeeD stability enables unsupervised anomaly-detection rejection with bounds on rejection rate and expected prediction cost.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection with Rejection

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have made significant progress in generating naturalistic images from textual inputs, and demonstrate the capacity to learn and represent complex visual-semantic relationships. While these diffusion models have achieved remarkable success, the underlying mechanisms driving their performance are not yet fully accounted for, with many unanswered questions surrounding what they learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize. Our work presents Diffusion Partial Information Decomposition (DiffusionPID), a novel technique that applies information-theoretic principles to decompose the input text prompt into its elementary components, enabling a detailed examination of how individual tokens and their interactions shape the generated image. We introduce a formal approach to analyze the uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy terms by applying PID to the denoising model at both the image and pixel level. This approach enables us to characterize how individual tokens and their interactions affect the model output. We first present a fine-grained analysis of characteristics utilized by the model to uniquely localize specific concepts, we then apply our approach in bias analysis and show it can recover gender and ethnicity biases. Finally, we use our method to visually characterize word ambiguity and similarity from the model’s perspective and illustrate the efficacy of our method for prompt intervention. Our results show that PID is a potent tool for evaluating and diagnosing text-to-image diffusion models. Link to project page: https://rbz-99.github.io/Diffusion-PID/.

paragraphs: DiffusionPID investigates how words in a text prompt influence images produced by diffusion models. A prompt contains individual concepts, but its effect also depends on relationships among words. The paper introduces an information-theoretic approach for examining those contributions, addressing questions about how these models represent visual meaning and why their behavior can be difficult to interpret.

The method applies partial information decomposition to the denoising model at both image and pixel levels. It separates unique information associated with individual tokens, redundant information shared across tokens, and synergistic information arising from their interactions. This provides a framework for asking both where a concept is expressed and how combinations of words shape the output.

The authors use the method to analyze concept localization, recover gender and ethnicity biases, and visualize word ambiguity and similarity from the model’s perspective. They also demonstrate its usefulness for prompt intervention. These applications position DiffusionPID as a diagnostic tool: its contribution is an account of token effects and interactions that can support closer examination of generated images.
summary.tldr: DiffusionPID separates individual and interacting token contributions to diagnose how text prompts shape diffusion-generated images.

title: Diffusion PID: Interpreting Diffusion via Partial Information Decomposition

abstract: Inverse molecular design with diffusion models holds great potential for advancements in material and drug discovery. Despite success in unconditional molecule generation, integrating multiple properties such as synthetic score and gas permeability as condition constraints into diffusion models remains unexplored. We present the Graph Diffusion Transformer (Graph DiT) for multi-conditional molecular generation. Graph DiT has a condition encoder to learn the representation of numerical and categorical properties and utilizes a Transformer-based graph denoiser to achieve molecular graph denoising under conditions. Unlike previous graph diffusion models that add noise separately on the atoms and bonds in the forward diffusion process, we propose a graph-dependent noise model for training Graph DiT, designed to accurately estimate graph-related noise in molecules. We extensively validate the Graph DiT for multi-conditional polymer and small molecule generation. Results demonstrate our superiority across metrics from distribution learning to condition control for molecular properties. A polymer inverse design task for gas separation with feedback from domain experts further demonstrates its practical utility. The code is available at https://github.com/liugangcode/Graph-DiT.

paragraphs: Inverse molecular design starts with desired properties and seeks molecules that satisfy them. The paper addresses how diffusion models can generate molecular graphs while accounting for several property constraints at once. Examples include synthetic score and gas permeability, making the task more directed than generating molecules without requested properties.

Graph DiT combines a condition encoder with a Transformer-based graph denoiser. The encoder represents both numerical and categorical property requirements, while the denoiser uses those representations during molecular generation. The authors also introduce graph-dependent noise for training, departing from approaches that add noise independently to atoms and bonds. This design aims to better account for noise associated with molecular graph structure.

Evaluations cover multi-conditional generation of polymers and small molecules. The authors report stronger results across measures of distribution learning and control over molecular properties. A polymer design task for gas separation, incorporating feedback from domain experts, further demonstrates practical utility. Together, these findings support combining property conditioning with graph-aware diffusion when searching for molecules with multiple requested characteristics.
summary.tldr: Graph DiT combines multiple property conditions with graph-dependent diffusion to improve controlled generation of polymers and small molecules.

title: Graph Diffusion Transformers for Multi-Conditional Molecular Generation

abstract: This paper introduces the Quadratic Quantum Variational Monte Carlo (Q$^2$VMC) algorithm, an innovative algorithm in quantum chemistry that significantly enhances the efficiency and accuracy of solving the Schrödinger equation. Inspired by the discretization of imaginary-time Schrödinger evolution, Q$^2$VMC employs a novel quadratic update mechanism that integrates seamlessly with neural network-based ansatzes. Our extensive experiments showcase Q$^2$VMC's superior performance, achieving faster convergence and lower ground state energies in wavefunction optimization across various molecular systems, without additional computational cost. This study not only advances the field of computational quantum chemistry but also highlights the important role of discretized evolution in variational quantum algorithms, offering a scalable and robust framework for future quantum research.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Q²VMC, an algorithm for improving wavefunction optimization in quantum chemistry. The underlying goal is to solve the Schrödinger equation efficiently and accurately across molecular systems. Its contribution centers on changing the optimization update used with neural-network representations of wavefunctions.

The update is inspired by discretizing imaginary-time Schrödinger evolution: translating that evolution into computational steps motivates a quadratic update mechanism. Q²VMC is designed to integrate with neural-network ansatzes, the parameterized wavefunction forms being optimized. This connects the update rule to the structure of the underlying evolution rather than treating optimization as an unrelated component.

Across the molecular systems studied, the authors report faster convergence and lower ground-state energies without additional computational cost. Faster convergence means that the optimization reaches its result more quickly, while the reported energy improvements support the claimed gains in wavefunction optimization. The findings highlight discretized evolution as a useful source of algorithm design for variational quantum methods and motivate the proposed framework's further use in quantum-chemistry research.
summary.tldr: Q²VMC uses a quadratic update inspired by imaginary-time evolution to achieve faster wavefunction optimization and lower reported ground-state energies without added computational cost.

title: Quadratic Quantum Variational Monte Carlo

abstract: Alignment techniques are critical in ensuring that large language models (LLMs) output helpful and harmless content by enforcing the LLM-generated content to align with human preferences. However, the existence of noisy preferences (NPs), where the responses are mistakenly labelled as chosen or rejected, could spoil the alignment, thus making the LLMs generate useless and even malicious content. Existing methods mitigate the issue of NPs from the loss perspective by adjusting the alignment loss based on a clean validation dataset.Orthogonal to these loss-oriented methods, we propose perplexity-aware correction (PerpCorrect) from the data perspective for robust alignment which detects and corrects NPs based on the differences between the perplexity of the chosen and rejected responses (dubbed as PPLDiff). Intuitively, a higher PPLDiff indicates a higher probability of the NP because a rejected/chosen response which is mistakenly labelled as chosen/rejected is less preferable to be generated by an aligned LLM, thus having a higher/lower perplexity.PerpCorrect works in three steps: (1) PerpCorrect aligns a surrogate LLM using the clean validation data to make the PPLDiff able to distinguish clean preferences (CPs) and NPs. (2) PerpCorrect further aligns the surrogate LLM by incorporating the reliable clean training data whose PPLDiff is extremely small and reliable noisy training data whose PPLDiff is extremely large after correction to boost the discriminatory power.(3) Detecting and correcting NPs according to the PPLDiff obtained by the aligned surrogate LLM to obtain a denoised training dataset for robust alignment.Comprehensive experiments validate that our proposed PerpCorrect can achieve state-of-the-art alignment performance under NPs.Notably, PerpCorrect demonstrates practical utility by requiring only a modest amount of validation data and being compatible with various alignment techniques. Our code is available at [PerpCorrect](https://github.com/luxinyayaya/PerpCorrect).

paragraphs: Preference-based alignment can be undermined when desirable and undesirable responses are assigned the wrong labels. PerpCorrect addresses these errors by correcting the training data. Its central signal is the perplexity difference between chosen and rejected responses, measured using an aligned surrogate language model.

The method first aligns the surrogate on clean validation data so that this difference can help distinguish reliable preferences from mislabeled ones. It then strengthens the surrogate using highly reliable training examples: pairs with extremely small differences are treated as clean, while pairs with extremely large differences are incorporated after correction. The refined surrogate subsequently identifies and corrects noise across the training dataset.

The intuition is probabilistic: a larger perplexity difference suggests a greater chance that the preference labels are wrong, because an aligned model should be less inclined to generate an undesirable response. Experiments report leading alignment performance under noisy preferences. The method requires a modest amount of clean validation data and works with multiple alignment techniques, making data correction a complementary route to improving robustness.
summary.tldr: PerpCorrect uses an aligned surrogate model’s perplexity differences to detect and repair mislabeled preference pairs before alignment training.

title: Perplexity-aware Correction for Robust Alignment with Noisy Preferences

abstract: Verbal and visual-spatial information processing are two critical subsystems that activate different brain regions and often collaborate together for cognitive reasoning. Despite the rapid advancement of LLM-based reasoning, the mainstream frameworks, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and its variants, primarily focus on the verbal dimension, resulting in limitations in tackling reasoning problems with visual and spatial clues. To bridge the gap, we propose a novel dual-modality reasoning framework called Vision-Augmented Prompting (VAP). Upon receiving a textual problem description, VAP automatically synthesizes an image from the visual and spatial clues by utilizing external drawing tools. Subsequently, VAP formulates a chain of thought in both modalities and iteratively refines the synthesized image. Finally, a conclusive reasoning scheme based on self-alignment is proposed for final result generation. Extensive experiments are conducted across four versatile tasks, including solving geometry problems, Sudoku, time series prediction, and travelling salesman problem. The results validated the superiority of VAP over existing LLMs-based reasoning frameworks.

paragraphs: Many language-model reasoning methods organize their work entirely as text, even when a problem contains useful spatial or visual relationships. Vision-Augmented Prompting addresses this mismatch by giving the reasoning process a visual representation to work with. Its motivation is that verbal and visual-spatial processing can make complementary contributions to solving a problem.

Starting from a textual description, the framework extracts visual and spatial clues and uses external drawing tools to synthesize an image. It then develops a chain of thought across text and images, refining the image as reasoning proceeds. A final reasoning stage based on self-alignment produces the answer, making the visual component part of an iterative process.

The authors evaluate the framework on geometry problems, Sudoku, time-series prediction, and the travelling salesman problem. They report better results than the existing language-model reasoning frameworks evaluated. These findings support the value of constructing and revising visual representations for the tested tasks, extending reasoning beyond a purely verbal sequence of intermediate steps.
summary.tldr: Vision-Augmented Prompting turns spatial clues into revisable images and combines visual and textual reasoning to improve performance on four tasks.

title: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Vision-Augmented Prompting

abstract: The operations and maintenance of satellite networks heavily depend on traffic measurements. Due to the large-scale and highly dynamic nature of satellite networks, global measurement encounters significant challenges in terms of complexity and overhead. Estimating global network traffic data from partial traffic measurements is a promising solution. However, the majority of current estimation methods concentrate on low-rank linear decomposition, which is unable to accurately estimate. The reason lies in its inability to capture the intricate nonlinear spatio-temporal relationship found in large-scale, highly dynamic traffic data. This paper proposes Satformer, an accurate and robust method for estimating traffic data in satellite networks. In Satformer, we innovatively incorporate an adaptive sparse spatio-temporal attention mechanism. In the mechanism, more attention is paid to specific local regions of the input tensor to improve the model's sensitivity on details and patterns. This method enhances its capability to capture nonlinear spatio-temporal relationships. Experiments on small, medium, and large-scale satellite networks datasets demonstrate that Satformer outperforms mathematical and neural baseline methods notably. It provides substantial improvements in reducing errors and maintaining robustness, especially for larger networks. The approach shows promise for deployment in actual systems.

paragraphs: Satellite network operation depends on knowing traffic conditions, but measuring an entire large, rapidly changing network creates substantial overhead. Satformer tackles the alternative of estimating global traffic from partial measurements. The paper identifies nonlinear relationships across space and time as a central challenge for approaches based on low-rank linear decomposition.

Its proposed solution uses adaptive sparse spatio-temporal attention. The mechanism concentrates attention on selected local regions of the traffic tensor, increasing sensitivity to details and patterns within the measurements. This design aims to capture the nonlinear spatial and temporal relationships that are difficult to represent through the linear decomposition methods discussed in the paper.

Experiments use datasets for small, medium, and large satellite networks. The authors report lower estimation errors and better robustness than mathematical and neural baselines, with especially strong benefits for larger networks. These findings support the proposed attention mechanism as a way to reconstruct network-wide traffic from limited observations and suggest potential for deployment in actual systems.
summary.tldr: Satformer uses adaptive sparse attention to estimate satellite network traffic more accurately and robustly from partial measurements.

title: Satformer: Accurate and Robust Traffic Data Estimation for Satellite Networks

abstract: We consider the challenging problem of estimating causal effects from purely observational data in the bi-directional Mendelian randomization (MR), where some invalid instruments, as well as unmeasured confounding, usually exist. To address this problem, most existing methods attempt to find proper valid instrumental variables (IVs) for the target causal effect by expert knowledge or by assuming that the causal model is a one-directional MR model. As such, in this paper, we first theoretically investigate the identification of the bi-directional MR from observational data. In particular, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which valid IV sets are correctly identified such that the bi-directional MR model is identifiable, including the causal directions of a pair of phenotypes (i.e., the treatment and outcome).Moreover, based on the identification theory, we develop a cluster fusion-like method to discover valid IV sets and estimate the causal effects of interest.We theoretically demonstrate the correctness of the proposed algorithm.Experimental results show the effectiveness of our method for estimating causal effects in both one-directional and bi-directional MR models.

paragraphs: This paper studies causal effect estimation in bi-directional Mendelian randomization, where two phenotypes may influence one another. The setting is difficult because the data are observational, some candidate instruments are invalid, and unmeasured confounding may be present. Existing approaches often depend on expert selection of instruments or assume a one-directional causal model.

The authors first investigate identifiability: the conditions under which the observational data can determine the causal model. They provide necessary and sufficient conditions for correctly identifying valid instrument sets so that the bi-directional model, including causal directions between the two phenotypes, is identifiable. This makes instrument validity and direction discovery central parts of the analysis.

Using that theory, the paper develops a cluster fusion-like method to discover valid instrument sets and estimate the causal effects of interest. It provides a theoretical correctness result for the algorithm and reports effective estimation in experiments with both one-directional and bi-directional models. The contribution connects conditions for identifying the model to a concrete estimation procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes identification conditions and an estimation method for bi-directional Mendelian randomization with some invalid instruments.

title: Identification and Estimation of the Bi-Directional MR with Some Invalid Instruments

abstract: This paper investigates a novel lossy compression framework operating under logarithmic loss, designed to handle situations where the reconstruction distribution diverges from the source distribution. This framework is especially relevant for applications that require joint compression and retrieval, and in scenarios involving distributional shifts due to processing. We show that the proposed formulation extends the classical minimum entropy coupling framework by integrating a bottleneck, allowing for controlled variability in the degree of stochasticity in the coupling.We explore the decomposition of the Minimum Entropy Coupling with Bottleneck (MEC-B) into two distinct optimization problems: Entropy-Bounded Information Maximization (EBIM) for the encoder, and Minimum Entropy Coupling (MEC) for the decoder. Through extensive analysis, we provide a greedy algorithm for EBIM with guaranteed performance, and characterize the optimal solution near functional mappings, yielding significant theoretical insights into the structural complexity of this problem.Furthermore, we illustrated the practical application of MEC-B through experiments in Markov Coding Games (MCGs) under rate limits. These games simulate a communication scenario within a Markov Decision Process, where an agent must transmit a compressed message from a sender to a receiver through its actions. Our experiments highlighted the trade-offs between MDP rewards and receiver accuracy across various compression rates, showcasing the efficacy of our method compared to conventional compression baseline.

paragraphs: This paper studies lossy compression when reconstructed outputs follow a different distribution from the original source. Its formulation uses logarithmic loss and is motivated by settings combining compression with retrieval or involving distribution changes caused by processing. It extends minimum entropy coupling by adding a bottleneck that controls how much randomness the relationship between source and reconstruction can contain.

The authors divide the resulting problem into two parts. The encoder solves Entropy-Bounded Information Maximization, while the decoder solves a minimum entropy coupling problem. This separation makes the respective responsibilities explicit. For the encoder problem, they develop a greedy algorithm with a performance guarantee and analyze optimal solutions near functional mappings.

The results illustrate how changing the compression rate affects both task rewards and the receiver's accuracy, and show effectiveness relative to a conventional compression baseline. The framework thus connects compression structure with the competing demands of acting and communicating.
summary.tldr: MEC-B adds a bottleneck to minimum entropy coupling, separating encoder and decoder optimization for compression with differing source and reconstruction distributions.

title: Minimum Entropy Coupling with Bottleneck

abstract: The essence of multi-modal fusion lies in exploiting the complementary information inherent in diverse modalities.However, most prevalent fusion methods rely on traditional neural architectures and are inadequately equipped to capture the dynamics of interactions across modalities, particularly in presence of complex intra- and inter-modality correlations.Recent advancements in State Space Models (SSMs), notably exemplified by the Mamba model, have emerged as promising contenders. Particularly, its state evolving process implies stronger modality fusion paradigm, making multi-modal fusion on SSMs an appealing direction. However, fusing multiple modalities is challenging for SSMs due to its hardware-aware parallelism designs. To this end, this paper proposes the Coupled SSM model, for coupling state chains of multiple modalities while maintaining independence of intra-modality state processes. Specifically, in our coupled scheme, we devise an inter-modal hidden states transition scheme, in which the current state is dependent on the states of its own chain and that of the neighbouring chains at the previous time-step. To fully comply with the hardware-aware parallelism, we obtain the global convolution kernel by deriving the state equation while introducing the historical state.Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSEI, CH-SIMS, CH-SIMSV2 through multi-domain input verify the effectiveness of our model compared to current state-of-the-art methods, improved F1-Score by 0.4%, 0.9%, and 2.3% on the three datasets respectively, 49% faster inference and 83.7% GPU memory save. The results demonstrate that Coupled Mamba model is capable of enhanced multi-modal fusion.

paragraphs: Multimodal fusion combines complementary information from different input types. Coupled Mamba addresses the difficulty of modeling relationships both within each modality and across modalities as their internal states evolve. It uses state space models, whose changing hidden states offer a way to represent these interactions, while accounting for the parallel computation requirements that make Mamba efficient.

The architecture gives each modality its own state chain and couples those chains through their transitions. A current state depends on previous states from its own chain and neighboring chains, while the within-modality state processes retain their independence. The authors derive a global convolution kernel using historical state information to make this coupled formulation compatible with hardware-aware parallelism.

Experiments on CMU-MOSEI, CH-SIMS, and CH-SIMSV2 report F1 improvements of 0.4%, 0.9%, and 2.3%, respectively, over current leading methods. The abstract also reports 49% faster inference and 83.7% lower GPU memory use. These results support the proposed combination of richer cross-modal interaction modeling and efficient computation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Coupled Mamba connects modality-specific state chains to improve multimodal fusion while reporting faster inference and lower GPU memory use.

title: Coupled Mamba: Enhanced Multimodal Fusion with Coupled State Space Model

abstract: Global stability and robustness guarantees in learned dynamical systems are essential to ensure well-behavedness of the systems in the face of uncertainty. We present Extended Linearized Contracting Dynamics (ELCD), the first neural network-based dynamical system with global contractivity guarantees in arbitrary metrics. The key feature of ELCD is a parametrization of the extended linearization of the nonlinear vector field. In its most basic form, ELCD is guaranteed to be (i) globally exponentially stable, (ii) equilibrium contracting, and (iii) globally contracting with respect to some metric. To allow for contraction with respect to more general metrics in the data space, we train diffeomorphisms between the data space and a latent space and enforce contractivity in the latent space, which ensures global contractivity in the data space. We demonstrate the performance of ELCD on the high dimensional LASA, multi-link pendulum, and Rosenbrock datasets.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamical system involves modeling how a state changes over time, but a good fit alone does not establish stable behavior. This paper introduces Extended Linearized Contracting Dynamics, or ELCD, to give neural dynamical systems global contractivity guarantees. Contractivity concerns trajectories drawing closer under a chosen way of measuring distance, making the metric part of the guarantee.

ELCD builds its guarantees into a parameterization of the nonlinear vector field's extended linearization. In its basic form, the system is globally exponentially stable, contracts toward its equilibrium, and is globally contracting under some metric. These are properties of the construction, rather than conclusions drawn only from the observed trajectories in an experiment.

To support more general metrics in the data space, the authors learn diffeomorphisms: smooth, invertible transformations between data and latent spaces. They enforce contraction in the latent space, which ensures global contraction in the data space. Demonstrations use high-dimensional LASA, multi-link pendulum, and Rosenbrock datasets. The contribution combines learnable nonlinear dynamics with global guarantees, while using learned coordinate transformations to broaden the metrics those guarantees can accommodate.
summary.tldr: ELCD learns neural dynamical systems with global contraction guarantees using extended linearization and invertible transformations into a contracting latent space.

title: Learning Neural Contracting Dynamics: Extended Linearization and Global Guarantees

abstract: Distributed learning is essential to train machine learning algorithms across *heterogeneous* agents while maintaining data privacy. We conduct an asymptotic analysis of Unified Distributed SGD (UD-SGD), exploring a variety of communication patterns, including decentralized SGD and local SGD within Federated Learning (FL), as well as the increasing communication interval in the FL setting. In this study, we assess how different sampling strategies, such as *i.i.d.* sampling, shuffling, and Markovian sampling, affect the convergence speed of UD-SGD by considering the impact of agent dynamics on the limiting covariance matrix as described in the Central Limit Theorem (CLT). Our findings not only support existing theories on linear speedup and asymptotic network independence, but also theoretically and empirically show how efficient sampling strategies employed by individual agents contribute to overall convergence in UD-SGD. Simulations reveal that a few agents using highly efficient sampling can achieve or surpass the performance of the majority employing moderately improved strategies, providing new insights beyond traditional analyses focusing on the worst-performing agent.

paragraphs: Distributed learning combines updates from agents whose data and behavior may differ. This paper asks how each agent's sampling strategy influences the progress of the whole system. It studies Unified Distributed SGD across communication arrangements that include decentralized learning and local training in federated learning, including federated settings with increasing intervals between communications.

The analysis focuses on long-run behavior through the limiting covariance in a Central Limit Theorem. This describes the fluctuations relevant to convergence near the limiting solution. The authors compare independent sampling, shuffling, and Markovian sampling to understand how the dynamics of individual agents contribute to those fluctuations. Their results also support established conclusions about linear speedup and asymptotic network independence.

This challenges an exclusively worst-agent-centered interpretation without claiming that the weakest agent never matters.
summary.tldr: Long-run analysis and simulations show that a few agents with highly efficient sampling can substantially improve distributed SGD convergence.

title: Does Worst-Performing Agent Lead the Pack? Analyzing Agent Dynamics in Unified Distributed SGD

abstract: Going beyond mimicking limited human experiences, recent studies show initial evidence that, like humans, large language models (LLMs) are capable of improving their abilities purely by self-correction, i.e., correcting previous responses through self-examination, as seen in models like OpenAI o1. Nevertheless, little is known about how such capabilities arise. In this work, based on a simplified setup akin to an alignment task, we theoretically analyze self-correction from an in-context learning perspective, showing that when LLMs give relatively accurate self-examinations as rewards, they are capable of refining responses in an in-context way. Notably, going beyond previous theories on over-simplified linear transformers, our theoretical construction underpins the roles of several key designs of realistic transformers for self-correction: softmax attention, multi-head attention, and the MLP block. We validate these findings extensively on synthetic datasets. Inspired by these findings, we propose a simple self-correction strategy, Checking as Context (CaC), which finds novel applications in alleviating social bias and defending against LLM jailbreaks. We believe that these findings will inspire further research on understanding, exploiting, and enhancing self-correction for building better foundation models. Code is at https://github.com/yifeiwang77/Self-Correction.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a language model can improve an answer by examining its own earlier response. It studies self-correction as a form of in-context learning: the model uses information within the ongoing interaction to refine its output. The theoretical analysis uses a simplified setting resembling an alignment task.

The central result is conditional. When the model’s self-examinations provide relatively accurate rewards, the authors show that it can refine responses through context. Their construction also explains roles for softmax attention, multiple attention heads, and the transformer’s multilayer perceptron block. This connects the analysis to architectural components used in realistic transformers, extending beyond theories restricted to simplified linear versions.

The authors validate their findings on synthetic datasets and introduce Checking as Context, a self-correction strategy inspired by the analysis. They apply it to reducing social bias and resisting jailbreaks. These results support a specific account of self-correction in which sufficiently informative self-evaluation helps guide improvement; the accuracy of that evaluation remains central to the theoretical claim.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how relatively accurate self-evaluation can enable language models to improve responses through in-context learning.

title: A Theoretical Understanding of Self-Correction through In-context Alignment

abstract: We present NN4SysBench, a benchmark suite for neural network verification that is composed of applications from the domain of computer systems. We call these neural networks for computer systems or NN4Sys. NN4Sys is booming: there are many proposals for using neural networks in computer systems—for example, databases, OSes, and networked systems—many of which are safety critical. Neural network verification is a technique to formally verify whether neural networks satisfy safety properties. We however observe that NN4Sys has some unique characteristics that today’s verification tools overlook and have limited support. Therefore, this benchmark suite aims at bridging the gap between NN4Sys and the verification by using impactful NN4Sys applications as benchmarks to illustrate computer systems’ unique challenges. We also build a compatible version of NN4SysBench, so that today’s verifiers can also work on these benchmarks with approximately the same verification difficulties. The code is available at https://github.com/lydialin1212/NN4Sys_Benchmark.

paragraphs: Neural networks are increasingly proposed for use inside databases, operating systems, and networked systems. Many such applications are safety critical, making it useful to formally check whether their networks satisfy required properties. This paper argues that these computer-systems applications have characteristics that existing verification tools overlook or support only to a limited extent.

NN4SysBench assembles a benchmark suite from impactful applications in this area. Its purpose is to expose verification challenges through concrete systems workloads. By bringing these applications into a common suite, the authors create a basis for examining the gap between what systems need and what neural-network verification currently handles.

The paper also provides a compatible version of the benchmark that existing verifiers can process while retaining approximately the same verification difficulties. This makes the benchmark usable for present tools as well as relevant to future development. The contribution is evaluation infrastructure: it connects formal verification research with the distinctive requirements of neural networks deployed as components of computer systems.
summary.tldr: NN4SysBench brings computer-systems applications into neural-network verification benchmarks, including a version compatible with existing tools.

title: NN4SysBench: Characterizing Neural Network Verification for Computer Systems

abstract: Trained models are often composed with post-hoc transforms such as temperature scaling (TS), ensembling and stochastic weight averaging (SWA) to improve performance, robustness, uncertainty estimation, etc. However, such transforms are typically applied only after the base models have already been finalized by standard means. In this paper, we challenge this practice with an extensive empirical study. In particular, we demonstrate a phenomenon that we call post-hoc reversal, where performance trends are reversed after applying post-hoc transforms. This phenomenon is especially prominent in high-noise settings. For example, while base models overfit badly early in training, both ensembling and SWA favor base models trained for more epochs. Post-hoc reversal can also prevent the appearance of double descent and mitigate mismatches between test loss and test error seen in base models. Preliminary analyses suggest that these transforms induce reversal by suppressing the influence of mislabeled examples, exploiting differences in their learning dynamics from those of clean examples. Based on our findings, we propose post-hoc selection, a simple technique whereby post-hoc metrics inform model development decisions such as early stopping, checkpointing, and broader hyperparameter choices. Our experiments span real-world vision, language, tabular and graph datasets. On an LLM instruction tuning dataset, post-hoc selection results in >1.5x MMLU improvement compared to naive selection.

paragraphs: Models are often chosen before applying temperature scaling, ensembling, or stochastic weight averaging. This paper shows that such transformations can reverse the performance trends used to make the original choice. A model that looks worse before transformation may therefore be a better component of the final prediction system.

The authors call this phenomenon post-hoc reversal and find it especially prominent with high noise. For example, base models may overfit early even though ensembling and weight averaging favor longer training. Reversal can also remove the appearance of double descent and reduce disagreements between test loss and test error. Preliminary analysis suggests that suppressing the influence of mislabeled examples helps explain the behavior.

The proposed response is post-hoc selection: use performance after transformation to guide early stopping, checkpoint selection, and hyperparameter decisions. Experiments cover vision, language, tabular, and graph datasets. On one language-model instruction-tuning dataset, this approach produces more than a 1.5-fold MMLU improvement over naive selection. The practical lesson is to evaluate development choices in the form in which the model will ultimately be used.
summary.tldr: Post-training transformations can reverse model rankings, motivating selection based on the transformed system’s performance.

title: Post-Hoc Reversal: Are We Selecting Models Prematurely?

abstract: We aim to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) for embodied decision making. While a significant body of work has been leveraging LLMs for decision making in embodied environments, we still lack a systematic understanding of their performance because they are usually applied in different domains, for different purposes, and built based on different inputs and outputs. Furthermore, existing evaluations tend to rely solely on a final success rate, making it difficult to pinpoint what ability is missing in LLMs and where the problem lies, which in turn blocks embodied agents from leveraging LLMs effectively and selectively. To address these limitations, we propose a generalized interface (Embodied Agent Interface) that supports the formalization of various types of tasks and input-output specifications of LLM-based modules. Specifically, it allows us to unify 1) a broad set of embodied decision-making tasks involving both state and temporally extended goals, 2) four commonly-used LLM-based modules for decision making: goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, and transition modeling, and 3) a collection of fine-grained metrics that break down evaluation into error types, such as hallucination errors, affordance errors, and various types of planning errors. Overall, our benchmark offers a comprehensive assessment of LLMs’ performance for different subtasks, pinpointing the strengths and weaknesses in LLM-powered embodied AI systems and providing insights into the effective and selective use of LLMs in embodied decision making.

paragraphs: Evaluating language models as embodied decision makers is difficult when systems use different tasks, inputs, outputs, and responsibilities. A final success rate also hides why an agent failed. Embodied Agent Interface addresses these problems by providing a common way to formalize tasks and the specifications of language-model components.

The interface covers goals about states as well as goals extending over time. It organizes four common model responsibilities: interpreting goals, breaking them into subgoals, sequencing actions, and modeling transitions. This shared structure allows evaluation to focus on particular decision-making functions instead of treating the entire agent as one indivisible system.

Its metrics distinguish error types, including hallucinations, affordance errors, and several planning errors. The resulting benchmark is designed to reveal strengths and weaknesses at the subtask level. This matters for deciding where a language model can contribute effectively within an embodied system, because the same overall failure can arise from very different problems in understanding, planning, or predicting action outcomes.
summary.tldr: Embodied Agent Interface standardizes embodied decision-making evaluations and breaks failures down by model responsibility and error type.

title: Embodied Agent Interface: Benchmarking LLMs for Embodied Decision Making

abstract: Recent open-world 3D representation learning methods using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to align 3D point clouds with image-text information have shown superior 3D zero-shot performance. However, CAD-rendered images for this alignment often lack realism and texture variation, compromising alignment robustness. Moreover, the volume discrepancy between 3D and 2D pretraining datasets highlights the need for effective strategies to transfer the representational abilities of VLMs to 3D learning. In this paper, we present OpenDlign, a novel open-world 3D model using depth-aligned images generated from a diffusion model for robust multimodal alignment. These images exhibit greater texture diversity than CAD renderings due to the stochastic nature of the diffusion model. By refining the depth map projection pipeline and designing depth-specific prompts, OpenDlign leverages rich knowledge in pre-trained VLM for 3D representation learning with streamlined fine-tuning. Our experiments show that OpenDlign achieves high zero-shot and few-shot performance on diverse 3D tasks, despite only fine-tuning 6 million parameters on a limited ShapeNet dataset. In zero-shot classification, OpenDlign surpasses previous models by 8.0\% on ModelNet40 and 16.4\% on OmniObject3D. Additionally, using depth-aligned images for multimodal alignment consistently enhances the performance of other state-of-the-art models.

Depth-aligned images also consistently improve other evaluated models, suggesting that the alignment data contribute value beyond OpenDlign's own architecture.
summary.tldr: OpenDlign uses diffusion-generated, depth-aligned images to transfer vision-language knowledge into stronger 3D point-cloud representations.

title: OpenDlign: Open-World Point Cloud Understanding with Depth-Aligned Images

abstract: Human feedback is central to the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, open questions remain about the methods (how), domains (where), people (who) and objectives (to what end) of feedback processes. To navigate these questions, we introduce PRISM, a new dataset which maps the sociodemographics and stated preferences of 1,500 diverse participants from 75 countries, to their contextual preferences and fine-grained feedback in 8,011 live conversations with 21 LLMs. With PRISM, we contribute (i) wider geographic and demographic participation in feedback; (ii) census-representative samples for two countries (UK, US); and (iii) individualised ratings that link to detailed participant profiles, permitting personalisation and attribution of sample artefacts. We target subjective and multicultural perspectives on value-laden and controversial issues, where we expect interpersonal and cross-cultural disagreement. We use PRISM in three case studies to demonstrate the need for careful consideration of which humans provide alignment data.

paragraphs: Human feedback shapes language-model alignment, but whose feedback is collected matters when people disagree about desirable behavior. PRISM studies that issue by linking participants' backgrounds and stated preferences to their judgments during actual model conversations. It focuses on subjective, value-laden, and controversial topics where interpersonal and cultural differences are expected.

The dataset contains feedback from 1,500 participants across 75 countries, covering 8,011 live conversations with 21 language models. It includes samples representative of the census populations of the United Kingdom and United States. Individual ratings connect to detailed participant profiles, allowing researchers to investigate personalization and effects associated with the composition of the sample.

The authors use three case studies to demonstrate why alignment research should carefully consider the people providing its data. PRISM's contribution is both broader participation and a structure that preserves who expressed each preference in which context. This enables analysis of differences among people and groups that would be difficult to investigate from feedback disconnected from participant information.
summary.tldr: PRISM links diverse participants' profiles to conversational feedback, enabling analysis of whose preferences shape language-model alignment.

title: The PRISM Alignment Dataset: What Participatory, Representative and Individualised Human Feedback Reveals About the Subjective and Multicultural Alignment of Large Language Models

abstract: As machine learning (ML) models are increasingly used in social domains to make consequential decisions about humans, they often have the power to reshape data distributions. Humans, as strategic agents, continuously adapt their behaviors in response to the learning system. As populations change dynamically, ML systems may need frequent updates to ensure high performance. However, acquiring high-quality *human-annotated* samples can be highly challenging and even infeasible in social domains. A common practice to address this issue is using the model itself to annotate unlabeled data samples. This paper investigates the long-term impacts when ML models are retrained with *model-annotated* samples when they incorporate human strategic responses. We first formalize the interactions between strategic agents and the model and then analyze how they evolve under such dynamic interactions. We find that agents are increasingly likely to receive positive decisions as the model gets retrained, whereas the proportion of agents with positive labels may decrease over time. We thus propose a *refined retraining process* to stabilize the dynamics. Last, we examine how algorithmic fairness can be affected by these retraining processes and find that enforcing common fairness constraints at every round may not benefit the disadvantaged group in the long run. Experiments on (semi-)synthetic and real data validate the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: When a model makes decisions about people, those people may change their behavior in response. This changes the data the model encounters and can create pressure to retrain it. The paper studies what happens when new training labels come from the model itself, especially where obtaining high-quality human annotations is difficult.

The authors formalize the interaction between strategic people and repeated model retraining. In their analysis, people become increasingly likely to receive favorable decisions, even though the proportion with genuinely positive labels may decrease. This separates two quantities that can otherwise appear interchangeable: receiving a positive model decision and belonging to the positive underlying category.

The paper proposes a refined retraining process to stabilize these dynamics and also examines fairness over time. It finds that imposing common fairness constraints in every round may fail to benefit the disadvantaged group in the long run. Experiments using synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real data support the theoretical findings. The results make the evolving feedback between behavior, generated labels, and retraining central to evaluating such systems.
summary.tldr: Repeated retraining on model-generated labels can produce harmful feedback with strategic human behavior, motivating a more stable retraining process.

title: Automating Data Annotation under Strategic Human Agents: Risks and Potential Solutions

abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative AI has raised significant questions regarding its ability to produce creative and novel outputs. Our recent work investigates this question within the domain of chess puzzles and presents an AI system designed to generate puzzles characterized by aesthetic appeal, novelty, counter-intuitive and unique solutions. We briefly outline our methodology, with a detailed discussion in the technical paper. To assess our system's creativity, we presented a curated booklet of AI-generated puzzles to three world-renowned experts: International Master for chess compositions Amatzia Avni, Grandmaster Jonathan Levitt, and Grandmaster Matthew Sadler. All three are noted authors on chess aesthetics and the evolving role of computers in the game. They were asked to select their favorites and explain what made them appealing, considering qualities such as their creativity, level of challenge, or aesthetic design. This paper compiles these selected puzzles, integrating expert analysis to explore the elements that render them counter-intuitive and beautiful.
