paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to convex optimization: simulated annealing, which uses random walks, and interior-point methods that follow a central path. The authors show that simulated annealing is directly equivalent, in a particular sense, to central-path optimization using the entropic universal barrier. The connection provides a way to transfer ideas between these methods.

One consequence is a new temperature schedule for simulated annealing, motivated by how interior-point algorithms follow their central paths. Under the membership-oracle model, where access to a convex set is through tests of whether points belong to it, this schedule improves the state-of-the-art time complexity for convex optimization.

A second consequence is an efficient randomized interior-point method with an efficiently computable universal barrier for any convex set described by a membership oracle. Previously, efficiently computable barriers were available only for particular convex sets. The importance of the equivalence is therefore algorithmic: it yields both a faster annealing approach and a broader way to construct usable interior-point methods.
summary.tldr: A qualified equivalence between simulated annealing and interior-point methods yields faster convex optimization and an efficiently computable universal barrier.

title: Faster Convex Optimization: Simulated Annealing with an Efficient Universal Barrier

abstract: A softmax operator applied to a set of values acts somewhat like the maximization function and somewhat like an average. In sequential decision making, softmax is often used in settings where it is necessary to maximize utility but also to hedge against problems that arise from putting all of one’s weight behind a single maximum utility decision. The Boltzmann softmax operator is the most commonly used softmax operator in this setting, but we show that this operator is prone to misbehavior. In this work, we study a differentiable softmax operator that, among other properties, is a non-expansion ensuring a convergent behavior in learning and planning. We introduce a variant of SARSA algorithm that, by utilizing the new operator, computes a Boltzmann policy with a state-dependent temperature parameter. We show that the algorithm is convergent and that it performs favorably in practice.

The Boltzmann softmax operator is the most commonly used softmax operator in this setting, but we show that this operator is prone to misbehavior. In this work, we study a differentiable softmax operator that, among other properties, is a non-expansion ensuring a convergent behavior in learning and planning. We introduce a variant of SARSA algorithm that, by utilizing the new operator, computes a Boltzmann policy with a state-dependent temperature parameter. We show that the algorithm is convergent and that it performs favorably in practice.

paragraphs: A softmax operator combines values in a way that lies between selecting the largest and taking an average. In sequential decision making, this can help favor high-value choices while avoiding complete commitment to a single option. The paper examines the commonly used Boltzmann softmax operator and shows that it can exhibit problematic behavior.

The authors study an alternative differentiable operator with a non-expansion property. In plain terms, applying it does not enlarge differences between value inputs. This mathematical feature supports convergent behavior in learning and planning, connecting the choice of value-combination rule to the stability of the larger decision-making procedure.

They also introduce a variant of SARSA that uses the new operator. The resulting algorithm computes a Boltzmann policy whose temperature varies by state, allowing the policy's degree of concentration to depend on the situation. The paper establishes convergence for this algorithm and reports favorable practical performance. Its contribution combines an operator-level property with a concrete learning algorithm built around that property.
summary.tldr: A differentiable, non-expanding softmax operator supports a convergent SARSA variant with state-dependent Boltzmann temperatures.

title: An Alternative Softmax Operator for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In value-based reinforcement learning methods such as deep Q-learning, function approximation errors are known to lead to overestimated value estimates and suboptimal policies. We show that this problem persists in an actor-critic setting and propose novel mechanisms to minimize its effects on both the actor and the critic. Our algorithm builds on Double Q-learning, by taking the minimum value between a pair of critics to limit overestimation. We draw the connection between target networks and overestimation bias, and suggest delaying policy updates to reduce per-update error and further improve performance. We evaluate our method on the suite of OpenAI gym tasks, outperforming the state of the art in every environment tested.
originalAbstract: In value-based reinforcement learning methods such as deep Q-learning, function approximation errors are known to lead to overestimated value estimates and suboptimal policies. We show that this problem persists in an actor-critic setting and propose novel mechanisms to minimize its effects on both the actor and the critic. Our algorithm builds on Double Q-learning, by taking the minimum value between a pair of critics to limit overestimation. We draw the connection between target networks and overestimation bias, and suggest delaying policy updates to reduce per-update error and further improve performance. We evaluate our method on the suite of OpenAI gym tasks, outperforming the state of the art in every environment tested.

paragraphs: An actor-critic learner uses estimated values to guide improvements to its policy. If those estimates are too optimistic, policy learning can follow misleading signals. This paper shows that overestimation caused by function approximation, already recognized in value-based reinforcement learning, also affects actor-critic methods. The problem therefore concerns both the accuracy of the critic and the decisions learned by the actor.

The proposed algorithm builds on Double Q-learning and uses the smaller estimate from two critics to limit overestimation. It also connects target networks with overestimation bias and proposes updating the policy less frequently. Delaying those updates is intended to reduce the error introduced at each policy update, complementing the more conservative use of critic estimates.

On the OpenAI Gym environments evaluated, the method outperforms the reported state of the art in every tested environment. These findings support addressing approximation error as a practical route to better actor-critic learning, with the empirical claim applying to the environments included in the evaluation.
summary.tldr: Using the smaller of two critic estimates and delaying policy updates reduces the effects of approximation error in actor-critic learning.

title: Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods

abstract: Backpropagation-based visualizations have been proposed to interpret convolutional neural networks (CNNs), however a theory is missing to justify their behaviors: Guided backpropagation (GBP) and deconvolutional network (DeconvNet) generate more human-interpretable but less class-sensitive visualizations than saliency map. Motivated by this, we develop a theoretical explanation revealing that GBP and DeconvNet are essentially doing (partial) image recovery which is unrelated to the network decisions. Specifically, our analysis shows that the backward ReLU introduced by GBP and DeconvNet, and the local connections in CNNs are the two main causes of compelling visualizations. Extensive experiments are provided that support the theoretical analysis.
originalAbstract: Backpropagation-based visualizations have been proposed to interpret convolutional neural networks (CNNs), however a theory is missing to justify their behaviors: Guided backpropagation (GBP) and deconvolutional network (DeconvNet) generate more human-interpretable but less class-sensitive visualizations than saliency map. Motivated by this, we develop a theoretical explanation revealing that GBP and DeconvNet are essentially doing (partial) image recovery which is unrelated to the network decisions. Specifically, our analysis shows that the backward ReLU introduced by GBP and DeconvNet, and the local connections in CNNs are the two main causes of compelling visualizations. Extensive experiments are provided that support the theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Visualizations of convolutional neural networks can look convincing without clearly explaining a prediction. This paper investigates a particular puzzle: guided backpropagation and DeconvNet tend to produce images that humans find easier to interpret, yet those images respond less to the chosen class than ordinary saliency maps do. The authors seek a theoretical explanation for that mismatch.

Their analysis finds that guided backpropagation and DeconvNet largely perform partial recovery of the input image, in a way unrelated to the network's decisions. Two ingredients explain the visually compelling results: the backward ReLU operation used by these methods and the local connections in convolutional networks. Those mechanisms help explain why recognizable image content can appear in the visualization.

The paper supports its theoretical account with extensive experiments. The central implication is that visual clarity alone does not establish that a method explains a classifier's decision. For the methods studied, an appealing reconstruction of image content can account for interpretability to a human viewer while also explaining weak sensitivity to the predicted class.
summary.tldr: The paper explains why guided backpropagation and DeconvNet can produce compelling images through partial image recovery unrelated to network decisions.

title: A Theoretical Explanation for Perplexing Behaviors of Backpropagation-based Visualizations

abstract: Off-policy learning is key to scaling up reinforcement learning as it allows to learn about a target policy from the experience generated by a different behavior policy. Unfortunately, it has been challenging to combine off-policy learning with function approximation and multi-step bootstrapping in a way that leads to both stable and efficient algorithms. In this work, we show that the Tree Backup and Retrace algorithms are unstable with linear function approximation, both in theory and in practice with specific examples. Based on our analysis, we then derive stable and efficient gradient-based algorithms using a quadratic convex-concave saddle-point formulation. By exploiting the problem structure proper to these algorithms, we are able to provide convergence guarantees and finite-sample bounds. The applicability of our new analysis also goes beyond Tree Backup and Retrace and allows us to provide new convergence rates for the GTD and GTD2 algorithms without having recourse to projections or Polyak averaging.

Unfortunately, it has been challenging to combine off-policy learning with function approximation and multi-step bootstrapping in a way that leads to both stable and efficient algorithms. In this work, we show that the Tree Backup and Retrace algorithms are unstable with linear function approximation, both in theory and in practice with specific examples. Based on our analysis, we then derive stable and efficient gradient-based algorithms using a quadratic convex-concave saddle-point formulation. By exploiting the problem structure proper to these algorithms, we are able to provide convergence guarantees and finite-sample bounds. The applicability of our new analysis also goes beyond Tree Backup and Retrace and allows us to provide new convergence rates for the GTD and GTD2 algorithms without having recourse to projections or Polyak averaging.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses experience from one behavior policy to learn about another target policy. Combining this with function approximation and updates that use multiple time steps can be difficult to stabilize. This paper shows, through theoretical analysis and concrete practical examples, that Tree Backup and Retrace can be unstable with linear function approximation.

The authors use that analysis to derive stable, efficient algorithms based on gradients. Their construction expresses the learning problem as a quadratic convex-concave saddle-point problem. This mathematical structure lets them establish convergence guarantees and finite-sample bounds, connecting the proposed update rules to explicit statements about their learning behavior.

The analysis also extends beyond the two motivating algorithms. It yields new convergence rates for GTD and GTD2 without requiring projections or Polyak averaging. The contribution thus includes both a diagnosis of instability in existing methods and an analytical route to alternatives whose convergence can be established for the studied function-approximation setting.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes instability in Tree Backup and Retrace with linear approximation and derives gradient-based alternatives with convergence guarantees.

title: Convergent Tree Backup and Retrace with Function Approximation

abstract: In order to make good decision under uncertainty an agent must learn from observations. To do so, two of the most common frameworks are Contextual Bandits and Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). In this paper, we study whether there exist algorithms for the more general framework (MDP) which automatically provide the best performance bounds for the specific problem at hand without user intervention and without modifying the algorithm. In particular, it is found that a very minor variant of a recently proposed reinforcement learning algorithm for MDPs already matches the best possible regret bound $\tilde O (\sqrt{SAT})$ in the dominant term if deployed on a tabular Contextual Bandit problem despite the agent being agnostic to such setting.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits and Markov decision processes are two common ways to model learning through decisions under uncertainty. This paper asks whether an algorithm designed for the more general MDP setting can automatically enjoy stronger performance guarantees when the actual problem has the simpler structure of a contextual bandit.

When deployed on a tabular contextual bandit problem, it matches the best possible regret bound in the dominant term: approximately the square root of SAT, up to logarithmic factors. The agent does not need to be told that it is operating in the bandit setting.

The result shows that a general-purpose reinforcement learning procedure can adapt to this particular simpler structure without user intervention or a setting-specific algorithm change at deployment. Its precision matters: the optimality statement concerns the dominant regret term for tabular contextual bandits. This gives a concrete example of problem-dependent guarantees within a broader reinforcement learning framework.
summary.tldr: A small variant of an MDP learning algorithm achieves the optimal dominant regret term on tabular contextual bandits without knowing the setting.

title: Problem Dependent Reinforcement Learning Bounds Which Can Identify Bandit Structure in MDPs

abstract: We study the problem of learning-to-learn: infer- ring a learning algorithm that works well on a family of tasks sampled from an unknown distribution. As class of algorithms we consider Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) on the true risk regularized by the square euclidean distance from a bias vector. We present an average excess risk bound for such a learning algorithm that quantifies the potential benefit of using a bias vector with respect to the unbiased case. We then propose a novel meta-algorithm to estimate the bias term online from a sequence of observed tasks. The small memory footprint and low time complexity of our approach makes it appealing in practice while our theoretical analysis provides guarantees on the generalization properties of the meta-algorithm on new tasks. A key feature of our results is that, when the number of tasks grows and their vari- ance is relatively small, our learning-to-learn approach has a significant advantage over learning each task in isolation by standard SGD without a bias term. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in practice.

paragraphs: This paper studies how experience with earlier tasks can improve learning on new tasks drawn from an unknown distribution. They then introduce a meta-algorithm that estimates the bias online as tasks arrive. This identifies task relatedness as part of the setting supporting the benefit. Numerical experiments also demonstrate the method's effectiveness, complementing the theoretical account of when shared experience can help.
summary.tldr: An online meta-algorithm learns a shared regularization bias that can improve SGD on new tasks when enough sufficiently related tasks are available.

title: Learning-to-Learn Stochastic Gradient Descent with Biased Regularization

abstract: Generative models have proven to be an outstanding tool for representing high-dimensional probability distributions and generating realistic looking images. An essential characteristic of generative models is their ability to produce multi-modal outputs. However, while training, they are often susceptible to mode collapse, that is models are limited in mapping input noise to only a few modes of the true data distribution. In this work, we draw inspiration from Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to propose an unsupervised penalty loss that alleviates mode collapse while producing higher quality samples. DPP is an elegant probabilistic measure used to model negative correlations within a subset and hence quantify its diversity. We use DPP kernel to model the diversity in real data as well as in synthetic data. Then, we devise an objective term that encourages generator to synthesize data with a similar diversity to real data. In contrast to previous state-of-the-art generative models that tend to use additional trainable parameters or complex training paradigms, our method does not change the original training scheme. Embedded in an adversarial training and variational autoencoder, our Generative DPP approach shows a consistent resistance to mode-collapse on a wide-variety of synthetic data and natural image datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, and CelebA, while outperforming state-of-the-art methods for data-efficiency, generation quality, and convergence-time whereas being 5.8x faster than its closest competitor.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce plausible images while covering only a small portion of the variety in its training data. This failure, called mode collapse, limits its ability to represent a distribution with several distinct kinds of outputs. The paper introduces a penalty that encourages generated samples to reflect the diversity found in real samples.

The approach draws on determinantal point processes, which model negative correlations within a collection and thereby quantify diversity. It uses a DPP kernel to describe diversity in both real and generated data, then adds an objective term encouraging agreement between them. This supplies an unsupervised training signal while preserving the model’s original training scheme.

The authors incorporate Generative DPP into adversarial training and a variational autoencoder. Across synthetic and natural-image datasets, they report consistent resistance to mode collapse and improvements in data efficiency, generation quality, and convergence time. They also report being 5.8 times faster than the closest competitor in their comparison. These findings support diversity matching as a practical addition to the tested generative models.
summary.tldr: Generative DPP adds a diversity-matching penalty that reduces mode collapse and improves sample quality in the reported evaluations.

title: GDPP: Learning Diverse Generations using Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Domain adaptation enables knowledge transfer from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. A mainstream approach is adversarial feature adaptation, which learns domain-invariant representations through aligning the feature distributions of both domains. However, a theoretical prerequisite of domain adaptation is the adaptability measured by the expected risk of an ideal joint hypothesis over the source and target domains. In this respect, adversarial feature adaptation may potentially deteriorate the adaptability, since it distorts the original feature distributions when suppressing domain-specific variations. To this end, we propose Transferable Adversarial Training (TAT) to enable the adaptation of deep classifiers. The approach generates transferable examples to fill in the gap between the source and target domains, and adversarially trains the deep classifiers to make consistent predictions over the transferable examples. Without learning domain-invariant representations at the expense of distorting the feature distributions, the adaptability in the theoretical learning bound is algorithmically guaranteed. A series of experiments validate that our approach advances the state of the arts on a variety of domain adaptation tasks in vision and NLP, including object recognition, learning from synthetic to real data, and sentiment classification.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. A common strategy aligns their feature distributions. This paper highlights a potential problem: suppressing domain-specific variation can distort those distributions and worsen adaptability, measured through the expected risk of an ideal hypothesis shared by both domains.

Transferable Adversarial Training addresses this by generating examples that bridge the source and target domains. It then adversarially trains the classifier to make consistent predictions over those examples. The approach is designed to support transfer without relying on feature-distribution distortion to produce domain-invariant representations, and it algorithmically guarantees the adaptability component of the theoretical learning bound.

The authors report advances over state-of-the-art methods across these adaptation tasks. The contribution joins a concern about the theoretical conditions for successful transfer with a training procedure that directly addresses it, supported by empirical comparisons across different application types.
summary.tldr: Transferable Adversarial Training bridges domains with generated examples and prediction consistency while preserving adaptability in the theoretical bound.

title: Transferable Adversarial Training: A General Approach to Adapting Deep Classifiers

abstract: The pioneering work of sparse local embeddings for extreme classification (SLEEC) (Bhatia et al., 2015) has shown great promise in multi-label learning. Unfortunately, the statistical rate of convergence and oracle property of SLEEC are still not well understood. To fill this gap, we present a unified framework for SLEEC with nonconvex penalty. Theoretically, we rigorously prove that our proposed estimator enjoys oracle property (i.e., performs as well as if the underlying model were known beforehand), and obtains a desirable statistical convergence rate. Moreover, we show that under a mild condition on the magnitude of the entries in the underlying model, we are able to obtain an improved convergence rate. Extensive numerical experiments verify our theoretical findings and the superiority of our proposed estimator.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label learning must predict relevant labels from a very large label set. Sparse local embeddings, exemplified by SLEEC, had shown strong practical promise, but their statistical convergence and oracle behavior were not well understood. This paper builds a theoretical framework for a related estimator with nonconvex regularization.

The proposed framework combines the SLEEC setting with a nonconvex penalty. The authors prove an oracle property, meaning that the estimator can perform as well as if the underlying model were known beforehand in the formal setting analyzed. They also establish a statistical convergence rate and show that an additional condition on the sizes of underlying model entries yields an improved rate.

Extensive numerical experiments support the theory and show advantages over the compared estimators. The work therefore adds statistical justification to a successful approach for large label spaces while proposing an estimator with favorable measured behavior. The oracle statement is a conditional theoretical property, not a claim that the algorithm is given the true model during training.
summary.tldr: A nonconvex sparse-embedding estimator for extreme multi-label learning gains oracle and convergence guarantees.

title: Sparse Extreme Multi-label Learning with Oracle Property

abstract: We propose a new class of probabilistic neural-symbolic models, that have symbolic functional programs as a latent, stochastic variable. Instantiated in the context of visual question answering, our probabilistic formulation offers two key conceptual advantages over prior neural-symbolic models for VQA. Firstly, the programs generated by our model are more understandable while requiring less number of teaching examples. Secondly, we show that one can pose counterfactual scenarios to the model, to probe its beliefs on the programs that could lead to a specified answer given an image. Our results on the CLEVR and SHAPES datasets verify our hypotheses, showing that the model gets better program (and answer) prediction accuracy even in the low data regime, and allows one to probe the coherence and consistency of reasoning performed.

paragraphs: This paper develops visual question-answering models in which symbolic programs are latent stochastic variables. The program represents a reasoning procedure, while the probabilistic formulation allows uncertainty over which program applies. This gives the model an explicit reasoning structure that can be examined alongside its predicted answer.

The authors identify two advantages over prior neural-symbolic approaches. The generated programs are more understandable while requiring fewer teaching examples, and the model supports counterfactual questions about which programs could produce a specified answer for a given image. Such queries allow inspection of the model's beliefs about possible reasoning paths, extending interpretation beyond reading a single predicted program.

Results on CLEVR and SHAPES support these claims. The model improves program and answer prediction accuracy even when data are limited, and its probabilistic structure allows the coherence and consistency of reasoning to be probed. The contribution therefore combines predictive learning with a way to investigate how alternative symbolic explanations relate to the image and the proposed answer.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic symbolic programs improve reported visual question-answering accuracy and enable counterfactual inspection of reasoning.

title: Probabilistic Neural Symbolic Models for Interpretable Visual Question Answering

abstract: Monte Carlo (MC) permutation test is considered the gold standard for statistical hypothesis testing, especially when standard parametric assumptions are not clear or likely to fail. However, in modern data science settings where a large number of hypothesis tests need to be performed simultaneously, it is rarely used due to its prohibitive computational cost. In genome-wide association studies, for example, the number of hypothesis tests $m$ is around $10^6$ while the number of MC samples $n$ for each test could be greater than $10^8$, totaling more than $nm$=$10^{14}$ samples. In this paper, we propose \texttt{A}daptive \texttt{M}C multiple \texttt{T}esting (\texttt{AMT}) to estimate MC p-values and control false discovery rate in multiple testing. The algorithm outputs the same result as the standard full MC approach with high probability while requiring only $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}m)$ samples. This sample complexity is shown to be optimal. On a Parkinson GWAS dataset, the algorithm reduces the running time from 2 months for full MC to an hour. The \texttt{AMT} algorithm is derived based on the theory of multi-armed bandits.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo permutation tests can support statistical testing when standard parametric assumptions are uncertain or unsuitable. Their computational burden becomes severe when many hypotheses must be tested together: a large simulation budget for each test is multiplied across the entire collection. The paper addresses this scaling problem while retaining the multiple-testing decisions of a full Monte Carlo procedure with high probability.

The proposed Adaptive Monte Carlo Multiple Testing algorithm, AMT, draws on multi-armed bandit theory to allocate simulation effort adaptively. It estimates Monte Carlo p-values and controls the false discovery rate. Its stated sample requirement scales as roughly the number of hypotheses times the square root of the full per-test budget, with logarithmic factors suppressed, rather than their direct product.

The authors prove that this sample complexity is optimal and that AMT agrees with the full procedure with high probability. On a Parkinson genome-wide association dataset, they report reducing runtime from two months to one hour. The result demonstrates that adaptive simulation can make an otherwise costly testing procedure practical while providing a probabilistic agreement guarantee.
summary.tldr: AMT adaptively allocates Monte Carlo samples to reproduce full multiple-testing results with high probability at substantially lower computational cost.

title: Adaptive Monte Carlo Multiple Testing via Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We study Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method with constant step-size and momentum parameters in the stochastic approximation setting (unbiased gradients with bounded variance) and the finite-sum setting (where randomness is due to sampling mini-batches). To build better insight into the behavior of Nesterov’s method in stochastic settings, we focus throughout on objectives that are smooth, strongly-convex, and twice continuously differentiable. In the stochastic approximation setting, Nesterov’s method converges to a neighborhood of the optimal point at the same accelerated rate as in the deterministic setting. Perhaps surprisingly, in the finite-sum setting, we prove that Nesterov’s method may diverge with the usual choice of step-size and momentum, unless additional conditions on the problem related to conditioning and data coherence are satisfied. Our results shed light as to why Nesterov’s method may fail to converge or achieve acceleration in the finite-sum setting.

paragraphs: Nesterov's accelerated gradient method is designed to speed optimization, but randomness can change its convergence behavior. This paper studies the method with fixed step size and momentum in two stochastic settings. Throughout, the objective is assumed to be smooth, strongly convex, and twice continuously differentiable, giving the analysis a specific mathematical scope.

In stochastic approximation, gradients are unbiased and have bounded variance. Under this setup, the method approaches a neighborhood of the optimum at the same accelerated rate as in the deterministic setting. The neighborhood qualification matters: the result describes accelerated approach near the solution in the presence of gradient noise.

The finite-sum setting, where randomness comes from sampling mini-batches, behaves differently. With the usual step-size and momentum choices, the method may diverge unless additional conditions involving conditioning and data coherence hold. These results help explain why acceleration or even convergence can fail in mini-batch optimization despite the objective satisfying the stated smoothness and convexity assumptions.
summary.tldr: Nesterov's method approaches an optimum neighborhood quickly under bounded-variance unbiased noise, but usual parameters can cause divergence in finite-sum settings.

title: On the Convergence of Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient Method in Stochastic Settings

abstract: Retrosynthetic planning is a critical task in organic chemistry which identifies a series of reactions that can lead to the synthesis of a target product. The vast number of possible chemical transformations makes the size of the search space very big, and retrosynthetic planning is challenging even for experienced chemists. However, existing methods either require expensive return estimation by rollout with high variance, or optimize for search speed rather than the quality. In this paper, we propose Retro*, a neural-based A*-like algorithm that finds high-quality synthetic routes efficiently. It maintains the search as an AND-OR tree, and learns a neural search bias with off-policy data. Then guided by this neural network, it performs best-first search efficiently during new planning episodes. Experiments on benchmark USPTO datasets show that, our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art with respect to both the success rate and solution quality, while being more efficient at the same time.

These findings support combining learned guidance with structured search to address route quality and computational effort together. The reported contribution is an efficient method for finding high-quality synthetic routes, supported by benchmark comparisons on all three aspects.
summary.tldr: Retro* uses neural guidance within an A*-like search to find better synthetic routes more efficiently on USPTO benchmarks.

title: Retro*: Learning Retrosynthetic Planning with Neural Guided A* Search

abstract: We propose a neural network-based approach that computes a stable and generalizing metric (LSiM) to compare data from a variety of numerical simulation sources. We focus on scalar time-dependent 2D data that commonly arises from motion and transport-based partial differential equations (PDEs). Our method employs a Siamese network architecture that is motivated by the mathematical properties of a metric. We leverage a controllable data generation setup with PDE solvers to create increasingly different outputs from a reference simulation in a controlled environment. A central component of our learned metric is a specialized loss function that introduces knowledge about the correlation between single data samples into the training process. To demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing metrics for vector spaces and other learned, image-based metrics, we evaluate the different methods on a large range of test data. Additionally, we analyze generalization benefits of an adjustable training data difficulty and demonstrate the robustness of LSiM via an evaluation on three real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Comparing numerical simulations requires a measure of how different their outputs are. This paper learns such a measure, called LSiM, for scalar, time-dependent two-dimensional data, particularly data from motion and transport equations. The goal is a comparison method that remains stable and generalizes across simulation sources.

The method uses a Siamese neural network architecture motivated by mathematical properties of a metric. Training data come from a controlled simulation setup that produces outputs increasingly different from a reference. A specialized loss incorporates information about correlations among samples, allowing training to use relationships across the generated data rather than only isolated comparisons.

Across a broad collection of test data, the authors report better performance than existing vector-space metrics and learned image-based metrics. They also examine how adjustable training-data difficulty affects generalization and demonstrate robustness on three real-world datasets. The work shows how controlled simulation generation and a relationship-aware training objective can support learning a useful measure of similarity for this type of numerical output.
summary.tldr: LSiM learns simulation similarity from controlled PDE outputs and sample relationships, outperforming comparison metrics in the reported evaluations.

title: Learning Similarity Metrics for Numerical Simulations

abstract: Optimization models with non-convex constraints arise in many tasks in machine learning, e.g., learning with fairness constraints or Neyman-Pearson classification with non-convex loss. Although many efficient methods have been developed with theoretical convergence guarantees for non-convex unconstrained problems, it remains a challenge to design provably efficient algorithms for problems with non-convex functional constraints. This paper proposes a class of subgradient methods for constrained optimization where the objective function and the constraint functions are weakly convex and nonsmooth. Our methods solve a sequence of strongly convex subproblems, where a quadratic regularization term is added to both the objective function and each constraint function. Each subproblem can be solved by various algorithms for strongly convex optimization. Under a uniform Slater’s condition, we establish the computation complexities of our methods for finding a nearly stationary point.

paragraphs: Nonconvex constraints arise in learning problems such as fairness-constrained optimization and Neyman-Pearson classification with nonconvex loss. These constraints make it difficult to extend convergence guarantees from unconstrained optimization. This paper considers problems where both the objective and constraint functions are weakly convex and may be nonsmooth.

The proposed subgradient methods replace the original task with a sequence of strongly convex subproblems. To construct each one, the methods add quadratic regularization to the objective and to every constraint function. Each resulting subproblem can then be handled by various algorithms designed for strongly convex optimization, providing flexibility in how the inner problems are solved.

Under a uniform Slater’s condition, the authors establish computational complexity guarantees for reaching a nearly stationary point. The assumption is part of the stated theoretical result, and the target is near stationarity. The contribution supplies an analyzed route for handling nonsmooth objectives and nonconvex functional constraints together through a sequence of more tractable optimization problems.
summary.tldr: Quadratic regularization yields strongly convex subproblems and conditional complexity guarantees for weakly convex, nonsmooth constrained optimization.

title: Quadratically Regularized Subgradient Methods for Weakly Convex Optimization with Weakly Convex Constraints

abstract: Policies for partially observed Markov decision processes can be efficiently learned by imitating expert policies generated using asymmetric information. Unfortunately, existing approaches for this kind of imitation learning have a serious flaw: the expert does not know what the trainee cannot see, and as a result may encourage actions that are sub-optimal or unsafe under partial information. To address this issue, we derive an update which, when applied iteratively to an expert, maximizes the expected reward of the trainee’s policy. Using this update, we construct a computationally efficient algorithm, adaptive asymmetric DAgger (A2D), that jointly trains the expert and trainee policies. We then show that A2D allows the trainee to safely imitate the modified expert, and outperforms policies learned either by imitating a fixed expert or through direct reinforcement learning.

Using this update, we construct a computationally efficient algorithm, adaptive asymmetric DAgger (A2D), that jointly trains the expert and trainee policies. We then show that A2D allows the trainee to safely imitate the modified expert, and outperforms policies learned either by imitating a fixed expert or through direct reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: An agent with partial observations can learn by imitating an expert that has access to more information. However, this information advantage creates a problem: an expert may recommend an action whose value depends on details the trainee cannot observe. Existing asymmetric imitation approaches can consequently encourage behavior that is suboptimal or unsafe for the trainee.

The paper derives an update that adapts the expert to this information mismatch. Applied iteratively, the update maximizes the expected reward of the trainee’s policy. The authors use it to build adaptive asymmetric DAgger, or A2D, a computationally efficient algorithm that trains the expert and trainee together rather than treating the expert’s behavior as fixed.

The authors show that the trainee can safely imitate the modified expert and that A2D outperforms learning from a fixed expert or through direct reinforcement learning. The central contribution is to make the teacher responsive to what the learner can perceive. This aligns the demonstration policy with the information available when the trainee must actually choose an action.
summary.tldr: A2D jointly adapts an informed expert and a partially observing trainee so the expert supplies behavior the trainee can safely imitate.

title: Robust Asymmetric Learning in POMDPs

abstract: Data-parallel distributed training (DDT) has become the de-facto standard for accelerating the training of most deep learning tasks on massively parallel hardware. In the DDT paradigm, the communication overhead of gradient synchronization is the major efficiency bottleneck. A widely adopted approach to tackle this issue is gradient sparsification (GS). However, the current GS methods introduce significant new overhead in compressing the gradients, outweighing the communication overhead and becoming the new efficiency bottleneck. In this paper, we propose DRAGONN, a randomized hashing algorithm for GS in DDT. DRAGONN can significantly reduce the compression time by up to 70% compared to state-of-the-art GS approaches, and achieve up to 3.52x speedup in total training throughput.

paragraphs: Data-parallel training spreads neural-network training across multiple computing devices. The devices must synchronize their gradients, and that communication can become a major obstacle to faster training. Gradient sparsification addresses the problem by reducing the gradient information that needs to be communicated, making synchronization less demanding.

However, producing the compressed gradients also takes computation. The paper identifies this compression work as a substantial overhead in existing sparsification methods: the effort spent preparing a smaller message can outweigh the communication benefit. DRAGONN addresses this part of the process with a randomized hashing algorithm for gradient sparsification. Its purpose is to make compression itself fast enough to improve the complete training workflow.

The reported results show compression-time reductions of up to 70% compared with state-of-the-art sparsification approaches, alongside total training throughput improvements of up to 3.52 times. These are reported maximum gains, rather than guarantees for every training configuration. The findings emphasize that distributed-training efficiency depends on both communication volume and the computational cost of achieving that reduction.
summary.tldr: DRAGONN uses randomized hashing to accelerate gradient compression, reporting up to 3.52 times higher distributed-training throughput.

title: DRAGONN: Distributed Randomized Approximate Gradients of Neural Networks

abstract: Major Internet advertising platforms offer budget pacing tools as a standard service for advertisers to manage their ad campaigns. Given the inherent non-stationarity in an advertiser’s value and also competing advertisers’ values over time, a commonly used approach is to learn a target expenditure plan that specifies a target spend as a function of time, and then run a controller that tracks this plan. This raises the question: how many historical samples are required to learn a good expenditure plan ? We study this question by considering an advertiser repeatedly participating in $T$ second-price auctions, where the tuple of her value and the highest competing bid is drawn from an unknown time-varying distribution. The advertiser seeks to maximize her total utility subject to her budget constraint. Prior work has shown the sufficiency of $T\log T$ samples per distribution to achieve the optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$-regret. We dramatically improve this state-of-the-art and show that just one sample per distribution is enough to achieve the near-optimal $\tilde O(\sqrt{T})$-regret, while still being robust to noise in the sampling distributions.

paragraphs: An advertiser must spread a limited budget across auctions whose opportunities change over time. A common strategy first learns a target spending plan and then uses a controller to follow it. This paper asks how much historical information is sufficient to learn a good plan when both the advertiser’s value and competing bids are non-stationary.

The analysis considers T second-price auctions. At each time, the advertiser’s value and the highest competing bid come from an unknown, time-varying distribution. The goal is to maximize total utility without exceeding the budget. Earlier work established that T log T samples from each distribution suffice for an optimal regret rate proportional to the square root of T.

The paper shows that one sample from each distribution is sufficient for a near-optimal square-root regret rate, up to logarithmic factors. It also establishes robustness to noise in the sampling distributions. The reduction concerns samples per time-specific distribution, not one sample for the entire auction sequence, making the result a substantial reduction in historical-data requirements within the stated model.
summary.tldr: One sample per time-varying auction distribution suffices for near-optimal budget-pacing regret, with robustness to sampling-distribution noise.

title: Robust Budget Pacing with a Single Sample

abstract: To achieve scalable and accurate inference for latent Gaussian processes, we propose a variational approximation based on a family of Gaussian distributions whose covariance matrices have sparse inverse Cholesky (SIC) factors. We combine this variational approximation of the posterior with a similar and efficient SIC-restricted Kullback-Leibler-optimal approximation of the prior. We then focus on a particular SIC ordering and nearest-neighbor-based sparsity pattern resulting in highly accurate prior and posterior approximations. For this setting, our variational approximation can be computed via stochastic gradient descent in polylogarithmic time per iteration. We provide numerical comparisons showing that the proposed double-Kullback-Leibler-optimal Gaussian-process approximation (DKLGP) can sometimes be vastly more accurate for stationary kernels than alternative approaches such as inducing-point and mean-field approximations at similar computational complexity.

This paper proposes a variational family of Gaussian distributions whose covariance matrices have sparse inverse Cholesky factors. The sparse factor structure provides a way to restrict the computation while still representing dependencies within the Gaussian distribution.

The method approximates both the posterior and the prior using related sparse structures and Kullback–Leibler objectives. This pairing gives the approach its name, double-Kullback–Leibler-optimal Gaussian-process approximation, or DKLGP. Numerical comparisons show that, with stationary kernels, DKLGP can sometimes be vastly more accurate than inducing-point or mean-field alternatives at similar computational complexity. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is possible and empirically demonstrated, while the efficient computation result depends on the selected sparse construction.
summary.tldr: DKLGP sparsely approximates both Gaussian-process prior and posterior, sometimes delivering much higher accuracy at comparable computational cost.

title: Variational Sparse Inverse Cholesky Approximation for Latent Gaussian Processes via Double Kullback-Leibler Minimization

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are able to achieve high classification accuracy on many important real world datasets, but provide no rigorous notion of predictive uncertainty. Quantifying the confidence of GNN models is difficult due to the dependence between datapoints induced by the graph structure. We leverage recent advances in conformal prediction to construct prediction sets for node classification in inductive learning scenarios. We do this by taking an existing approach for conformal classification that relies on exchangeable data and modifying it by appropriately weighting the conformal scores to reflect the network structure. We show through experiments on standard benchmark datasets using popular GNN models that our approach provides tighter and better calibrated prediction sets than a naive application of conformal prediction.

We do this by taking an existing approach for conformal classification that relies on exchangeable data and modifying it by appropriately weighting the conformal scores to reflect the network structure. We show through experiments on standard benchmark datasets using popular GNN models that our approach provides tighter and better calibrated prediction sets than a naive application of conformal prediction.

paragraphs: A graph neural network can classify nodes accurately without giving a rigorous account of uncertainty in individual predictions. This paper addresses that gap by constructing prediction sets: collections of candidate labels for a node. The focus is inductive node classification, where uncertainty must be handled while accounting for the relationships encoded by the graph.

The authors adapt an existing conformal classification approach that relies on exchangeable data. Graph connections induce dependence between observations, making a direct application difficult. Their modification weights the conformal scores to reflect network structure, allowing the construction of prediction sets to incorporate information about how the observations are related.

Experiments using popular graph neural networks on standard benchmark datasets produce tighter and better calibrated prediction sets than a naive application of conformal prediction. Tighter sets narrow the candidate labels, while better calibration improves how well the sets reflect uncertainty. The reported result is an empirical improvement from making conformal scoring sensitive to graph structure, rather than treating connected observations as interchangeable inputs.
summary.tldr: Weighting conformal scores by graph structure yields tighter, better calibrated node-classification prediction sets in benchmark experiments.

title: Distribution Free Prediction Sets for Node Classification

abstract: This paper reveals a new appeal of the recently emerged large-kernel Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets): as the teacher in Knowledge Distillation (KD) for small-kernel ConvNets. While Transformers have led state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in various fields with ever-larger models and labeled data, small-kernel ConvNets are considered more suitable for resource-limited applications due to the efficient convolution operation and compact weight sharing. KD is widely used to boost the performance of small-kernel ConvNets. However, previous research shows that it is not quite effective to distill knowledge (e.g., global information) from Transformers to small-kernel ConvNets, presumably due to their disparate architectures. We hereby carry out a first-of-its-kind study unveiling that modern large-kernel ConvNets, a compelling competitor to Vision Transformers, are remarkably more effective teachers for small-kernel ConvNets, due to more similar architectures. Our findings are backed up by extensive experiments on both logit-level and feature-level KD "out of the box", with no dedicated architectural nor training recipe modifications. Notably, we obtain the best-ever pure ConvNet under 30M parameters with 83.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, outperforming current SOTA methods including ConvNeXt V2 and Swin V2. We also find that beneficial characteristics of large-kernel ConvNets, e.g., larger effective receptive fields, can be seamlessly transferred to students through this large-to-small kernel distillation. Code is available at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/SLaK.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network using information from a teacher. This paper asks which teachers work well for small-kernel convolutional networks, which are attractive for resource-limited applications. Transferring knowledge from Transformers has previously been less effective, with architectural differences suggested as a reason.

The authors study large-kernel convolutional networks as teachers and find them substantially more effective for these students. Their architectural similarity offers a route for transferring useful information between the networks. Experiments cover distillation through both output predictions and internal features, using existing methods without specialized changes to architecture or training recipes.

The study reports a pure convolutional model with fewer than 30 million parameters reaching 83.1% top-1 ImageNet accuracy, outperforming the named contemporary methods in the abstract. It also finds that students can inherit characteristics such as larger effective receptive fields. These results make teacher compatibility an important part of the distillation story: the tested large-kernel teachers help compact students acquire useful properties while retaining a convolutional architecture.
summary.tldr: Large-kernel convolutional networks prove more effective than Transformers as teachers for small-kernel ConvNets in the reported distillation experiments.

title: Are Large Kernels Better Teachers than Transformers for ConvNets?

abstract: In this work we perform symbolic discovery of differential operators in a situation where there is sparse experimental data. This small data regime in machine learning can be made tractable by providing our algorithms with prior information about the underlying dynamics. Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have been very successful in this regime (reconstructing entire ODE solutions using only a single point or entire PDE solutions with very few measurements of the initial condition). The Universal PINN approach (UPINN) adds a neural network that learns a representation of unknown hidden terms in the differential equation. The algorithm yields both a surrogate solution to the differential equation and a black-box representation of the hidden terms. These hidden term neural networks can then be converted into symbolic equations using symbolic regression techniques like AI Feynman. In order to achieve convergence of the neural networks, we provide our algorithms with (noisy) measurements of both the initial condition as well as (synthetic) experimental data obtained at later times. We demonstrate strong performance of UPINNs even when provided with very few measurements of noisy data in both the ODE and PDE regime.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover unknown terms in differential equations from sparse measurements. Prior knowledge of the dynamics helps make the small-data problem tractable. The Universal Physics-Informed Neural Network approach extends physics-informed learning by adding a neural network specifically tasked with representing hidden terms in the equation.

The method produces two outputs: a surrogate solution to the differential equation and a learned, initially black-box description of its unknown terms. Symbolic regression tools such as AI Feynman can then convert the hidden-term representation into symbolic equations. This separates fitting the missing dynamics from expressing them in an interpretable mathematical form.

To obtain convergence, the authors provide noisy measurements of initial conditions together with synthetic experimental observations at later times. Their demonstrations show strong performance with very few noisy measurements in both ordinary and partial differential equation settings. The stated data setup is important: the approach combines prior dynamical information with observations over time, using that combination to reconstruct solutions and support symbolic discovery of unknown operators.
summary.tldr: Universal PINNs learn unknown differential-equation terms from sparse noisy observations and enable their conversion into symbolic equations.

title: Universal Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Symbolic Differential Operator Discovery with Sparse Data

abstract: We present a constraint-based algorithm for learning causal structures from observational time-series data, in the presence of latent confounders. We assume a discrete-time, stationary structural vector autoregressive process, with both temporal and contemporaneous causal relations. One may ask if temporal and contemporaneous relations should be treated differently. The presented algorithm gradually refines a causal graph by learning long-term temporal relations before short-term ones, where contemporaneous relations are learned last. This ordering of causal relations to be learnt leads to a reduction in the required number of statistical tests. We validate this reduction empirically and demonstrate that it leads to higher accuracy for synthetic data and more plausible causal graphs for real-world data compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to infer causal relationships from observational time series when some confounding variables are hidden. It assumes a stationary structural vector autoregressive process in discrete time. The causal structure can include both relationships across time steps and contemporaneous relationships between variables within the same time step.

The proposed constraint-based algorithm gradually refines a causal graph in a particular order. It learns longer-term temporal relationships first, moves toward shorter-term relationships, and considers contemporaneous relationships last. This ordering reduces the number of statistical tests required. The key methodological choice is therefore how to organize the discovery process across different temporal distances.

Experiments confirm the reduction in testing and associate it with higher causal-discovery accuracy on synthetic data. For real-world data, the resulting graphs are reported to be more plausible than those from leading alternatives. These findings support ordered refinement as a useful approach within the assumed time-series setting, while the real-data claim concerns plausibility rather than verified recovery of every causal relationship.
summary.tldr: Learning long-term causal links before shorter-term and simultaneous links reduces testing and improves time-series causal discovery.

title: From Temporal to Contemporaneous Iterative Causal Discovery in the Presence of Latent Confounders

abstract: Recent end-to-end multi-object detectors simplify the inference pipeline by removing hand-crafted processes such as non-maximum suppression (NMS). However, during training, they still heavily rely on heuristics and hand-crafted processes which deteriorate the reliability of the predicted confidence score. In this paper, we propose a novel framework to train an end-to-end multi-object detector consisting of only two terms: negative log-likelihood (NLL) and a regularization term. In doing so, the multi-object detection problem is treated as density estimation of the ground truth bounding boxes utilizing a regularized mixture density model. The proposed end-to-end multi-object Detection with a Regularized Mixture Model (D-RMM) is trained by minimizing the NLL with the proposed regularization term, maximum component maximization (MCM) loss, preventing duplicate predictions. Our method reduces the heuristics of the training process and improves the reliability of the predicted confidence score. Moreover, our D-RMM outperforms the previous end-to-end detectors on MS COCO dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/lhj815/D-RMM.

paragraphs: End-to-end object detectors simplify prediction by eliminating hand-designed steps such as non-maximum suppression. Their training can nevertheless retain substantial heuristic machinery. This paper argues that those training choices can undermine the reliability of confidence scores and proposes a more compact probabilistic formulation of multi-object detection.

D-RMM treats the ground-truth bounding boxes as data whose density should be modeled by a regularized mixture. Training uses only two terms: negative log-likelihood and a regularizer called maximum component maximization. The likelihood term fits the observed boxes, while the regularizer is designed to prevent duplicate predictions. Together, they connect the detection objective with an explicit model of the box distribution.

The authors report that this formulation reduces training heuristics and improves confidence-score reliability. D-RMM also outperforms previous end-to-end detectors on MS COCO in the reported evaluation. The contribution concerns both the organization of training and its resulting predictions: a simpler objective supports competitive detection while addressing duplication and the trustworthiness of predicted confidence.
summary.tldr: D-RMM trains object detection as regularized density estimation, reducing heuristics while improving confidence reliability and reported detection performance.

title: End-to-End Multi-Object Detection with a Regularized Mixture Model

abstract: We consider the problem of localizing change points in high-dimensional linear regression. We propose an Approximate Message Passing (AMP) algorithm for estimating both the signals and the change point locations. Assuming Gaussian covariates, we give an exact asymptotic characterization of its estimation performance in the limit where the number of samples grows proportionally to the signal dimension. Our algorithm can be tailored to exploit any prior information on the signal, noise, and change points. It also enables uncertainty quantification in the form of an efficiently computable approximate posterior distribution, whose asymptotic form we characterize exactly. We validate our theory via numerical experiments, and demonstrate the favorable performance of our estimators on both synthetic data and images.

paragraphs: A regression relationship can change across a sequence of observations, making it necessary to estimate both the underlying signals and the locations where they change. This paper addresses that joint problem in high dimensions, where the signal has many components relative to the available observations.

The authors propose an Approximate Message Passing algorithm that estimates signals and change points together. The algorithm can incorporate prior information about the signals, observation noise, and change-point locations. It also produces an efficiently computable approximate posterior distribution, providing a way to express uncertainty rather than returning only a single set of estimates.

Under Gaussian covariates, the paper exactly characterizes asymptotic estimation performance when sample count and signal dimension grow proportionally. It also characterizes the asymptotic form of the approximate posterior. Numerical experiments validate the theory, and results on synthetic data and images demonstrate favorable estimator performance. The contribution connects a computational procedure with precise predictions about its behavior under a specified high-dimensional model, while extending its output to uncertainty quantification.
summary.tldr: An Approximate Message Passing method jointly estimates regression signals and change points, with uncertainty estimates and exact asymptotic analysis under Gaussian covariates.

title: Inferring Change Points in High-Dimensional Linear Regression via Approximate Message Passing

abstract: Collective action in machine learning is the study of the control that a coordinated group can have over machine learning algorithms. While previous research has concentrated on assessing the impact of collectives against Bayes (sub-)optimal classifiers, this perspective is limited in that it does not account for the choice of learning algorithm. Since classifiers seldom behave like Bayes classifiers and are influenced by the choice of learning algorithms along with their inherent biases, in this work we initiate the study of how the choice of the learning algorithm plays a role in the success of a collective in practical settings. Specifically, we focus on distributionally robust optimization (DRO), popular for improving a worst group error, and on the ubiquitous stochastic gradient descent (SGD), due to its inductive bias for "simpler" functions. Our empirical results, supported by a theoretical foundation, show that the effective size and success of the collective are highly dependent on properties of the learning algorithm. This highlights the necessity of taking the learning algorithm into account when studying the impact of collective action in machine learning.

paragraphs: A coordinated group can influence a machine-learning system through collective action involving its data. Prior analyses often evaluated that influence against idealized Bayes classifiers. This paper argues that real learning algorithms have their own biases, which can materially change how much influence a collective achieves.

The authors focus on distributionally robust optimization and stochastic gradient descent. The former is motivated by improving worst-group error, while the latter has a preference for simpler functions. They investigate how these algorithmic properties affect both the effective size of a collective and the success of its attempted influence.

Empirical results, supported by theoretical analysis, show strong dependence on the learning algorithm. The contribution is to make algorithm choice an explicit part of collective-action analysis instead of assuming that all sufficiently accurate classifiers respond similarly. The abstract does not specify a universal direction of the effect; whether a collective gains influence depends on the relevant algorithmic properties and setting.
summary.tldr: The success of collective influence on machine learning depends strongly on the learning algorithm and its inductive biases.

title: The Role of Learning Algorithms in Collective Action

abstract: We study continual pretraining recipe for scaling language models’ context lengths to 128K, with a focus on data engineering. We hypothesize that long context modeling, in particular the ability to utilize information at arbitrary input locations, is a capability that is mostly already acquired through large-scale pretraining, and that this capability can be readily extended to contexts substantially longer than seen during training (e.g., 4K to 128K) through lightweight continual pretraining on appropriate data mixture. We investigate the quantity and quality of the data for continual pretraining: (1) for quantity, we show that 500 million to 5 billion tokens are enough to enable the model to retrieve information anywhere within the 128K context; (2) for quality, our results equally emphasize domain balance and length upsampling. Concretely, naïvely upsampling longer data on certain domains like books, a common practice of existing work, gives suboptimal performance; a balanced domain mixture is equally important. We demonstrate that continual pretraining of the full model on 1B-5B tokens of such data is an effective and affordable strategy for scaling the context length of language models to 128K. Our recipe outperforms strong open-source long-context models and closes the gap to frontier models like GPT-4 128K.

paragraphs: This paper studies how continued pretraining can extend language models to contexts of 128,000 tokens. Its starting hypothesis is that large-scale pretraining already develops much of the ability to use information at arbitrary input positions. An appropriate additional training mixture may then extend that capability far beyond the context lengths previously encountered.

The study examines both data quantity and data composition. It reports that 500 million to five billion tokens can enable retrieval of information throughout a 128,000-token context. The composition results emphasize two requirements together: increasing the representation of long examples and maintaining balance across domains. Simply emphasizing long material from domains such as books produces suboptimal results.

The authors present full-model continued pretraining on one to five billion suitably mixed tokens as an effective, affordable recipe. Their models outperform strong open-source long-context models and narrow the gap to GPT-4 128K. These findings make data engineering central to the proposed extension strategy, while the idea that the underlying capability is largely acquired earlier remains the paper’s motivating hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Balanced domains and increased exposure to long examples make continued pretraining an effective route to 128,000-token language-model contexts.

title: Data Engineering for Scaling Language Models to 128K Context

abstract: This paper presents an efficient and scalable incomplete multi-view clustering method, referred to as Enhanced Dictionary-Induced tenSorized incomplete multi-view clustering with Gaussian errOr raNk minimization (EDISON). Specifically, EDISON employs an enhanced dictionary representation strategy as the foundation for inferring missing data and constructing anchor graphs, ensuring robustness to less-than-ideal data and maintaining high computational efficiency. Additionally, we introduce Gaussian error rank as a concise approximation of the true tensor rank, facilitating a comprehensive exploration of the diverse information encapsulated by various singular values in tensor data. Additionally, we integrate a hyper-anchor graph Laplacian manifold regularization into the tensor representation, allowing for the simultaneous utilization of inter-view high-order correlations and intra-view local correlations. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the EDISON model in both effectiveness and efficiency compared to SOTA methods.

Its goal is to maintain useful clustering structure without making computation prohibitively expensive.

The method begins with an enhanced dictionary representation, which supports both estimating missing information and building anchor graphs. It then introduces Gaussian error rank as an approximation to tensor rank. This component is intended to account for information carried by different singular values in the tensor representation, rather than overlooking their varied contributions.

These components connect efficient representation, recovery of missing information, and preservation of relational structure. Extensive experiments report better effectiveness and efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined design for the incomplete multi-view clustering problems evaluated.
summary.tldr: EDISON combines dictionary representations, tensor-rank approximation, and graph regularization to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of incomplete multi-view clustering.

title: EDISON: Enhanced Dictionary-Induced Tensorized Incomplete Multi-View Clustering with Gaussian Error Rank Minimization

abstract: Despite large neural networks demonstrating remarkable abilities to complete different tasks, they require excessive memory usage to store the optimization states for training. To alleviate this, the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is proposed to reduce the optimization states by training fewer parameters. However, LoRA restricts overall weight update matrices to be low-rank, limiting the model performance. In this work, we investigate the dynamics of LoRA and identify that it can be approximated by a random projection. Based on this observation, we propose Flora, which is able to achieve high-rank updates by resampling the projection matrices while enjoying the sublinear space complexity of optimization states. We conduct experiments across different tasks and model architectures to verify the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires memory for optimization states as well as model parameters. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, reduces that burden by training fewer parameters. Its restriction of overall weight updates to low-rank matrices can also limit model performance, creating a tension between training memory and the flexibility of the updates.

The authors analyze LoRA's learning dynamics and find that they can be approximated by a random projection. This interpretation suggests a way to keep updates compact without permanently confining their overall effect to low rank. Their method, Flora, resamples projection matrices so that it can achieve high-rank updates while keeping optimization-state space complexity sublinear.

Experiments across different tasks and model architectures support the effectiveness of this approach. The conceptual contribution is to view low-rank adaptation through the lens of gradient compression. That perspective motivates changing the projections over time, preserving the memory advantage of compact optimization states while allowing a more flexible accumulated change to the model.
summary.tldr: Flora resamples gradient projections to enable high-rank model updates while retaining sublinear memory use for optimization states.

title: Flora: Low-Rank Adapters Are Secretly Gradient Compressors

abstract: Federated learning is a promising distributed machine learning paradigm that can effectively exploit large-scale data without exposing users’ privacy. However, it may incur significant communication overhead, thereby potentially impairing the training efficiency. To address this challenge, numerous studies suggest binarizing the model updates. Nonetheless, traditional methods usually binarize model updates in a post-training manner, resulting in significant approximation errors and consequent degradation in model accuracy. To this end, we propose Federated Binarization-Aware Training (FedBAT), a novel framework that directly learns binary model updates during the local training process, thus inherently reducing the approximation errors. FedBAT incorporates an innovative binarization operator, along with meticulously designed derivatives to facilitate efficient learning. In addition, we establish theoretical guarantees regarding the convergence of FedBAT. Extensive experiments are conducted on four popular datasets. The results show that FedBAT significantly accelerates the convergence and exceeds the accuracy of baselines by up to 9%, even surpassing that of FedAvg in some cases.

paragraphs: Federated learning distributes training across participants, but communicating model updates can become a substantial cost. Representing those updates in binary form reduces what must be transmitted. The difficulty is that converting updates to binary after local training can introduce large approximation errors, damaging the accuracy of the resulting model.

FedBAT makes binary updates part of local training itself. Instead of learning an update and only afterward compressing it into binary form, participants directly learn binary model updates. The framework introduces a binarization operator and specially designed derivatives that enable this learning process. This connects communication constraints to optimization, allowing training to account for the representation that will actually be exchanged.

The paper establishes convergence guarantees and evaluates FedBAT on four datasets. The experiments report significantly faster convergence and accuracy improvements over baselines of up to 9%, with performance exceeding FedAvg in some cases. The findings support learning with binarization in mind as a way to reduce the accuracy cost of compact communication; the reported advantage over FedAvg is explicitly conditional on the evaluated case.
summary.tldr: FedBAT learns binary model updates during local federated training, reducing approximation errors and improving reported convergence and accuracy.

title: FedBAT: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning via Learnable Binarization

abstract: The Robust Satisficing (RS) model is an emerging approach to robust optimization, offering streamlined procedures and robust generalization across various applications. However, the statistical theory of RS remains unexplored in the literature. This paper fills in the gap by comprehensively analyzing the theoretical properties of the RS model. Notably, the RS structure offers a more straightforward path to deriving statistical guarantees compared to the seminal Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO), resulting in a richer set of results. In particular, we establish two-sided confidence intervals for the optimal loss without the need to solve a minimax optimization problem explicitly. We further provide finite-sample generalization error bounds for the RS optimizer. Importantly, our results extend to scenarios involving distribution shifts, where discrepancies exist between the sampling and target distributions. Our numerical experiments show that the RS model consistently outperforms the baseline empirical risk minimization in small-sample regimes and under distribution shifts. Furthermore, compared to the DRO model, the RS model exhibits lower sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning, highlighting its practicability for robustness considerations.

paragraphs: Robust Satisficing is an approach to robust optimization whose statistical foundations are the focus of this paper. The authors examine what can be guaranteed about its loss and generalization, including when the distribution supplying the data differs from the distribution of interest. This connects the optimization procedure to uncertainty about how its solution will perform.

The analysis establishes two-sided confidence intervals for the optimal loss without explicitly solving a minimax optimization problem. It also provides finite-sample bounds on the generalization error of the Robust Satisficing optimizer. The authors argue that the structure of the model offers a more direct route to statistical guarantees than Distributionally Robust Optimization, enabling a richer collection of results.
