It also exhibits lower sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning than Distributionally Robust Optimization. These findings combine theoretical guarantees with practical evidence that the approach can be useful when data are limited or the target distribution differs from the sampling distribution.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes statistical guarantees for Robust Satisficing and reports practical advantages with limited data and distribution shifts.

title: Statistical Properties of Robust Satisficing

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning (RL), updating the value function with the discrete-time Bellman Equation often encounters challenges due to the limited scope of available data. This limitation stems from the Bellman Equation, which cannot accurately predict the value of unvisited states. To address this issue, we have introduced an innovative solution that bridges the continuous- and discrete-time RL methods, capitalizing on their advantages. Our method uses a discrete-time RL algorithm to derive the value function from a dataset while ensuring that the function’s first derivative aligns with the local characteristics of states and actions, as defined by the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation in continuous RL. We provide practical algorithms for both deterministic policy gradient methods and stochastic policy gradient methods. Experiments on the D4RL dataset show that incorporating the first-order information significantly improves policy performance for offline RL problems.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an available dataset rather than continually collecting new experience. Limited data coverage makes value estimation difficult, particularly for states absent from the dataset. This paper addresses that problem by combining the usual discrete-time value-learning approach with information drawn from continuous-time reinforcement learning.

It also constrains the function’s first derivative to agree with local state and action characteristics described by the continuous-time Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. This adds information about how values should change locally to the value relationships supplied by discrete-time Bellman updates.

The authors provide practical versions for both deterministic and stochastic policy-gradient methods. Experiments on D4RL show that adding this first-order information significantly improves offline policy performance. The contribution is therefore a way to enrich value-function training using local dynamics, with implementations spanning two policy-learning settings. The reported results support the usefulness of that additional structure when learning from a fixed dataset with limited coverage.
summary.tldr: Combining discrete-time value learning with continuous-time derivative constraints improves offline reinforcement learning performance on D4RL.

title: Enhancing Value Function Estimation through First-Order State-Action Dynamics in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep equilibrium models (DEQs), as typical implicit neural networks, have demonstrated remarkable success on various tasks. There is, however, a lack of theoretical understanding of the connections and differences between implicit DEQs and explicit neural network models. In this paper, leveraging recent advances in random matrix theory (RMT), we perform an in-depth analysis on the eigenspectra of the conjugate kernel (CK) and neural tangent kernel (NTK) matrices for implicit DEQs, when the input data are drawn from a high-dimensional Gaussia mixture. We prove that, in this setting, the spectral behavior of these Implicit-CKs and NTKs depend on the DEQ activation function and initial weight variances, but only via a system of four nonlinear equations. As a direct consequence of this theoretical result, we demonstrate that a shallow explicit network can be carefully designed to produce the same CK or NTK as a given DEQ. Despite derived here for Gaussian mixture data, empirical results show the proposed theory and design principles also apply to popular real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models are implicit neural networks, and their relationship to ordinary explicit networks is not fully understood. This paper investigates that relationship through two mathematical descriptions of network behavior: the conjugate kernel and the neural tangent kernel. It focuses on the eigenvalue patterns of their matrices.

Using random matrix theory, the authors analyze inputs drawn from a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture. In this setting, they prove that the kernels' spectral behavior depends on activation functions and initial weight variances through a system of just four nonlinear equations. This provides a compact description of how those design choices influence the analyzed kernels.

The result enables a carefully designed shallow explicit network to reproduce the conjugate kernel or neural tangent kernel of a given equilibrium model. The equivalence concerns these kernel descriptions, rather than an unrestricted identity between all aspects of the networks. Although the theory is derived for Gaussian-mixture inputs, experiments on popular real-world datasets support the broader usefulness of its analysis and design principles.
summary.tldr: For high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, a compact kernel analysis shows how shallow explicit networks can match key kernels of deep equilibrium models.

title: Deep Equilibrium Models are Almost Equivalent to Not-so-deep Explicit Models for High-dimensional Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: We introduce a novel framework of combinatorial multi-armed bandits (CMAB) with multivariant and probabilistically triggering arms (CMAB-MT), where the outcome of each arm is a $d$-dimensional multivariant random variable and the feedback follows a general arm triggering process. Compared with existing CMAB works, CMAB-MT not only enhances the modeling power but also allows improved results by leveraging distinct statistical properties for multivariant random variables. For CMAB-MT, we propose a general 1-norm multivariant and triggering probability-modulated smoothness condition, and an optimistic CUCB-MT algorithm built upon this condition. Our framework can include many important problems as applications, such as episodic reinforcement learning (RL) and probabilistic maximum coverage for goods distribution, all of which meet the above smoothness condition and achieve matching or improved regret bounds compared to existing works. Through our new framework, we build the first connection between the episodic RL and CMAB literature, by offering a new angle to solve the episodic RL through the lens of CMAB, which may encourage more interactions between these two important directions.

paragraphs: Combinatorial bandit problems involve learning which combinations of uncertain choices produce good outcomes. This paper broadens that framework so each arm produces a multidimensional random outcome and feedback arrives through a general probabilistic triggering process. The resulting CMAB-MT framework can represent richer observations and interactions than formulations with simpler arm outcomes.

The authors introduce a smoothness condition that accounts for both multidimensional outcomes and arm-triggering probabilities. They then build an optimistic algorithm, CUCB-MT, around that condition. The approach uses distinct statistical properties of multivariant random variables to obtain improved results, making the richer representation useful for analysis as well as modeling.

Applications include episodic reinforcement learning and probabilistic maximum coverage for distributing goods. These problems satisfy the proposed condition and receive regret bounds matching or improving prior results. Regret measures the cost of learning through uncertain choices. By expressing episodic reinforcement learning through this bandit framework, the paper provides a connection that may enable further exchange of methods between the two research areas.
summary.tldr: CMAB-MT models multidimensional bandit outcomes and probabilistic feedback, yielding matching or improved regret bounds for applications including episodic reinforcement learning.

title: Combinatorial Multivariant Multi-Armed Bandits with Applications to Episodic Reinforcement Learning and Beyond

abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) is a vital technique for network compression and acceleration, gaining prominence as model sizes increase. This paper addresses a critical challenge in PTQ: the severe impact of outliers on the accuracy of quantized transformer architectures. Specifically, we introduce the concept of ‘reconstruction granularity’ as a novel solution to this issue, which has been overlooked in previous works. Our work provides theoretical insights into the role of reconstruction granularity in mitigating the outlier problem in transformer models. This theoretical framework is supported by empirical analysis, demonstrating that varying reconstruction granularities significantly influence quantization performance. Our findings indicate that different architectural designs necessitate distinct optimal reconstruction granularities. For instance, the multi-stage Swin Transformer architecture benefits from finer granularity, a deviation from the trends observed in ViT and DeiT models. We further develop an algorithm for determining the optimal reconstruction granularity for various ViT models, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in PTQ. For example, applying our method to $4$-bit quantization, the Swin-Base model achieves a Top-1 accuracy of $82.24%$ on the ImageNet classification task. This result surpasses the RepQ-ViT by $3.92%$ ($82.24%$ VS $78.32%$). Similarly, our approach elevates the ViT-Small to a Top-1 accuracy of $80.50%$, outperforming NoisyQuant by $3.64%$ ($80.50%$ VS $76.86%$). Codes are available in Supplementary Materials.

title: Outlier-aware Slicing for Post-Training Quantization in Vision Transformer

abstract: Can we identify the weights of a neural network by probing its input-output mapping? At first glance, this problem seems to have many solutions because of permutation, overparameterisation and activation function symmetries. Yet, we show that the incoming weight vector of each neuron is identifiable up to sign or scaling, depending on the activation function. Our novel method ’Expand-and-Cluster’ can identify layer sizes and weights of a target network for all commonly used activation functions. Expand-and-Cluster consists of two phases: (i) to relax the non-convex optimisation problem, we train multiple overparameterised student networks to best imitate the target function; (ii) to reverse engineer the target network’s weights, we employ an ad-hoc clustering procedure that reveals the learnt weight vectors shared between students – these correspond to the target weight vectors. We demonstrate successful weights and size recovery of trained shallow and deep networks with less than 10% overhead in the layer size and describe an ’ease-of-identifiability’ axis by analysing 150 synthetic problems of variable difficulty.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a neural network’s internal weights can be recovered by observing its input-output behavior. Several symmetries make this difficult: neurons can be permuted, networks can be overparameterized, and activation functions introduce additional equivalences. The authors show that each neuron’s incoming weight vector is identifiable up to a sign or scaling ambiguity, depending on the activation function.

Expand-and-Cluster turns that result into a two-step recovery method. First, multiple oversized student networks are trained to imitate the target network. This expansion relaxes the nonconvex optimization problem. A tailored clustering procedure then finds weight vectors shared across the trained students, identifying those shared vectors with the target network’s weights.

The method is designed to recover both layer sizes and weights for commonly used activation functions. The authors demonstrate recovery for trained shallow and deep networks with less than 10% layer-size overhead. They also analyze 150 synthetic problems to characterize an axis of recovery difficulty. Together, these results examine both what can be identified and how difficult identification is in practice.
summary.tldr: Training oversized imitators and clustering their shared weights can recover network sizes and weights, subject to activation-dependent sign or scaling ambiguities.

title: Expand-and-Cluster: Parameter Recovery of Neural Networks

abstract: The ability of machine learning (ML) algorithms to generalize well to unseen data has been studied through the lens of information theory, by bounding the generalization error with the input-output mutual information (MI), i.e., the MI between the training data and the learned hypothesis. Yet, these bounds have limited practicality for modern ML applications (e.g., deep learning), due to the difficulty of evaluating MI in high dimensions. Motivated by recent findings on the compressibility of neural networks, we consider algorithms that operate by slicing the parameter space, i.e., trained on random lower-dimensional subspaces. We introduce new, tighter information-theoretic generalization bounds tailored for such algorithms, demonstrating that slicing improves generalization. Our bounds offer significant computational and statistical advantages over standard MI bounds, as they rely on scalable alternative measures of dependence, i.e., disintegrated mutual information and $k$-sliced mutual information. Then, we extend our analysis to algorithms whose parameters do not need to exactly lie on random subspaces, by leveraging rate-distortion theory. This strategy yields generalization bounds that incorporate a distortion term measuring model compressibility under slicing, thereby tightening existing bounds without compromising performance or requiring model compression. Building on this, we propose a regularization scheme enabling practitioners to control generalization through compressibility. Finally, we empirically validate our results and achieve the computation of non-vacuous information-theoretic generalization bounds for neural networks, a task that was previously out of reach.

paragraphs: Information-theoretic generalization bounds relate performance on unseen data to dependence between training data and the learned model. Their practical use in deep learning is limited by the difficulty of measuring mutual information in high dimensions. This paper studies slicing: training within randomly selected, lower-dimensional subspaces of parameter space.

The authors derive tighter bounds tailored to sliced training, using disintegrated mutual information and k-sliced mutual information as more scalable dependence measures. Their analysis demonstrates improved generalization through slicing. They then extend the framework to models whose parameters do not lie exactly within random subspaces, using rate-distortion theory to account for the discrepancy.

That extension introduces a distortion term measuring how compressible a model is under slicing. It tightens existing bounds without requiring the model to be compressed or sacrificing performance. The authors also propose regularization that lets practitioners influence generalization through compressibility. Experiments validate the results and produce non-vacuous information-theoretic bounds for neural networks, meaning bounds informative enough to provide a substantive guarantee.
summary.tldr: Slicing parameter space yields more tractable generalization bounds, with an extension that connects neural-network compressibility to informative guarantees.

title: Slicing Mutual Information Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks

abstract: Recent studies have shown that the domain matching of text representations will help improve the generalization ability of asymmetrical domains text matching tasks. This requires that the distribution of text representations should be as similar as possible, similar to matching with heterogeneous data domains, in order to make the data after feature extraction indistinguishable. However, how to match the distribution of text representations remains an open question, and the role of text representations distribution match is still unclear. In this work, we explicitly narrow the distribution of text representations by matching them with the same prior distribution. We theoretically prove that narrowing the distribution of text representations in asymmetrical domains text matching is equivalent to optimizing the information bottleneck (IB). Since the interaction between text representations plays an important role in asymmetrical domains text matching, IB does not restrict the interaction between text representations. Therefore, we propose the adequacy of interaction and the incompleteness of a single text representation on the basis of IB and obtain the representation matching information bottleneck (RMIB). We theoretically prove that the constraints on text representations in RMIB is equivalent to maximizing the mutual information between text representations on the premise that the task information is given. On four text matching models and five text matching datasets, we verify that RMIB can improve the performance of asymmetrical domains text matching. Our experimental code is available at https://github.com/chenxingphh/rmib.

We theoretically prove that narrowing the distribution of text representations in asymmetrical domains text matching is equivalent to optimizing the information bottleneck (IB). Since the interaction between text representations plays an important role in asymmetrical domains text matching, IB does not restrict the interaction between text representations. Therefore, we propose the adequacy of interaction and the incompleteness of a single text representation on the basis of IB and obtain the representation matching information bottleneck (RMIB). We theoretically prove that the constraints on text representations in RMIB is equivalent to maximizing the mutual information between text representations on the premise that the task information is given. On four text matching models and five text matching datasets, we verify that RMIB can improve the performance of asymmetrical domains text matching. Our experimental code is available at https://github.com/chenxingphh/rmib.

paragraphs: Matching texts from asymmetric domains requires comparing representations that can have different distributions. Bringing those distributions closer can help generalization, but the paper asks how to do this and why it works. Its starting approach matches both text representations to the same prior distribution, providing a common target for their alignment.

The authors prove that this distribution-narrowing objective is equivalent to optimizing an information bottleneck in the studied setting. They then address something that the bottleneck alone does not constrain: interactions between the two text representations. Their representation matching information bottleneck, RMIB, adds requirements concerning sufficient interaction and the incompleteness of either representation considered alone.

The paper proves that RMIB's representation constraints are equivalent to maximizing mutual information between the representations when task information is given. This provides a theoretical account of how their relationship should be structured. Experiments involving four text matching models and five datasets show performance improvements, supporting the usefulness of combining distribution matching with explicit attention to interaction.
summary.tldr: RMIB combines distribution matching with constraints on interactions between text representations, providing theoretical connections and improved text matching results.

title: RMIB: Representation Matching Information Bottleneck for Matching Text Representations

abstract: Machine unlearning, the study of efficiently removing the impact of specific training instances on a model, has garnered increased attention in recent years due to regulatory guidelines such as the Right to be Forgotten. Achieving precise unlearning typically involves fully retraining the model and is computationally infeasible in case of very large models such as Large Language Models (LLMs). To this end, recent work has proposed several algorithms which approximate the removal of training data without retraining the model. These algorithms crucially rely on access to the model parameters in order to update them, an assumption that may not hold in practice due to computational constraints or having only query access to the LLMs. In this work, we propose a new class of unlearning methods for LLMs called “In-Context Unlearning.” This method unlearns instances from the model by simply providing specific kinds of inputs in context, without the need to update model parameters. To unlearn specific training instances, we present these instances to the LLMs at inference time along with labels that differ from their ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrate that in-context unlearning performs on par with, or in some cases outperforms other state-of-the-art methods that require access to model parameters, effectively removing the influence of specific instances on the model while preserving test accuracy.

This paper considers a different access pattern: changing the information supplied to the model at inference time, without updating its weights.

These examples become the mechanism for altering the model’s responses. The method therefore makes the inference-time context the point of intervention, addressing situations where computational constraints or query-only access prevent parameter updates.

The authors report reduced influence of the selected instances while preserving test accuracy. These are empirical findings about the proposed contextual intervention. The contribution is an alternative route to unlearning behavior that operates through supplied inputs and expands the range of access conditions under which unlearning methods can be applied.
summary.tldr: In-context unlearning uses deliberately relabeled examples at inference time to reduce selected training instances’ influence without changing model parameters.

title: In-Context Unlearning: Language Models as Few-Shot Unlearners

abstract: Recent diffusion models provide a promising zero-shot solution to noisy linear inverse problems without retraining for specific inverse problems. In this paper, we reveal that recent methods can be uniformly interpreted as employing a Gaussian approximation with hand-crafted isotropic covariance for the intractable denoising posterior to approximate the conditional posterior mean. Inspired by this finding, we propose to improve recent methods by using more principled covariance determined by maximum likelihood estimation. To achieve posterior covariance optimization without retraining, we provide general plug-and-play solutions based on two approaches specifically designed for leveraging pre-trained models with and without reverse covariance. We further propose a scalable method for learning posterior covariance prediction based on representation with orthonormal basis. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly enhance reconstruction performance without requiring hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models can help reconstruct signals from noisy linear measurements without being retrained for each inverse problem. This paper examines an approximation underlying recent methods: they use a Gaussian denoising posterior with a hand-designed isotropic covariance to estimate a conditional posterior mean. That covariance describes uncertainty in an overly uniform way.

The authors replace this handcrafted choice with covariance determined through maximum likelihood estimation. They develop plug-and-play approaches for pretrained models both with and without reverse covariance, allowing posterior covariance optimization without retraining. They also propose a scalable method that learns to predict posterior covariance using a representation built from an orthonormal basis.

The experiments show significant reconstruction improvements without requiring hyperparameter tuning. The central finding is that the uncertainty approximation is a useful point of intervention when adapting diffusion models to inverse problems. Improving covariance can strengthen reconstruction while retaining the ability to reuse pretrained models, and the separate learned representation addresses scalability of covariance prediction.
summary.tldr: Principled posterior covariance estimates improve diffusion-based reconstruction from noisy linear measurements without requiring hyperparameter tuning in the reported experiments.

title: Improving Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems Using Optimal Posterior Covariance

abstract: Optimization layers in deep neural networks have enjoyed a growing popularity in structured learning, improving the state of the art on a variety of applications. Yet, these pipelines lack interpretability since they are made of two opaque layers: a highly non-linear prediction model, such as a deep neural network, and an optimization layer, which is typically a complex black-box solver. Our goal is to improve the transparency of such methods by providing counterfactual explanations. We build upon variational autoencoders a principled way of obtaining counterfactuals: working in the latent space leads to a natural notion of plausibility of explanations. We finally introduce a variant of the classic loss for VAE training that improves their performance in our specific structured context. These provide the foundations of CF-OPT, a first-order optimization algorithm that can find counterfactual explanations for a broad class of structured learning architectures. Our numerical results show that both close and plausible explanations can be obtained for problems from the recent literature.

Understanding their outputs is difficult because both stages can be opaque. CF-OPT addresses this problem with counterfactual explanations: changes to an input that would lead the combined system to produce a different decision.

The method uses a variational autoencoder to search within a learned latent representation. This gives the search a notion of plausibility, helping distinguish meaningful alternatives from arbitrary input changes. The authors also modify the autoencoder’s training loss to improve its suitability for this structured prediction setting, connecting the representation-learning step to the explanation task.

These components support a first-order optimization algorithm applicable to a broad class of structured learning architectures. Numerical results on problems from the literature show that it can find explanations that are both close to the original input and plausible. Those two properties address complementary needs: an explanation should describe a modest change while still resembling a credible alternative input.
summary.tldr: CF-OPT searches a learned latent space for close, plausible input changes that explain structured prediction decisions.

title: CF-OPT: Counterfactual Explanations for Structured Prediction

abstract: Previous work in fair machine learning has characterised the Fair Bayes Optimal Classifier (BOC) on a given distribution for both deterministic and randomized classifiers. We study the robustness of the Fair BOC to adversarial noise in the data distribution. Kearns & Li (1988) implies that the accuracy of the deterministic BOC without any fairness constraints is robust (Lipschitz) to malicious noise in the data distribution. We demonstrate that their robustness guarantee breaks down when we add fairness constraints. Hence, we consider the randomized Fair BOC, and our central result is that its accuracy is robust to malicious noise in the data distribution. Our robustness result applies to various fairness constraints—Demographic Parity, Equal Opportunity, Predictive Equality. Beyond robustness, we demonstrate that randomization leads to better accuracy and efficiency. We show that the randomized Fair BOC is nearly-deterministic, and gives randomized predictions on at most one data point, hence availing numerous benefits of randomness, while using very little of it.

paragraphs: A fair Bayes optimal classifier seeks the best accuracy available on a distribution while satisfying a fairness constraint. This paper investigates how its accuracy responds when an adversary perturbs that distribution. Existing robustness guarantees for an unconstrained deterministic optimal classifier can fail once fairness constraints are imposed.

The authors show that allowing randomized predictions restores robustness of the optimal fair classifier's accuracy to malicious distribution noise. Their result covers Demographic Parity, Equal Opportunity, and Predictive Equality. The central distinction concerns accuracy under perturbation: deterministic fair optimization can lose a robustness property that is available to the randomized formulation.

The paper also reports accuracy and efficiency benefits from randomization and shows that the randomized fair optimal classifier can be nearly deterministic, randomizing on at most one data point. Thus, the theoretical benefits do not require randomness throughout its predictions. The result makes a case for treating a small amount of randomization as a meaningful design choice when seeking accurate fair classifiers whose optimal accuracy remains robust to adversarial changes in the data distribution.
summary.tldr: Randomization restores accuracy robustness for fair Bayes optimal classifiers under adversarial distribution noise, while requiring randomness at at most one data point.

title: Optimal Fair Learning Robust to Adversarial Distribution Shift

abstract: Modern sequence models (e.g., Transformers and linear RNNs) emerged as dominant backbones of recent deep learning frameworks, mainly due to their efficiency, representational power, and/or ability to capture long-range dependencies. Recently, adopting these sequence models for graph-structured data has gained popularity as the alternative to Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs). There is, however, a lack of a common foundation about what constitutes a good graph sequence model, and a mathematical description of the benefits and deficiencies in adopting different sequence models for learning on graphs. To this end, we introduce the Graph Sequence Model (GSM), a unifying framework for applying sequence models to graph data. The GSM framework allows us to understand, evaluate, and compare the power of different sequence model backbones in graph tasks. Building on this insight, we propose GSM++, a fast hybrid model that hierarchically tokenizes the graph using Hierarchical Affinity Clustering (HAC) and then encodes these sequences via a hybrid architecture. The theoretical and experimental findings confirm that GSM++ outperforms baseline models on most benchmarks.

paragraphs: Sequence models are increasingly used to learn from graphs, extending architectures designed for ordered inputs to data organized by connections. The paper asks how to compare these choices systematically. Different sequence backbones offer different combinations of efficiency, representational power, and ability to capture distant relationships, making a shared framework useful.

The authors introduce the Graph Sequence Model framework, or GSM, to describe how sequence models operate on graph data. It provides a common basis for examining and comparing the power of different backbones on graph tasks. This makes architectural choices easier to study within one mathematical description.

Using insights from that framework, the authors build GSM++, a fast hybrid model. It first organizes a graph into hierarchical tokens using Hierarchical Affinity Clustering, then processes the resulting sequences with a hybrid architecture. The paper combines theoretical analysis with experiments and reports that GSM++ beats baseline models on most benchmarks. The contribution therefore links a general framework for understanding graph sequence models with a concrete architecture whose reported gains cover most, rather than all, evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: A unified framework for graph sequence models motivates GSM++, a hierarchical hybrid architecture that outperforms baselines on most evaluated benchmarks.

title: Best of Both Worlds: Advantages of Hybrid Graph Sequence Models

abstract: In this paper, we investigate how to push the performance limits of serving Deep Neural Network (DNN) models on CPU-based servers. Specifically, we observe that while intra-operator parallelism across multiple threads is an effective way to reduce inference latency, it provides diminishing returns. Our primary insight is that instead of running a single instance of a model with all available threads on a server, running multiple instances each with smaller batch sizes and fewer threads for intra-op parallelism can provide lower inference latency. However, the right configuration is hard to determine manually since it is workload- (DNN model and batch size used by the serving system) and deployment-dependent (number of CPU cores on server). We present Packrat, a new serving system for online inference that given a model and batch size ($B$) algorithmically picks the optimal number of instances ($i$), the number of threads each should be allocated ($t$), and the batch sizes each should operate on ($b$) that minimizes latency. Packrat is built as an extension to TorchServe and supports online reconfigurations to avoid serving downtime. Averaged across a range of batch sizes, Packrat improves inference latency by 1.43$\times$ to 1.83$\times$ on a range of commonly used DNNs.

paragraphs: Giving a neural network more CPU threads can reduce inference latency, but the benefit diminishes as more threads cooperate on the same operation. This paper investigates an alternative allocation: run several copies of the model, each processing a smaller batch with fewer threads. Depending on the workload and server, that arrangement can complete inference sooner.

The difficulty is choosing the configuration. The appropriate number of model instances, threads per instance, and batch sizes depends on the model, the serving batch size, and available CPU cores. Packrat automates this choice, algorithmically selecting these quantities to minimize latency for the given setup. It extends TorchServe and supports changing configurations while continuing to serve requests.

Across the tested neural networks, the authors report latency improvements of 1.43× to 1.83× when averaged across a range of batch sizes. The result shows that resource allocation within a CPU server can materially affect inference speed. Packrat makes this allocation an explicit optimization problem instead of relying on a single model instance using all available threads.
summary.tldr: Packrat reduces CPU inference latency by automatically choosing model instance counts, thread allocations, and batch sizes.

title: Auto-reconfiguration for Latency Minimization in CPU-based DNN Serving

abstract: The use of machine learning to estimate the energy of a group of atoms, and the forces that drive them to more stable configurations, have revolutionized the fields of computational chemistry and materials discovery. In this domain, rigorous enforcement of symmetry and conservation laws has traditionally been considered essential. For this reason, interatomic forces are usually computed as the derivatives of the potential energy, ensuring energy conservation. Several recent works have questioned this physically constrained approach, suggesting that directly predicting the forces yields a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency – and that energy conservation can be learned during training. This work investigates the applicability of such non-conservative models in microscopic simulations. We identify and demonstrate several fundamental issues, from ill-defined convergence of geometry optimization to instability in various types of molecular dynamics. Contrary to the case of rotational symmetry, energy conservation is hard to learn, monitor, and correct for. The best approach to exploit the acceleration afforded by direct force prediction might be to use it in tandem with a conservative model, reducing – rather than eliminating – the additional cost of backpropagation, but avoiding the pathological behavior associated with non-conservative forces.

paragraphs: Atomistic machine-learning models estimate energies and the forces that move atoms. Computing forces as derivatives of a potential energy enforces energy conservation. Direct force prediction can offer computational savings, but it removes that built-in guarantee, raising the question of whether training can adequately recover the missing physical constraint.

The paper investigates direct, non-conservative force models in microscopic simulations. It demonstrates problems including ill-defined convergence during geometry optimization and instability in several forms of molecular dynamics. The authors find that energy conservation is difficult to learn, monitor, and correct, unlike the comparison they draw with rotational symmetry. Prediction accuracy and speed therefore need to be considered alongside the behavior of the resulting simulation.

The authors suggest that combining direct force prediction with a conservative model might offer the best use of the acceleration. Such a combination could reduce the extra backpropagation cost while avoiding the pathological behavior associated with non-conservative forces. This is presented as a possible practical direction, rather than an established universally optimal solution.
summary.tldr: Direct force prediction can cause problematic atomistic simulations, motivating possible combinations with energy-conserving models.

title: The dark side of the forces: assessing non-conservative force models for atomistic machine learning

abstract: Post-training compression reduces the computational and memory costs of large language models (LLMs), enabling resource-efficient deployment. However, existing compression benchmarks focus narrowly on language modeling (e.g., perplexity) and natural language understanding tasks (e.g., GLUE accuracy), ignoring the agentic capabilities—workflow, tool use/function call, long-context understanding and real-world application. We introduce the Agent Compression Benchmark (ACBench), the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating how compression impacts LLMs’ agentic abilities. ACBench spans (1) 12 tasks across 4 capabilities (e.g., WorfBench for workflow generation, Needle-in-Haystack for long-context retrieval), (2) 4-bit quantization (GPTQ, AWQ) and 50% pruning (Wanda, SparseGPT), and (3) 15 models, including small (Gemma-2B), standard (Qwen2.5-7B), and distilled reasoning LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill). Our experiments reveal compression tradeoffs: 4-bit quantization preserves workflow generation and tool use (1%–3% drop) but degrades real-world application accuracy by 10%–15%. We introduce ERank, Top-k Ranking Correlation and Energy to systematize analysis. ACBench provides actionable insights for optimizing LLM compression in agentic scenarios, bridging the gap between algorithmic efficiency and real-world applicability.

summary.tldr: ACBench finds that compression affects agent capabilities unevenly, with 4-bit quantization preserving some skills better than real-world application accuracy.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression

abstract: We initiate a study of algorithms for model training with user-level differential privacy (DP), where each example may be attributed to multiple users, which we call the multi-attribution model. We first provide a carefully chosen definition of user-level DP under the multi-attribution model. Training in the multi-attribution model is facilitated by solving the contribution bounding problem, i.e. the problem of selecting a subset of the dataset for which each user is associated with a limited number of examples. We propose a greedy baseline algorithm for the contribution bounding problem. We then empirically study this algorithm for a synthetic logistic regression task and a transformer training task, including studying variants of this baseline algorithm that optimize the subset chosen using different techniques and criteria. We find that the baseline algorithm remains competitive with its variants in most settings, and build a better understanding of the practical importance of a bias-variance tradeoff inherent in solutions to the contribution bounding problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies private model training when a single training example can belong to several users. It calls this the multi-attribution setting and develops a user-level differential-privacy definition for it. The central issue is that controlling one person's contribution becomes more complicated when examples are shared across people rather than attributed to only one user.

The authors formulate contribution bounding as a dataset-selection problem: choose a subset in which each user is associated with only a limited number of examples. They propose a greedy baseline and examine variants that optimize the selected subset using different techniques and criteria. This makes the selection step a concrete part of enabling private training under shared attribution.

Experiments cover a synthetic logistic-regression task and a transformer-training task. The simple greedy algorithm remains competitive with its variants in most settings. The study also identifies the practical importance of a bias-variance tradeoff in contribution bounding. Its findings suggest that selecting a privacy-compatible subset requires attention to statistical effects, beyond simply enforcing the per-user contribution limit.
summary.tldr: The paper defines user-level privacy for shared training examples and studies greedy contribution bounding as a practical training ingredient.

title: It’s My Data Too: Private ML for Datasets with Multi-User Training Examples

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful generative models, but their high computational cost in iterative sampling remains a significant bottleneck. In this work, we present an in-depth and insightful study of state-of-the-art acceleration techniques for diffusion models, including caching and quantization, and reveal their limitations in computation error and generation quality. To break these limits, this work introduces Modulated Diffusion (MoDiff), an innovative, rigorous, and principled framework that accelerates generative modeling through modulated quantization and error compensation. MoDiff not only inherits the advantages of existing caching and quantization methods but also serves as a general framework to accelerate all diffusion models. The advantages of MoDiff are supported by solid theoretical insight and analysis. In addition, extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and LSUN demonstrate that MoDiff significantly reduces activation quantization from 8 bits to 3 bits without performance degradation in post-training quantization (PTQ). Our code implementation is available at https://github.com/WeizhiGao/MoDiff.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate outputs through iterative sampling, which can make generation computationally expensive. This paper examines two acceleration strategies, caching and quantization, and studies how their computational errors affect generation quality. Its starting point is that accelerating the repeated computation requires managing the errors introduced by those shortcuts.

The proposed framework, Modulated Diffusion or MoDiff, combines modulated quantization with error compensation. It is designed to retain advantages of existing caching and quantization approaches while addressing their limitations. The authors support the framework with theoretical analysis and present it as generally applicable to diffusion models, connecting acceleration to explicit treatment of approximation error.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and LSUN show activation quantization reduced from eight bits to three bits without performance degradation in the reported post-training-quantization setting. This is the concrete empirical result behind the method's promise: substantially lower activation precision can remain compatible with generation quality when accompanied by the proposed modulation and compensation. The reported evidence establishes that outcome on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: MoDiff combines modulated quantization and error compensation, enabling three-bit activations without reported performance loss on CIFAR-10 and LSUN.

title: Modulated Diffusion: Accelerating Generative Modeling with Modulated Quantization

abstract: Label distribution learning (LDL) is a novel machine learning paradigm that can handle label ambiguity. This paper focuses on the interpretability issue of label distribution learning. Existing local interpretability models are mainly designed for single-label learning problems and are difficult to directly interpret label distribution learning models. In response to this situation, we propose an improved local interpretable model-agnostic explanations algorithm that can effectively interpret any black-box model in label distribution learning. To address the label dependency problem, we introduce the feature attribution distribution matrix and derive the solution formula for explanations under the label distribution form. Meanwhile, to enhance the transparency and trustworthiness of the explanation algorithm, we provide an analytical solution and derive the boundary conditions for explanation convergence and stability. In addition, we design a feature selection scoring function and a fidelity metric for the explanation task of label distribution learning. A series of numerical experiments and human experiments were conducted to validate the performance of the proposed algorithm in practical applications. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves high fidelity, consistency, and trustworthiness in explaining LDL models.

Explaining such a model requires accounting for relationships among labels. This paper adapts local, model-agnostic explanation methods, which are mainly designed for single-label predictions, to this richer output structure.

The authors provide an analytical solution and conditions governing explanation convergence and stability. These components make the explanation procedure itself more transparent by describing how its answers are obtained and when their behavior is controlled.

title: LIMEFLDL: A Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations Approach for Label Distribution Learning

abstract: Dynamic graphs evolve continuously, presenting challenges for traditional graph learning due to their changing structures and temporal dependencies. Recent advancements have shown potential in addressing these challenges by developing suitable meta-learning-based dynamic graph neural network models. However, most meta-learning approaches for dynamic graphs rely on fixed weight update parameters, neglecting the essential intrinsic complex high-order topological information of dynamically evolving graphs. We have designed Dowker Zigzag Persistence (DZP), an efficient and stable dynamic graph persistent homology representation method based on Dowker complex and zigzag persistence, to capture the high-order features of dynamic graphs. Armed with the DZP ideas, we propose TMetaNet, a new meta-learning parameter update model based on dynamic topological features. By utilizing the distances between high-order topological features, TMetaNet enables more effective adaptation across snapshots. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate TMetaNet’s state-of-the-art performance and resilience to graph noise, illustrating its high potential for meta-learning and dynamic graph analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lihaogx/TMetaNet.

paragraphs: Dynamic link prediction concerns relationships in graphs whose structure changes over time. Meta-learning methods can adapt graph models across successive snapshots, but the paper argues that fixed weight-update parameters overlook complex higher-order topology. Its approach makes information about changing graph structure part of the adaptation process, so updates can reflect differences between snapshots.

The authors first introduce Dowker Zigzag Persistence, or DZP, an efficient and stable representation of dynamic graphs built from Dowker complexes and zigzag persistence. This persistent-homology representation captures higher-order structural features. TMetaNet then uses distances between these features to guide meta-learning parameter updates, connecting the amount of structural change to how the model adapts.

The contribution has two linked parts: a representation of dynamic higher-order structure and an update mechanism that uses that representation to improve adaptation, rather than leaving the graph's structural evolution outside the update rule.
summary.tldr: TMetaNet guides adaptation across graph snapshots using distances between persistent higher-order topological features.

title: TMetaNet: Topological Meta-Learning Framework for Dynamic Link Prediction

abstract: We present Banyan, a model that efficiently learns semantic representations by leveraging explicit hierarchical structure. While transformers excel at scale, they struggle in low-resource settings. Conversely recent structured models have shown promise as efficient learners, but lack performance. Banyan bridges this gap with two key innovations: an entangled hierarchical tree structure and diagonalized message passing, enabling it to outperform larger transformer models with just 14 non-embedding parameters. It excels in low-resource settings, offering a viable alternative for under-represented languages and highlighting its potential for efficient, interpretable NLP in resource-constrained environments.

paragraphs: Banyan explores whether explicitly organizing a model’s computation can make semantic representation learning more efficient. The paper focuses on low-resource settings, where transformers struggle despite their success at larger scales. Structured models offer another route, but the authors identify their weaker performance as an obstacle to making them a useful alternative.

The proposed model combines an entangled hierarchical tree with diagonalized message passing. The tree supplies an explicit hierarchy, while message passing is the mechanism for exchanging information through that structure. Together, these choices build organization directly into the representation-learning process. The contribution is therefore an architectural approach to efficiency, with structure playing a central role in how the model learns.

The authors report that Banyan outperforms larger transformer models using just 14 non-embedding parameters. That qualification matters: the count excludes embedding parameters and is not a total model parameter count. The reported strength in low-resource settings supports Banyan as a potential option for under-represented languages. More broadly, the findings point toward efficient, interpretable language processing through explicit structure.
summary.tldr: Banyan uses explicit hierarchical structure to learn semantic representations efficiently, outperforming larger transformers with 14 non-embedding parameters in the reported results.

title: Banyan: Improved Representation Learning with Explicit Structure

abstract: Teaching large language models (LLMs) to critique and refine their outputs is crucial for building systems that can iteratively improve, yet it is fundamentally limited by the ability to provide accurate judgments and actionable suggestions. In this work, we study LLM critics for code generation and propose $\texttt{CTRL}$, a framework for $\texttt{C}$ritic $\texttt{T}$raining via $\texttt{R}$einforcement $\texttt{L}$earning, which trains a critic model to generate feedback that maximizes correction performance for a fixed generator model without human supervision. Our results demonstrate that critics trained with $\texttt{CTRL}$ significantly enhance pass rates and mitigate compounding errors across both base and stronger generator models. Furthermore, we show that these critic models act as accurate generative reward models and enable test-time scaling through iterative critique-revision, achieving up to 106.1% relative improvements across challenging code generation benchmarks.

paragraphs: A language model can revise code in response to feedback, but that feedback must correctly identify problems and suggest useful changes. This paper studies how to train a critic specifically for that role. Its framework, CTRL, uses reinforcement learning to make critiques more effective at helping another model correct its code.

The training objective is correction performance for a fixed generator model, and the procedure does not require human supervision. This ties the critic’s learning directly to the usefulness of its feedback. The reported results show that trained critics improve pass rates and reduce compounding errors with both base generators and stronger generator models.

The authors also find that the critics can serve as accurate generative reward models. Repeated rounds of critique and revision provide a way to improve performance by spending more computation at test time. Across challenging code-generation benchmarks, the paper reports relative improvements of up to 106.1%. That maximum describes the evaluated gains, while the broader contribution is training feedback around its ability to enable successful correction.
summary.tldr: CTRL trains code critics through reinforcement learning to provide feedback that improves correction and supports iterative critique-and-revision.

title: Teaching Language Models to Critique via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In open-environment applications, data are often collected from heterogeneous modalities with distinct encodings, resulting in feature space heterogeneity. This heterogeneity inherently induces label shift, making cross-modal knowledge transfer particularly challenging when the source and target data exhibit simultaneous heterogeneous feature spaces and shifted label distributions. Existing studies address only partial aspects of this issue, leaving the broader problem unresolved. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new concept of Heterogeneous Label Shift (HLS), targeting this critical but underexplored challenge. We first analyze the impact of heterogeneous feature spaces and label distribution shifts on model generalization and introduce a novel error decomposition theorem. Based on these insights, we propose a bound minimization HLS framework that decouples and tackles feature heterogeneity and label shift accordingly. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks for cross-modal classification validate the effectiveness and practical relevance of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Transferring a classifier between modalities can involve two changes at once: inputs use different representations, and class labels occur at different frequencies. The paper introduces Heterogeneous Label Shift to study this combined problem. Its motivation is that addressing only one part leaves important difficulties in cross-modal knowledge transfer unresolved.

The authors first analyze how feature-space differences and changes in label distributions affect generalization. They derive an error decomposition theorem, providing a theoretical way to separate contributions to prediction error. This separation then guides a learning framework that minimizes a bound while handling feature heterogeneity and label shift as distinct components.

Experiments across cross-modal classification benchmarks support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The main significance is the connection between the theoretical decomposition and the algorithm’s organization: the method explicitly accounts for both differences in how inputs are represented and differences in class prevalence. This provides a coordinated treatment of two shifts that occur together in the setting studied.
summary.tldr: Heterogeneous Label Shift jointly addresses changing input representations and class distributions through an error decomposition and bound-minimization framework.

title: Heterogeneous Label Shift: Theory and Algorithm

abstract: Through recognizing causal subgraphs, causal graph learning (CGL) has risen to be a promising approach for improving the generalizability of graph neural networks under out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. However, the empirical successes of CGL techniques are mostly exemplified in classification settings, while regression tasks, a more challenging setting in graph learning, are overlooked. We thus devote this work to tackling causal graph regression (CGR); to this end we reshape the processing of confounding effects in existing CGL studies, which mainly deal with classification. Specifically, we reflect on the predictive power of confounders in graph-level regression, and generalize classification-specific causal intervention techniques to regression through a lens of contrastive learning. Extensive experiments on graph OOD benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposals for CGR. The model implementation and the code are provided on https://github.com/causal-graph/CGR.

paragraphs: Graph models can perform well on familiar data yet struggle when the data distribution changes. Causal graph learning addresses this by identifying subgraphs that support more generalizable predictions. This paper examines graph regression, where the output is a numerical value, because most existing evidence for causal graph learning comes from classification tasks.

The authors revisit how these methods handle confounders: factors whose relationships with the graph and prediction target complicate causal interpretation. Their approach explicitly considers the predictive information confounders carry in graph-level regression. This makes the treatment of confounding a central design question rather than simply transferring the procedures used for categorical predictions.

They also adapt causal intervention techniques developed for classification through a contrastive-learning perspective, which reasons about relationships between examples. Experiments on graph benchmarks involving distribution shifts support the effectiveness of the resulting proposals. The contribution is a recipe for extending causal graph learning to numerical prediction, with particular attention to how confounding and intervention should be reconsidered for that setting.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts causal graph learning to regression by reconsidering confounders and reformulating intervention techniques through contrastive learning.

title: A Recipe for Causal Graph Regression: Confounding Effects Revisited

abstract: Existing PLMs generate protein sequences based on a single-condition constraint from a specific modality, struggling to simultaneously satisfy multiple constraints across different modalities. In this work, we introduce CFP-GEN, a novel diffusion language model for Combinatorial Functional Protein GENeration. CFP-GEN facilitates the de novo protein design by integrating multimodal conditions with functional, sequence, and structural constraints. Specifically, an Annotation-Guided Feature Modulation (AGFM) module is introduced to dynamically adjust the protein feature distribution based on composable functional annotations, e.g., GO terms, IPR domains and EC numbers. Meanwhile, the ResidueControlled Functional Encoding (RCFE) module captures residue-wise interaction to ensure more precise control. Additionally, off-the-shelf 3D structure encoders can be seamlessly integrated to impose geometric constraints. We demonstrate that CFP-GEN enables high-throughput generation of novel proteins with functionality comparable to natural proteins, while achieving a high success rate in designing multifunctional proteins.

paragraphs: Designing a protein can require satisfying several requirements at once, including desired functions, sequence constraints, and structural properties. Existing protein language models described in this paper typically condition generation on a single requirement from one information type. CFP-GEN introduces a diffusion language model that combines these different constraints when generating new protein sequences.

One component adjusts the model's protein features according to combinations of functional annotations, including GO terms, IPR domains, and EC numbers. Another captures interactions at the level of individual residues, providing finer control over the generated sequence. The framework can also incorporate existing three-dimensional structure encoders to bring geometric requirements into the generation process.

The authors report high-throughput generation of novel proteins whose functionality is comparable to that of natural proteins, together with a high success rate for multifunctional designs. These findings support the approach's ability to combine functional requirements rather than handle only isolated conditions. Its main contribution is coordinating broad functional instructions, residue-level control, and structural information within one generation framework.
summary.tldr: CFP-GEN combines functional, sequence, and structural constraints in a diffusion language model for generating multifunctional proteins.

title: CFP-Gen: Combinatorial Functional Protein Generation via Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a surge in the development of protein structural tokenization methods, which chunk protein 3D structures into discrete or continuous representations. Structure tokenization enables the direct application of powerful techniques like language modeling for protein structures, and large multimodal models to integrate structures with protein sequences and functional texts. Despite the progress, the capabilities and limitations of these methods remain poorly understood due to the lack of a unified evaluation framework. We first introduce StructTokenBench, a framework that comprehensively evaluates the quality and efficiency of structure tokenizers, focusing on fine-grained local substructures rather than global structures, as typical in existing benchmarks. Our evaluations reveal that no single model dominates all benchmarking perspectives. Observations of codebook under-utilization led us to develop AminoAseed, a simple yet effective strategy that enhances codebook gradient updates and optimally balances codebook size and dimension for improved tokenizer utilization and quality. Compared to the leading model ESM3, our method achieves an average of 6.31% performance improvement across 24 supervised tasks, with sensitivity and utilization rates increased by 12.83% and 124.03%, respectively. Source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/KatarinaYuan/StructTokenBench.

paragraphs: Protein structure tokenizers turn three-dimensional structures into representations that language-style and multimodal models can process. Comparing these tokenizers is difficult without a shared evaluation framework. StructTokenBench addresses this by assessing quality and efficiency with particular attention to local substructures, complementing evaluations centered on the global shape of a protein.

The benchmark finds that no tokenizer leads across every evaluation perspective. It also reveals underuse of codebooks, the collections of representations available to encode structure. Motivated by that observation, the authors introduce AminoAseed. The strategy improves gradient updates to codebook entries and balances codebook size with representation dimension to improve utilization and tokenizer quality.

summary.tldr: StructTokenBench exposes trade-offs in protein tokenizers, and AminoAseed improves codebook use with reported gains across 24 supervised tasks.

title: Protein Structure Tokenization: Benchmarking and New Recipe

abstract: Large repositories of image-caption pairs are essential for the development of vision-language models. However, these datasets are often extracted from noisy data scraped from the web, and contain many mislabeled instances. In order to improve the reliability of downstream models, it is important to identify and filter images with incorrect captions. However, beyond filtering based on image-caption embedding similarity, no prior works have proposed other methods to filter noisy multimodal data, or concretely assessed the impact of noisy captioning data on downstream training. In this work, we propose, theoretically justify, and empirically validate LEMoN, a method to identify label errors in image-caption datasets. Our method leverages the multimodal neighborhood of image-caption pairs in the latent space of contrastively pretrained multimodal models to automatically identify label errors. Through empirical evaluations across eight datasets and twelve baselines, we find that LEMoN outperforms the baselines by over 3% in label error detection, and that training on datasets filtered using our method improves downstream captioning performance by more than 2 BLEU points over noisy training.

paragraphs: Image-caption collections scraped from the web can contain incorrect descriptions, creating unreliable training material for vision-language models. A common filtering signal is the similarity between an image’s representation and its caption’s representation. LEMoN broadens the evidence used to judge a pair by considering its multimodal neighborhood.

The method operates in the latent space of a contrastively pretrained multimodal model, where images and captions have learned representations. It uses neighboring image-caption pairs to identify likely labeling errors automatically. The authors provide both theoretical justification and empirical validation for using this surrounding structure as evidence about whether a caption is appropriate.

Across eight datasets and twelve baselines, LEMoN improves label-error detection by more than 3%. Training on data filtered with LEMoN also improves downstream captioning by over two BLEU points compared with noisy training. These results connect the filtering method to two outcomes: detecting incorrect pairs and improving a model trained on the cleaned data. The downstream result makes the practical value of better error detection explicit.
summary.tldr: LEMoN detects incorrect image captions using nearby multimodal representations, with reported gains in both label-error detection and downstream captioning.

title: LEMoN: Label Error Detection using Multimodal Neighbors

abstract: We propose Network Automatic Relevance Determination (NARD), an extension of ARD for linearly probabilistic models, to simultaneously model sparse relationships between inputs $X \in \mathbb R^{d \times N}$ and outputs $Y \in \mathbb R^{m \times N}$, while capturing the correlation structure among the $Y$. NARD employs a matrix normal prior which contains a sparsity-inducing parameter to identify and discard irrelevant features, thereby promoting sparsity in the model. Algorithmically, it iteratively updates both the precision matrix and the relationship between $Y$ and the refined inputs. To mitigate the computational inefficiencies of the $\mathcal O(m^3 + d^3)$ cost per iteration, we introduce Sequential NARD, which evaluates features sequentially, and a Surrogate Function Method, leveraging an efficient approximation of the marginal likelihood and simplifying the calculation of determinant and inverse of an intermediate matrix. Combining the Sequential update with the Surrogate Function method further reduces computational costs. The computational complexity per iteration for these three methods is reduced to $\mathcal O(m^3+p^3)$, $\mathcal O(m^3 + d^2)$, $\mathcal O(m^3+p^2)$ respectively, where $p \ll d$ is the final number of features in the model. Our methods demonstrate significant improvements in computational efficiency with comparable performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

NARD employs a matrix normal prior which contains a sparsity-inducing parameter to identify and discard irrelevant features, thereby promoting sparsity in the model. paragraphs: Network Automatic Relevance Determination, or NARD, jointly addresses two modeling needs: identifying sparse relationships between inputs and outputs, and representing correlations among outputs. It extends automatic relevance determination for linear probabilistic models. A matrix normal prior includes a sparsity-promoting parameter that helps identify and discard irrelevant input features.

Training alternates between updating a precision matrix and updating the relationship between outputs and the remaining inputs. The original iteration cost is O(m³ + d³), where m is the number of outputs and d the number of input features. The paper introduces sequential feature evaluation and a surrogate approximation to the marginal likelihood to make these updates less expensive.

Sequential NARD reduces the cost to O(m³ + p³), the surrogate method to O(m³ + d²), and their combination to O(m³ + p²), where p is the final retained feature count and is much smaller than d. Synthetic and real-world experiments show significant efficiency gains with comparable performance. The improvements chiefly reduce the computational burden associated with input features.
summary.tldr: NARD models sparse input–output relationships and output correlations, with accelerated variants that substantially reduce per-iteration costs.

title: Efficient Network Automatic Relevance Determination

abstract: Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) underpins real-time monitoring in cloud services and web systems, allowing rapid identification of anomalies to prevent costly failures. Most TSAD methods driven by forecasting models tend to overfit by emphasizing minor fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that effective TSAD should focus on modeling "normal" behavior through smooth local patterns. To achieve this, we reformulate time series modeling as approximating the series with smooth univariate functions. The local smoothness of each univariate function ensures that the fitted time series remains resilient against local disturbances. However, a direct KAN implementation proves susceptible to these disturbances due to the inherently localized characteristics of B-spline functions. We thus propose KAN-AD, replacing B-splines with truncated Fourier expansions and introducing a novel lightweight learning mechanism that emphasizes global patterns while staying robust to local disturbances. On four popular TSAD benchmarks, KAN-AD achieves an average 15% improvement in detection accuracy (with peaks exceeding 27%) over state-of-the-art baselines. Remarkably, it requires fewer than 1,000 trainable parameters, resulting in a 50% faster inference speed compared to the original KAN, demonstrating the approach’s efficiency and practical viability.

paragraphs: Time-series anomaly detection supports monitoring systems by identifying unusual behavior before failures become costly. Forecasting-based methods can overfit small fluctuations, making them less effective at representing normal operation. This paper argues that useful normal-behavior models should capture smooth local patterns and remain resilient to small disturbances in the observed series.

The authors formulate time-series modeling as approximation with smooth functions of one variable. A direct Kolmogorov–Arnold Network implementation remains sensitive to disturbances because its B-spline functions are inherently localized. KAN-AD replaces these with truncated Fourier expansions and adds a lightweight learning mechanism that emphasizes global patterns. summary.tldr: KAN-AD uses Fourier-based smooth modeling to improve reported anomaly detection accuracy with fewer than 1,000 trainable parameters.

title: KAN-AD: Time Series Anomaly Detection with Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks

abstract: We formalize a new concept for LLMs, context-enhanced learning. It involves standard gradient-based learning on text except that the context is enhanced with additional data on which no auto-regressive gradients are computed. This setting is a gradient-based analog of usual in-context learning (ICL) and appears in some recent works. Using a multi-step reasoning task, we prove in a simplified setting that context-enhanced learning can be exponentially more sample-efficient than standard learning when the model is capable of ICL. At a mechanistic level, we find that the benefit of context-enhancement arises from a more accurate gradient learning signal. We also experimentally demonstrate that it appears hard to detect or recover learning materials that were used in the context during training. This may have implications for data security as well as copyright.

paragraphs: Context-enhanced learning adds information to the context used during ordinary gradient-based language-model training. The additional material is available to the model, but no autoregressive gradients are computed on that material itself. The paper formalizes this arrangement as a gradient-based counterpart to in-context learning and studies why it can help.

title: On the Power of Context-Enhanced Learning in LLMs

abstract: In mechanistic interpretability, recent work scrutinizes transformer “circuits”—sparse, mono or multi layer sub computations, that may reflect human understandable functions. Yet, these network circuits are rarely acid-tested for their stability across different instances of the same deep learning architecture. Without this, it remains unclear whether reported circuits emerge universally across labs or turn out to be idiosyncratic to a particular estimation instance, potentially limiting confidence in safety-critical settings. Here, we systematically study stability across-refits in increasingly complex transformer language models of various sizes. We quantify, layer by layer, how similarly attention heads learn representations across independently initialized training runs. Our rigorous experiments show that (1) middle-layer heads are the least stable yet the most representationally distinct; (2) deeper models exhibit stronger mid-depth divergence; (3) unstable heads in deeper layers become more functionally important than their peers from the same layer; (4) applying weight decay optimization substantially improves attention-head stability across random model initializations; and (5) the residual stream is comparatively stable. Our findings establish the cross-instance robustness of circuits as an essential yet underappreciated prerequisite for scalable oversight, drawing contours around possible white-box monitorability of AI systems.

paragraphs: An interpretable circuit found in one language model may not reappear in another model trained with the same architecture. This paper investigates that uncertainty by comparing attention-head representations across independently initialized training runs. The study examines models of varying size and complexity, asking how reproducible their internal components are at different depths.

The experiments find that middle-layer heads are least stable across runs while also being most distinct in their representations. Greater model depth brings stronger divergence around the middle. In deeper layers, unstable heads become more functionally important than other heads in the same layer, indicating that instability does not simply identify components with little effect on computation.

These findings distinguish reproducibility of individual heads from stability of the broader representations passing through the network. They motivate testing circuit robustness across independently trained instances before relying on a particular circuit for scalable oversight or conclusions about shared internal mechanisms.
summary.tldr: Attention heads vary substantially across independent training runs, especially at mid-depth, while weight decay improves stability and residual streams remain comparatively stable.

title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality

abstract: Continuous-Depth Neural Networks (CDNNs), including Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) and Liquid-Time-Constant Neural Networks (LTC-NN), suffer from high computational costs due to solving numerous nonlinear ODEs during training and inference. We introduce Continuous Depth Acceleration (CoDA), a framework that leverages Mori–Zwanzig/Koopman operator theory to replace continuous-depth layers requiring multiple nonlinear ODEs with a compact GRU module, a single low-dimensional linear ODE, and a dense layer. We prove PAC learnability of CoDA, establishing that this transformation preserves accuracy and can be applied repeatedly across multiple layers with unified backpropagation. Experiments on the Liquid Foundation Model (LFM-1.2B) demonstrate $6.7\times$ training speedup and $1.8\times$ inference speedup without loss of accuracy. Across six real-world LTC-NN applications, CoDA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art acceleration techniques—including neural flows, model order reduction, and variational formulations—in both training and inference time while maintaining competitive or superior accuracy. The implementation and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/ImpactLabASU/CoDA-ICML2026.

paragraphs: Continuous-depth neural networks describe transformations using differential equations, but repeatedly solving many nonlinear equations can make training and inference expensive. This paper introduces Continuous Depth Acceleration, or CoDA, to replace those costly layer computations with a more compact combination of recurrent, linear-dynamics, and dense components.

Drawing on Mori–Zwanzig and Koopman operator theory, CoDA substitutes a small GRU module, one low-dimensional linear ordinary differential equation, and a dense layer for a continuous-depth layer requiring multiple nonlinear equations. The authors prove a PAC learnability result supporting accuracy preservation. They also establish that the transformation can be repeated across multiple layers while retaining a unified backpropagation procedure.
