Across six real-world liquid-time-constant network applications, CoDA also beats the tested acceleration techniques in training and inference time while maintaining competitive or better accuracy. The contribution combines a theoretically supported replacement with measured computational savings in those evaluated models and applications.
summary.tldr: CoDA replaces expensive continuous-depth computations with compact GRU-based modules and linear dynamics, producing substantial measured speedups while preserving accuracy.

title: Efficient Continuous-Depth Modeling with GRU Equivalents

abstract: Existing data poisoning attacks on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems scale poorly because they require costly optimization of poisoned documents for each target phrase. We introduce Eyes-on-Me, a modular attack that decomposes an adversarial document into reusable Attention Attractors and Focus Regions. Attractors are optimized to direct attention to the Focus Region. Attackers can then insert semantic baits for the retriever or malicious instructions for the generator, adapting to new targets at near zero cost. This is achieved by steering a small subset of attention heads that we empirically identify as strongly correlated with attack success. Across 18 end-to-end RAG settings (3 datasets $\times$ 2 retrievers $\times$ 3 generators), Eyes-on-Me raises average attack success rates from 21.9 to 57.8 (+35.9 points, 2.6$\times$ over prior work). A single optimized attractor transfers to unseen black box retrievers and generators without retraining. Our findings establish a scalable paradigm for RAG data poisoning and show that modular, reusable components pose a practical threat to modern AI systems. They also reveal a strong link between attention concentration and model outputs, informing interpretability research.

paragraphs: Eyes-on-Me studies a scalability problem in attacks against retrieval-augmented generation: poisoned documents often require expensive optimization for each new target. The paper introduces a modular design that separates a reusable attention-directing component from the document region containing target-specific content. This separation reduces the work needed to adapt an attack.

The reusable components, called Attention Attractors, direct attention toward Focus Regions. Those regions can contain content aimed at influencing retrieval or instructions aimed at influencing generation. The approach steers a small subset of attention heads that the authors empirically identify as strongly correlated with attack success. Its central finding is that attention steering can transfer across different target contents and systems.

summary.tldr: Eyes-on-Me shows that reusable attention-steering components can make RAG poisoning more transferable and substantially increase attack success.

title: Eyes-on-Me: Scalable RAG Poisoning through Transferable Attention-Steering Attractors

abstract: Transferable jailbreaking attacks enable red-teaming of black-box large language models by optimizing adversarial prompts on open-source surrogates. A natural approach to improve transferability is multi-model training—optimizing against multiple source models simultaneously. Yet this approach has been largely abandoned, as it yields only marginal gains with standard optimizers. We argue the root cause is poor generalization: standard gradient descent lacks stability when aggregating gradients from diverse models. Since GCG and its variants implicitly perform SGD in discrete token space, they inherit this instability in multi-model settings. We address this with Lookahead-GCG, which combines: (1) Stochastic Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (SNAG), whose lookahead mechanism reduces sensitivity to individual gradient updates, providing stability for multi-model optimization; (2) embedding-space momentum accumulation, which enables SNAG in discrete token optimization; and (3) maximally distant initialization, which exploits SNAG’s improved generalization by starting from a universally beneficial point. Experiments show our method achieves 50.37% ASR on open-source and 34.03% on closed-source LLMs, outperforming GCG and TransferAttack with +11.78% gains from multi-model optimization.

paragraphs: Transferable adversarial prompts allow researchers to test black-box language models using attacks developed against accessible surrogate models. Optimizing across several surrogates seems promising, but standard methods have produced only modest benefits. This paper attributes that weakness to unstable optimization when gradients from different models are combined.

Lookahead-GCG applies a stochastic Nesterov optimization approach to reduce sensitivity to individual gradient updates. It combines this with momentum represented in embedding space, enabling the approach to work with discrete prompt tokens. summary.tldr: Lookahead-GCG improves reported jailbreak transferability by stabilizing adversarial prompt optimization across multiple surrogate models.

title: Lookahead-GCG: Improving Universal Multi-Model Optimization-Based Jailbreaking Attacks via Stochastic Nesterov Optimization

abstract: Reasoning segmentation is an emerging vision-language task that requires reasoning over intricate text queries to precisely segment objects. However, existing methods typically suffer from overthinking, generating verbose reasoning chains that interfere with object localization in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To address this issue, we propose DR$^2$Seg, a self-rewarding framework that improves both reasoning efficiency and segmentation accuracy without requiring extra thinking supervision. DR$^2$Seg employs a two-stage rollout strategy that decomposes reasoning segmentation into multimodal reasoning and referring segmentation. In the first stage, the model generates a self-contained description that explicitly specifies the target object. In the second stage, this description replaces the original complex query to verify its self-containment. Based on this design, two self-rewards are introduced to mitigate overthinking and the associated attention dispersion. Extensive experiments conducted on 3B and 7B variants of Qwen2.5-VL, as well as on both SAM2 and SAM3, demonstrate that DR$^2$Seg consistently improves reasoning efficiency and overall segmentation accuracy. The source code can be found at https://github.com/harrylin-hyl/DR2Seg.

paragraphs: Reasoning segmentation requires a model to interpret a complex textual request and identify the exact image region it describes. Long reasoning chains can interfere with this goal by dispersing attention and making object localization harder. DR²Seg addresses this overthinking problem through a self-rewarding framework that does not require additional supervision for the model's thinking.

The method divides each rollout into two stages. First, the model reasons over the image and query to produce a self-contained description of the target object. Second, that description replaces the original complex query for referring segmentation. This substitution checks whether the description contains enough information on its own. Two self-rewards built around this design discourage overthinking and its associated attention dispersion.

Experiments cover the 3B and 7B versions of Qwen2.5-VL and both SAM2 and SAM3. The authors report consistent improvements in reasoning efficiency and overall segmentation accuracy. These findings support making the intermediate reasoning product explicit and usable for localization, so that interpreting the request leads directly to identifying the intended object.
summary.tldr: DR²Seg turns complex queries into self-contained object descriptions, using two-stage self-rewards to improve reasoning efficiency and segmentation accuracy.

title: DR$^2$Seg: Decomposed Two-Stage Rollouts for Efficient Reasoning Segmentation in Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Graphs with heterophily, where adjacent nodes carry different labels, are prevalent in real-world applications, from social networks to molecular interactions. However, existing spectral Graph Neural Network (GNN) approaches tailored for heterophilous graph classification suffer from hub-dominated (node with large degree) aggregation and oversmoothing, as their suboptimal polynomial filters introduce approximation errors and blend distant signals. To address the degree-biased aggregation and suboptimal polynomial filtering, we introduce a Hierarchical Multi-view HAAR (HMH), a novel spectral graph-learning framework that scales in near-linear time. HMH first learns feature- and structure-aware signed affinities via a heterophily-aware encoder, then constructs a soft graph hierarchy guided by these embeddings. At each hierarchical level, HMH constructs a sparse, orthonormal, and locality-aware Haar basis to apply learnable spectral filters in the frequency domain. Finally, skip-connection unpooling layers combine outputs from all hierarchical levels back into the original graph, effectively preventing hub domination and long-range signal bottleneck (over-squashing). Experimentation shows that HMH outperforms state-of-the-art spectral baselines, achieving up to a 3 % improvement on node classification and 7 % on graph classification datasets, all while maintaining linear scalability. Our code is available at https://github.com/sazzad1008/Scalable-HMH101

paragraphs: Hierarchical Multi-view HAAR addresses graph learning when neighboring nodes often have different labels. In this setting, aggregation can become dominated by highly connected nodes, while spectral filtering can blur signals or introduce approximation errors. The proposed framework organizes information across a graph hierarchy to preserve useful distinctions and handle interactions at multiple scales.

HMH first learns signed affinities informed by node features and graph structure, then uses those embeddings to construct a soft hierarchy. At each level, a sparse, orthonormal Haar basis supports learnable filtering in the frequency domain while retaining locality. Skip connections and unpooling combine the hierarchical outputs back at the original graph resolution.

This construction targets hub domination, oversmoothing, and bottlenecks that compress long-range information. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art spectral baselines of up to 3% for node classification and 7% for graph classification, alongside linear scalability in the evaluations. The framework’s stated near-linear computational scaling makes its multiscale treatment relevant to larger graphs, rather than requiring a costly dense representation of their spectral structure.
summary.tldr: HMH uses a learned graph hierarchy and local Haar spectral filters to improve scalable learning on heterophilous graphs.

title: Hierarchical Multi Scale Graph Neural Networks: Scalable Heterophilous Learning with Oversmoothing and Oversquashing Mitigation

abstract: Activation steering offers a computationally efficient mechanism for controlling Large Language Models (LLMs) without fine-tuning. While effectively controlling target traits (e.g., persona), coherency degradation remains a major obstacle to safety and practical deployment. We hypothesize that this degradation stems from intervening on the residual stream, which indiscriminately affects aggregated features and inadvertently amplifies off-target noise. In this work, we identify a sparse subset of attention heads (only three heads) that independently govern persona and style formation, which we term Style Modulation Heads. Specifically, these heads can be localized via geometric analysis of internal representations, combining layer-wise cosine similarity and head-wise contribution scores. We demonstrate that intervention targeting only these specific heads achieves robust behavioral control while significantly mitigating the coherency degradation observed in residual stream steering. More broadly, our findings show that precise, component-level localization enables safer and more precise model control.

paragraphs: Activation steering changes a language model’s internal activity to control behavior without fine-tuning. It can adjust persona, but it can also make responses less coherent. This paper investigates a more targeted intervention, motivated by the hypothesis that changing the residual stream affects many aggregated features and amplifies unwanted signals.

The authors identify three attention heads that independently govern persona and style formation, naming them Style Modulation Heads. They locate these components through geometric analysis that combines cosine similarity across layers with scores measuring individual heads’ contributions. This creates a concrete procedure for identifying where to intervene within the model.

Steering only the identified heads produces robust behavioral control while substantially reducing the coherence degradation observed with residual-stream steering. The result supports locating specific components as a way to make control more precise. The proposed explanation for residual-stream degradation remains a hypothesis in the abstract, while the targeted heads and improved coherence are reported findings from the work.
summary.tldr: Targeting three identified style-related attention heads controls persona while reducing the coherence damage associated with residual-stream steering.

title: Steering at the Source: Style Modulation Heads for Robust Persona Control

abstract: Existing calibration methods for Large Language Models (LLMs) often overlook a critical dimension of trustworthiness: a model’s behavioral robustness to irrelevant or misleading information. In this paper, we argue that a model’s true confidence should reflect its stability under cognitive pressure. We introduce CaliDist, a novel post-hoc calibration approach that directly measures and penalizes a model’s susceptibility to distraction. CaliDist quantifies how an LLM’s predictions and uncertainty change when its input prompt is perturbed with semantic distractors. This stability (or lack thereof) signal is then used to adaptively scale the model’s initial confidence score. Our extensive experiments on seven Natural Language Understanding classification benchmarks using six distinct LLMs show that CaliDist consistently achieves lower Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier Score compared with strong baselines. Remarkably, our method reduces the ECE from 23% to 7% on average—a relative improvement of 70%—demonstrating that behavioral stability is a powerful signal for calibration. We make our code and datasets available at github.com/m-anas-j/CaliDist.

paragraphs: A language model’s confidence is useful only when it tracks how often its answers are correct. CaliDist examines an additional clue: whether the model remains stable when irrelevant or misleading information enters the prompt. The authors argue that confidence should account for this behavioral robustness, rather than relying only on the model’s initial score.

The method operates after prediction by introducing semantic distractors and measuring changes in both predictions and uncertainty. It uses those changes to adjust the original confidence score, penalizing susceptibility to distraction. This makes the calibration signal depend on observed behavior under altered inputs, connecting reported certainty to how easily the model’s judgment can be disturbed.

Across seven language-understanding classification benchmarks and six language models, CaliDist achieves lower Expected Calibration Error and Brier Score than strong baselines. Average calibration error falls from 23% to 7%, reported as a 70% relative improvement. These results support behavioral stability as a useful calibration signal in the evaluated classification settings.
summary.tldr: CaliDist improves confidence calibration by measuring how strongly distractions change a model’s predictions and uncertainty.

title: CaliDist: Calibrating Large Language Models via Behavioral Robustness to Distraction

abstract: Many modern retrieval problems are set-valued: given a broad intent, the system must return a collection of results that optimizes higherorder properties (e.g., diversity, coverage, complementarity, coherence) while staying grounded to a fixed database. Set-valued objectives are inherently non-decomposable and are not captured by existing supervised (query, content) datasets which only prioritize top-1 retrieval. While reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize set-level objectives via interaction, deploying an RL-tuned LLM for fan-out retrieval is prohibitively expensive at query time. Conversely, diffusion-based generative retrieval enables efficient single-pass fan-out in embedding space, but requires objective-aligned training targets. To address these issues, we propose R4T (Retrieve-for-Train), which uses RL once as an objective transducer in a three step process: (i) train a fan-out LLM with composite set-level rewards, (ii) synthesize objective-consistent training pairs, and (iii) train a lightweight diffusion retriever to model the conditional distribution of set-valued outputs. Across Polyvore and a music playlist dataset, R4T improves retrieval quality over strong baselines while reducing query-time fan-out latency by an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Some retrieval tasks require a useful collection of items rather than one highly relevant result. Qualities such as diversity, coverage, and compatibility depend on relationships within the collection, so optimizing individual query–item matches does not fully capture the objective. This paper studies how to learn those collection-level properties while keeping results grounded in a fixed database.

R4T, or Retrieve-for-Train, uses reinforcement learning during training to make that objective available to a cheaper retriever. First, it trains a language model to produce multiple retrieval outputs using combined set-level rewards. Next, it uses that model to create training pairs reflecting the desired properties. Finally, a lightweight diffusion model learns the conditional distribution of these collections in embedding space.

Experiments on Polyvore and a music playlist dataset report better retrieval quality than strong baselines, together with an order-of-magnitude reduction in query-time fan-out latency. The approach separates learning a complex collection objective from serving requests. The expensive reinforcement-trained model supplies supervision, while the diffusion retriever carries that learned behavior into a more efficient retrieval process.
summary.tldr: R4T transfers collection-level retrieval objectives from an RL-trained language model into a lightweight diffusion retriever, improving quality and reducing query latency.

title: Efficient, Property-Aligned Fan-Out Retrieval via RL-Compiled Diffusion

abstract: This paper presents OvisOCR, a lightweight and strictly end-to-end Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) tailored for document parsing. Unlike current methods that rely on complex "Crop-OCR-Merge’" cascades to handle high-resolution inputs, OvisOCR directly maps full-page visual signals to structured Markdown without localized slicing or layout detection dependencies. Through extensive evaluations on the OmniDocBench, OvisOCR achieves top-tier performance among all compared methods in all aspects, demonstrating that a compact E2E model can effectively “digest” the capabilities of intricate pipelines and surpass specialized and general methods. Technically, OvisOCR unifies fine-grained recognition and semantic correction in a single model by leveraging supervision bootstrapped from strong OCR engines and refined via general-model-based data cleaning. To balance the performance across diverse document constituents, we design category-specific reward mechanisms for distinct element types, such as dense text, complex tables, and formulas, and ensure the model enhances its formatting strengths for each modality concurrently. This approach effectively resolves the optimization conflict, guaranteeing that improvements in structural layout parsing do not come at the expense of omitting fine-grained textual details. Empirical results confirm that OvisOCR eliminates the error propagation inherent in split-and-merge architectures, offering a streamlined path for future document intelligence. Our model is available at https://huggingface.co/ATH-MaaS/OvisOCR.

abstract: Controlling autonomous systems under real-world conditions often requires policies that can be evaluated with low latency and minimal energy consumption. Unfortunately, these conditions are at odds with the use of high-precision deep neural networks as controllers. In this work, we introduce Differentiable Weightless Controllers (DWCs), a symbolic-differentiable architecture that learns flexible, non-linear, yet highly efficient control policies. DWCs can be trained end-to-end via gradient-based techniques, yet compile directly into FPGA-compatible circuits with few- or even single-clock-cycle latency and nanojoule-level energy cost per action. Across five MuJoCo benchmarks, including high-dimensional Humanoid, DWCs achieve returns competitive with standard deep policies (full-precision or quantized neural networks). Furthermore, DWCs exhibit structurally sparse and interpretable connectivity patterns, enabling direct inspection of which input values influence control decisions.

paragraphs: Autonomous systems need to turn observations into actions quickly and with little energy. High-precision neural controllers can make those deployment requirements difficult to meet. This paper introduces Differentiable Weightless Controllers, an architecture designed to learn flexible, nonlinear control policies while producing a particularly efficient hardware implementation.

The central idea is to connect gradient-based learning with symbolic circuit execution. Controllers can be trained end to end using gradient-based techniques, then compiled directly into circuits compatible with field-programmable gate arrays, or FPGAs. The abstract reports action evaluation in a few clock cycles, sometimes just one, with energy costs at the nanojoule level.

Across five MuJoCo benchmarks, including the high-dimensional Humanoid task, these controllers achieve returns competitive with standard full-precision and quantized neural policies. Their connectivity is also structurally sparse and interpretable, allowing inspection of which inputs influence decisions. The findings show that the proposed architecture can combine competitive benchmark control performance with low-cost circuit execution and a more inspectable decision structure.
summary.tldr: Differentiable Weightless Controllers learn competitive continuous-control policies that compile directly into fast, energy-efficient logic circuits.

title: Differentiable Weightless Controllers: Learning Logic Circuits for Continuous Control

abstract: Latent visual reasoning aims to mimic human’s imagination process by meditating through hidden states of Multimodal Large Language Models. While recognized as a promising paradigm for visual reasoning, the underlying mechanisms driving its effectiveness remain unclear. Motivated to demystify the true source of its efficacy, we investigate the validity of latent reasoning using Causal Mediation Analysis. We model the process as a causal chain: the input as the treatment, the latent tokens as the mediator, and the final answer as the outcome. Our findings uncover two critical disconnections: (a) Input-Latent Disconnect: dramatic perturbations on the input result in negligible changes to the latent tokens, suggesting that latent tokens do not effectively attend to the input sequence. (b) Latent-Answer Disconnect: perturbations on the latent tokens yield minimal impact on the final answer, indicating the limited causal effect latent tokens imposing on the outcome. Furthermore, extensive probing analysis reveals that latent tokens encode limited visual information and exhibit high similarity. Consequently, we challenge the necessity of latent reasoning and propose a straightforward alternative named CapImagine, which teaches the model to explicitly imagine using text. Experiments on vision-centric benchmarks show that CapImagine significantly outperforms complex latent-space baselines, highlighting the superior potential of visual reasoning through explicit imagination.

paragraphs: Latent visual reasoning aims to support visual problem solving through hidden intermediate tokens, loosely resembling an imagination process. This paper investigates whether those tokens actually connect the input to the answer. It uses causal mediation analysis, treating the input as the starting cause, latent tokens as intermediates, and the answer as the outcome.

The authors report two weak connections in the systems studied. Large input perturbations cause little change in latent tokens, and perturbing those tokens has little effect on final answers. Additional probes find limited visual information and high similarity among the tokens. These observations question how much the examined latent computations contribute to reasoning.

Motivated by that diagnosis, the authors introduce CapImagine, which teaches the model to express its imagined visual content through text. On vision-centric benchmarks, it substantially outperforms the evaluated latent-space baselines. The results support explicit textual imagination as an effective alternative in these experiments, while the causal findings specifically concern the latent reasoning behavior investigated.
summary.tldr: The studied latent visual reasoning tokens have weak causal influence, while explicit textual imagination improves benchmark performance.

title: Imagination Helps Visual Reasoning, But Not Yet in Latent Space

abstract: Flow-based generative models can be viewed through a physics lens: sampling transports a particle from noise to data by integrating a learned velocity field, and each sample corresponds to a trajectory with its own dynamical effort. Motivated by classical mechanics, we introduce Kinetic Path Energy (KPE), an action-like, per-sample diagnostic that measures the accumulated kinetic effort along an ordinary differential equation (ODE) trajectory. Empirically, KPE exhibits two robust correspondences: i higher KPE predicts stronger semantic fidelity; ii high-KPE trajectories land in sparse representation regions. We further provide theoretical guarantees linking trajectory energy to data sparsity. Paradoxically, this correlation is non-monotonic. At sufficiently high energy, generation can degenerate into memorization. Leveraging the closed-form formula of empirical flow matching, we show that extreme energies drive trajectories toward near-copies of training examples. This yields a Goldilocks principle and motivates Kinetic Trajectory Shaping (KTS), a training-free two-phase inference strategy that boosts early motion and enforces a late-time soft landing, reducing memorization and improving generation quality across benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Flow-based generators create samples by moving from noise toward data along a learned velocity field. This paper studies how much motion each individual sampling path accumulates. Its diagnostic, Kinetic Path Energy, measures the total kinetic effort along that path, providing a way to examine generation at the level of individual samples.

The authors report two empirical relationships: higher energy tends to accompany stronger semantic fidelity, and high-energy paths tend to end in sparsely populated representation regions. They also give theoretical guarantees connecting trajectory energy with data sparsity. However, the relationship between energy and useful generation is not uniformly positive. Their analysis of empirical flow matching shows that extreme energies can push outputs toward near-copies of training examples.

These findings motivate an intermediate-energy principle: additional motion can help, but excessive energy can encourage memorization. The proposed Kinetic Trajectory Shaping method increases early motion and softens the trajectory near its end. This two-phase sampling change requires no retraining and improves generation quality while reducing memorization across the reported benchmark tasks.
summary.tldr: Measuring sampling-path energy reveals a balance between semantic fidelity and memorization, motivating a training-free method that shapes early and late motion.

title: A Kinetic Energy Perspective of Flow Matching

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) possess intrinsic reasoning and world-knowledge capabilities, yet adapting them for dense retrieval remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on invasive parameter updates, such as full fine-tuning and LoRA, which may disrupt the pre-trained semantic space and impair the structured knowledge essential for reasoning. To address this, we propose SLQ, a parameter-efficient tuning framework that adapts MLLMs for retrieval while keeping the backbone entirely frozen. SLQ introduces a small set of Shared Latent Queries that are appended to both text and image tokens, leveraging the model’s native causal attention to aggregate multimodal context into a unified embedding space. Furthermore, to better evaluate retrieval beyond superficial pattern matching, we construct KARR-Bench, a benchmark designed for knowledge-aware reasoning retrieval. Extensive experiments show that SLQ outperforms full fine-tuning and LoRA on COCO and Flickr30K, while achieving competitive performance on MMEB and yielding substantial gains on KARR-Bench, validating that preserving the pre-trained representations via non-invasive adaptation is an effective strategy for MLLM-based retrieval. The code is available under: https://github.com/CnFaker/SLQ.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models contain useful semantic knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but adapting them for retrieval can alter the representations supporting those abilities. SLQ investigates how to build retrieval embeddings while keeping the model backbone entirely frozen. The aim is to preserve pretrained representations while learning a small adaptation component.

The method appends shared latent queries to both text and image tokens. Through the model’s existing causal attention, these queries gather information from the multimodal context into a common embedding space. This gives retrieval a trainable interface without changing the backbone parameters. The authors also introduce KARR-Bench to evaluate retrieval that requires knowledge-aware reasoning beyond superficial matching.

These findings support frozen-backbone adaptation as an effective retrieval strategy in the evaluated settings. The contribution connects parameter efficiency with preservation of pretrained structure, while testing the resulting embeddings on both established retrieval datasets and a reasoning-oriented benchmark.
summary.tldr: SLQ learns shared queries over a frozen multimodal model to produce strong retrieval embeddings while preserving backbone parameters.

title: SLQ: Bridging Modalities via Shared Latent Queries for Retrieval with Frozen MLLMs

abstract: Generating simulation-ready tabletop scenes from task instructions is an intriguing and promising research direction in the field of Embodied AI. However, existing task-to-scene generation methods rely exclusively on large language models (LLMs) to predict scene layouts, inevitably yielding object collisions or floating due to LLMs’ inherent limitations in 3D spatial reasoning. In this paper, we present STABLE, a semantics–physics dual-system tailored for simulation-ready tabletop scene generation. STABLE consists of two complementary modules: (i) a Semantic Reasoner, a fine-tuned LLM trained on a structured tabletop scene dataset to generate coarse layouts from input task instructions, and (ii) a Physics Corrector, a physics-aware flow-based denoising model that outputs pose updates to refine layouts, which ensures the physical plausibility of scenes while preserves semantic alignment with task instructions. STABLE adopts a progressive generation paradigm: by alternating between the Semantic Reasoner and Physics Corrector, it incrementally expands the scene from task-critical objects to background objects. Experiments demonstrate that STABLE successfully generates simulation-ready tabletop scenes that strictly conform to task instructions and significantly enhances the physical validity of scenes over prior art.

paragraphs: Creating a tabletop scene from a task description requires both understanding the requested arrangement and placing objects in physically plausible poses. Language-model layout predictions can produce collisions or floating objects because three-dimensional spatial reasoning is difficult. STABLE separates semantic planning and physical correction into complementary modules that work together to produce scenes ready for simulation.

A Semantic Reasoner, fine-tuned on structured tabletop scenes, generates a coarse layout from the task instructions. A Physics Corrector then uses a physics-aware flow-based denoising model to predict pose updates. These updates refine the arrangement while preserving its connection to the requested task. The system therefore explicitly couples the meaning of a scene with its physical validity.

Generation proceeds progressively, alternating the two modules as the scene grows from task-critical objects to background objects. This gives semantic planning and physical refinement recurring roles throughout construction. Experiments report simulation-ready scenes that strictly follow task instructions and substantially improve physical validity over prior approaches. The findings support combining language-based planning with learned physical correction for instruction-driven scene generation.
summary.tldr: STABLE alternates semantic layout generation and physical correction to create instruction-aligned tabletop scenes ready for simulation.

title: STABLE: Simulation-Ready Tabletop Layout Generation via a Semantics–Physics Dual System

abstract: Centralized multimodal learning commonly compresses language, acoustic, and visual signals into a single fused representation for prediction. While effective, this paradigm suffers from two limitations: modality dominance, where optimization gravitates towards the path of least resistance, ignoring weaker but informative modalities, and spurious modality coupling, where models overfit to incidental cross-modal correlations. To address these, we propose Group Cognition Learning (GCL), a governed collaboration paradigm that applies a two-stage protocol after modality-specific encoding. In Stage 1 (Selective Interaction), a Routing Agent proposes directed interaction routes, and an Auditing Agent assigns sample-wise gates to emphasize exchanges that yield positive marginal predictive gain while suppressing redundant coupling. In Stage 2 (Consensus Formation), a Public-Factor Agent maintains an explicit shared factor, and an Aggregation Agent produces the final prediction through contribution-aware weighting while keeping each modality representation as a specialization channel. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and MIntRec demonstrate that GCL mitigates dominance and coupling, establishing state-of-the-art results across both regression and classification benchmarks. Analysis experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of the design.

paragraphs: Combining language, sound, and visual information into one representation can cause a model to favor the easiest signal and overlook weaker but useful ones. It can also encourage reliance on incidental relationships between modalities. Group Cognition Learning addresses these problems through a governed collaboration process after each modality has been encoded separately.

The first stage controls information exchange. A Routing Agent proposes directed interactions, and an Auditing Agent assigns gates for each sample, emphasizing exchanges that add predictive value while suppressing redundant coupling. The second stage forms a consensus: a Public-Factor Agent maintains shared information, while an Aggregation Agent weights contributions to produce the final prediction.

Throughout this process, each modality retains a representation for its specialized information. Additional analyses support the design. The findings suggest that controlling which modalities exchange information, and how their contributions are combined, can improve multimodal prediction.
summary.tldr: Group Cognition Learning governs cross-modal exchanges and contribution weighting to reduce modality dominance and improve multimodal prediction.

title: Group Cognition Learning: Making Everything Better Through Governed Two-Stage Agents Collaboration

abstract: Stochastic-gradient MCMC methods enable scalable Bayesian posterior sampling but often suffer from sensitivity to minibatch size and gradient noise. To address this, we propose Stochastic Gradient Lattice Random Walk (SGLRW), an extension of the Lattice Random Walk discretisation. Unlike conventional Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD), SGLRW introduces stochastic noise only through the off-diagonal elements of the update covariance; this yields greater robustness to minibatch size while retaining asymptotic correctness. Furthermore, as a comparison we analyse a natural analogue of SGLD utilising gradient clipping. Experimental validation on Bayesian regression and classification demonstrates that SGLRW remains stable in regimes where SGLD fails, including in the presence of heavy-tailed gradient noise, and matches or improves predictive performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian posterior sampling can become computationally practical by estimating gradients from minibatches, but the resulting noise can make sampling unstable. Stochastic Gradient Lattice Random Walk addresses sensitivity to minibatch size and gradient noise through a different discretization of the sampling process. It extends an existing lattice random-walk approach.

The distinguishing feature is how stochastic noise enters the update covariance: SGLRW introduces it only through off-diagonal elements. The authors connect this design to greater robustness across minibatch sizes while retaining asymptotic correctness. They also analyze a gradient-clipped analogue of Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics as a comparison, examining another way to handle troublesome gradients.

Experiments on Bayesian regression and classification find that SGLRW stays stable in settings where SGLD fails, including settings with heavy-tailed gradient noise. Predictive performance matches or improves on the comparison method. The findings indicate that changing the structure of the sampling update can improve practical robustness while preserving the method's stated long-run correctness property.
summary.tldr: SGLRW changes the covariance structure of stochastic-gradient sampling to improve robustness while retaining asymptotic correctness.

title: Robust Stochastic Gradient Posterior Sampling with Lattice Based Discretisation

abstract: Reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence-based regularization with respect to a fixed reference policy is widely used in modern reinforcement learning to preserve the desired traits of the reference policy and sometimes to promote exploration (using uniform reference policy, known as entropy regularization). Beyond serving as a mere anchor, the reference policy can also be interpreted as encoding prior knowledge about good actions in the environment. In the context of alignment, recent game-theoretic approaches have leveraged KL regularization with pretrained language models as reference policies, achieving notable empirical success in self-play methods. Despite these advances, the theoretical benefits of KL regularization in game-theoretic settings remain poorly understood. In this work, we develop and analyze algorithms that provably achieve improved sample efficiency under KL regularization. We study both two-player zero-sum Matrix games and Markov games: for Matrix games, we propose OMG, an algorithm based on best response sampling with optimistic bonuses, and extend this idea to Markov games through the algorithm SOMG, which also uses best response sampling and a novel concept of superoptimistic bonuses. Both algorithms achieve a logarithmic regret in $T$ that scales inversely with the KL regularization strength $\beta$ in addition to the traditional $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret without the $\beta^{-1}$ dependence.

paragraphs: KL regularization encourages a learning policy to remain close to a fixed reference policy. That reference can preserve desired behavior or express prior knowledge about useful actions; a uniform reference gives entropy regularization. Although such regularization has worked empirically in game-based alignment methods, its theoretical benefits for learning in games have been less clear.

This paper develops algorithms for two-player zero-sum matrix games and Markov games. The matrix-game algorithm, OMG, combines best-response sampling with optimistic bonuses. SOMG extends this approach to Markov games and introduces superoptimistic bonuses. The analysis establishes improved sample-efficiency guarantees under KL regularization, giving a theoretical role to the reference-policy penalty beyond keeping policies anchored.

Both algorithms obtain regret bounds that grow logarithmically with the number of rounds, T, with an inverse dependence on regularization strength, beta. They also have the traditional approximately square-root-in-T guarantee without that inverse-beta dependence. Thus, the logarithmic result comes with an explicit tradeoff: its bound becomes less favorable as regularization weakens.
summary.tldr: New algorithms achieve logarithmic regret in KL-regularized zero-sum games, with bounds that depend inversely on regularization strength.

title: Achieving Logarithmic Regret in KL-Regularized Zero-Sum Markov Games

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) break the rigid left-to-right constraint of traditional LLMs, enabling token generation in arbitrary orders. Intuitively, this flexibility implies a solution space that strictly supersets the fixed autoregressive trajectory, theoretically unlocking superior reasoning potential. However, in this paper, we find that for general reasoning tasks (e.g., mathematics and coding), arbitrary order generation may in fact limit the reasoning potential of dLLMs. We observe that dLLMs tend to exploit this order flexibility to bypass high-uncertainty tokens that are crucial for exploration, which can lead to a premature collapse of solution coverage. This observation motivates a rethink of RL approaches for dLLMs, where considerable complexities, such as handling combinatorial trajectories and intractable likelihoods, are often devoted to preserving this flexibility. We show that effective reasoning can be elicited by simply forgoing arbitrary order and applying standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) instead. Our approach, JustGRPO, is minimalist yet surprisingly effective (e.g., 89.1% accuracy on GSM8K) while fully retaining the parallel decoding ability of dLLMs. Code: https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/JustGRPO.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate tokens in arbitrary orders, creating more possible generation paths than a fixed left-to-right process. This paper investigates why that freedom may fail to improve reasoning. On general reasoning tasks such as mathematics and coding, the authors observe behavior that can make the flexibility counterproductive.

The models tend to bypass highly uncertain tokens that are important for exploring possible solutions. Avoiding those choices can narrow solution coverage prematurely. This observation challenges the value of reinforcement learning machinery devoted to preserving arbitrary-order generation, especially when doing so introduces complicated trajectories and difficult likelihood calculations.

The proposed JustGRPO approach gives up arbitrary generation order and applies standard Group Relative Policy Optimization. It still retains parallel decoding, separating that efficiency benefit from order flexibility. The paper reports strong reasoning performance, including 89.1% accuracy on GSM8K. The result supports a simpler training route and shows that arbitrary order can be dispensable for effective reasoning in the evaluated setting; it does not establish that generation-order flexibility is always harmful.
summary.tldr: JustGRPO improves diffusion-model reasoning by dropping arbitrary generation order while retaining parallel decoding.

title: The Flexibility Trap: Rethinking the Value of Arbitrary Order in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Value factorization eases non-stationarity in MARL, but its static coordination assumptions hinder generalization on long-horizon tasks with shifting dependencies. Prior VQ-VAE methods abstract trajectories yet miss time-varying inter-agent dependencies. We present TACTIC, a CTDE framework with three components: (i) VQ-VAE-based trajectory abstraction that learns discrete task-semantic classes; (ii) semantic-conditioned sparse coordination graphs that adapt dependencies by pruning edges according to variance-based pairwise payoff sensitivity; and (iii) a pretrained, frozen trajectory-class predictor that conditions local policies while decoupling task recognition from control. On SMAC and SUMO, TACTIC shows strong overall competitiveness and adaptive coordination under sparse rewards and dynamic task structures.

TACTIC addresses this by connecting task recognition to sparse coordination graphs within a framework that uses centralized training and decentralized execution.

The central contribution is making trajectory abstraction useful for changing inter-agent coordination over time.
summary.tldr: TACTIC uses discrete task semantics to adapt sparse coordination graphs and condition local policies in multi-agent learning.

title: TACTIC: Task-Aware Sparse Coordination Graphs for Multi-Task Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) enables precise manipulation of individual atoms and molecules, offering a pathway to constructing nanoscale assemblies with rich quantum mechanical behavior. Despite its potential, STM-based fabrication remains limited by the inherent complexity of manipulation procedures and the extensive manual effort required. In this work, we take a substantial step toward autonomous manufacturing with STMs by introducing a novel AI-based planning framework for molecular assembly and a high-fidelity simulation environment. Our framework computes collision-free assembly plans that minimize the total distance traveled by molecules. Given an assignment of molecules to target positions, satisfiability solving is used to compute execution schedules in which each molecule has an empty corridor available when it is scheduled to move. Reinforcement learning (RL) agents then execute sequences of STM actions to manipulate molecules to their targets. We further introduce NanoAssemblyGym, a high-fidelity simulation environment for molecular manipulation built on the Gymnasium API, allowing seamless integration with existing RL libraries and workflows. Using NanoAssemblyGym, we demonstrate autonomous assembly of structures containing up to 420 molecules.

This paper combines planning, constraint solving, and reinforcement learning to automate molecular assembly. It also introduces a simulation environment for developing and evaluating the required manipulation behavior.

The planning framework computes collision-free assembly plans while minimizing the total distance molecules travel. Given an assignment of molecules to destinations, a satisfiability solver schedules their movements so that each molecule has an empty corridor when its turn arrives. Within this environment, they demonstrate autonomous assembly of structures containing up to 420 molecules. The contribution joins coordination across many molecules with learned execution of individual movements, showing how formal scheduling and learned control can work together in simulated nanoscale fabrication.
summary.tldr: Constraint-based scheduling and reinforcement learning enable simulated autonomous assembly of structures containing up to 420 molecules.

title: Efficient and Safe Molecular Assembly via Reinforcement Learning and Constraint Solving

abstract: A popular approach to post-training control of large language models (LLMs) is the steering of intermediate latent representations. Namely, identify a well-chosen direction depending on the task at hand and perturbs representations along this direction at inference time. While many propositions exist to pick this direction, considerably less is understood about how to choose the magnitude of the move, whereas its importance is clear: too little and the intended behavior does not emerge, too much and the model’s performance degrades beyond repair. In this work, we propose the first theoretical analysis of steering strength. We characterize its effect on next token probability, presence of a concept, and cross-entropy, deriving precise qualitative laws governing these quantities. Our analysis reveals surprising behaviors, including non-monotonic effects of steering strength. We validate our theoretical predictions empirically on eleven language models, ranging from a small GPT architecture to modern models.

paragraphs: Steering a language model changes its intermediate representations along a chosen direction during inference. Selecting the direction receives considerable attention, but the size of the intervention is equally consequential. A small change may fail to induce the intended behavior, while an excessive change can severely damage performance.

This paper develops a theoretical analysis of steering strength. It characterizes how intervention magnitude affects next-token probability, the presence of a concept, and cross-entropy. Examining these quantities together connects the immediate output distribution with the intended behavioral effect and with a measure of predictive performance.

The analysis produces qualitative laws, including non-monotonic behavior: increasing steering strength need not continue changing an outcome in the same direction. The authors empirically validate their predictions on eleven language models spanning a small GPT architecture and modern models. The findings establish that strength is a substantive part of the intervention, whose effects cannot generally be understood by assuming that more movement along a chosen direction always produces more of the desired behavior.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments show that steering strength can affect language-model behavior non-monotonically, making intervention magnitude crucial to effective control.

title: Towards Understanding Steering Strength

abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models and Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) have achieved remarkable progress in visual generation. However, their reliance on a single-pass generation paradigm limits their ability to handle complex prompts requiring iterative refinement. To enable multi-round Reflective Visual Generation (RVG), we formalize the Reason–Reflect–Rectify (R$^3$) loop as a core framework and introduce R$^3$-Bench, a benchmark of over 600 expert-annotated instances that quantifies iterative reasoning and rectification capabilities. Evaluation on R$^3$-Bench reveals a critical gap: while state-of-the-art models can identify generation errors, they fail to generate actionable rectification instructions. To bridge this gap, we propose R$^3$-Refiner, a dual-stage framework leveraging Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and a Hierarchical Reward Mechanism (HRM) to better align rectification with reflective reasoning. Experiments show that R$^3$-Refiner achieves significant improvements on R$^3$-Bench (+12.0% in Reflective Verdict Score, +9.0% in Rectification Score), and can be seamlessly integrated with various MLLMs to enhance the generation quality of different T2I models on GenEval++ and T2I-CompBench. Code is available at https://github.com/xiaomoguhz/R3-Bench.

paragraphs: Generating an image once leaves little room to correct mistakes in complex prompts. This paper formalizes a repeated Reason–Reflect–Rectify process: reason about the task, assess the generated result, and produce instructions for correction. It introduces R³-Bench, containing more than 600 expert-annotated instances, to evaluate the reasoning and correction abilities needed for this process.

Benchmark evaluations reveal a specific gap: the evaluated leading models can recognize generation errors but struggle to turn that recognition into actionable editing instructions. R³-Refiner addresses this gap through two stages of training that use Group Relative Policy Optimization and a hierarchical reward mechanism. The aim is to connect reflective judgments more closely to useful corrective actions.

The authors report improvements of 12.0% in Reflective Verdict Score and 9.0% in Rectification Score on R³-Bench. They also report improved image-generation quality on GenEval++ and T2I-CompBench when integrating the refiner with different multimodal and image-generation models. The findings emphasize that identifying an error and explaining how to fix it are distinct capabilities.
summary.tldr: R³-Bench evaluates iterative visual correction, and R³-Refiner trains models to turn detected image errors into more useful correction instructions.

title: Benchmarking and Evolving Reason-Reflect-Rectify for Reflective Visual Generation

abstract: Many optimizers can be interpreted as steepest-descent methods under norm-induced geometries, and thus inherit corresponding implicit biases. We introduce Orthogonal Lion which combines spectral control from orthogonalized update directions with $\ell_\infty$-style coordinate control from sign updates. OLion forms a Lion-style momentum direction, approximately orthogonalizes it via a few Newton–Schulz iterations, and then applies an entrywise sign, providing an efficient approximation to taking a maximal step over the intersection of the spectral and $\ell_\infty$ constraint sets (a scaled Hadamard-like set for matrix parameters). Despite the strong nonlinearity of orthogonalization and sign, we prove convergence under a mild, empirically verified diagonal-isotropy assumption. Across large-scale language and vision training, including GPT-2 and Llama pretraining, SiT image pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning, OLion matches or outperforms AdamW and Muon under comparable tuning while using only momentum-level optimizer state, and it mitigates optimizer mismatch when fine-tuning AdamW-pretrained checkpoints.

paragraphs: An optimizer’s update rule can favor particular geometric patterns in parameter changes. Orthogonal Lion, or OLion, combines two such influences: spectral control from orthogonalized directions and coordinate-level control from sign updates. The aim is to approximate a large step that respects both types of constraints for matrix parameters.

OLion first constructs a Lion-style momentum direction, approximately orthogonalizes it with a few Newton–Schulz iterations, and then takes the sign of each entry. The resulting update approximates optimization over an intersection of spectral and infinity-norm constraint sets. The authors prove convergence under a diagonal-isotropy assumption that they describe as mild and verify empirically; the guarantee depends on that assumption.

Evaluations span language and vision training, including GPT-2 and Llama pretraining, SiT image pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning. Under comparable tuning, OLion matches or exceeds AdamW and Muon while retaining only momentum-level optimizer state. It also reduces optimizer mismatch when fine-tuning checkpoints pretrained with AdamW, connecting the proposed geometry to practical training and adaptation results.
summary.tldr: OLion combines approximate orthogonalization and sign updates, delivering competitive training results with momentum-level optimizer state.

title: OLion: Approaching the Hadamard Ideal by Intersecting Spectral and $\ell_∞$ Implicit Biases

abstract: Recent genomic foundation models largely adopt large language model architectures that treat DNA as a one-dimensional token sequence. However, exhaustive sequential reading is structurally misaligned with sparse and discontinuous genomic semantics, leading to wasted computation on low-information background and preventing understanding-driven compression for long contexts. Here, we present OpticalDNA, a vision-based framework that reframes genomic modeling as Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-style document understanding. OpticalDNA renders DNA into structured visual layouts and trains an OCR-capable vision–language model with a visual DNA encoder and a document decoder, where the encoder produces compact, reconstructible visual tokens for high-fidelity compression. Building on this representation, OpticalDNA defines prompt-conditioned objectives over core genomic primitives—reading, region grounding, subsequence retrieval, and masked span completion—thereby learning layout-aware DNA representations that retain fine-grained genomic information under a reduced effective token budget. Across diverse genomic benchmarks, OpticalDNA consistently outperforms recent baselines; on sequences up to 450k bases, it achieves the best overall performance with nearly $20\times$ fewer effective tokens, and surpasses models with up to $985\times$ more activated parameters while tuning only 256k trainable parameters.

paragraphs: OpticalDNA treats DNA as a structured visual document. The paper argues that reading every position as a one-dimensional token sequence spends computation on low-information background and fits poorly with genomic meaning that can be sparse and discontinuous. Its alternative aims to preserve detailed information using a smaller effective token budget.

The framework renders DNA into visual layouts and trains an OCR-capable vision-language model with a visual DNA encoder and a document decoder. The encoder produces compact tokens from which the visual information can be reconstructed. Prompt-conditioned tasks cover reading, locating regions, retrieving subsequences, and completing masked spans, giving the representation several ways to retain and use genomic detail.

It also surpasses models with up to 985 times more activated parameters while tuning only 256,000 parameters. These are distinct efficiency measures: the reported trainable-parameter count describes what is tuned, rather than the entire model size.
summary.tldr: OpticalDNA models DNA as visual documents, reporting strong genomic performance with nearly 20 times fewer effective tokens on long sequences.

title: Rethinking Genomic Modeling Through Optical Character Recognition

abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) on open-ended tasks without ground-truth labels is increasingly done via the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm. A critical but under-modeled issue is that judge LLMs differ substantially in reliability; treating all judges equally can yield biased leaderboards and misleading uncertainty estimates—more data can make evaluation more confidently wrong under misspecified aggregation. We propose a judge-aware ranking framework that extends the Bradley-Terry-Luce model by introducing judge-specific discrimination parameters, jointly estimating latent model quality and judge reliability from pairwise comparisons without reference labels. We establish identifiability up to natural normalizations and prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, enabling confidence intervals for score differences and rank comparisons. Across multiple public benchmarks and a newly collected dataset, our method improves agreement with human preferences, achieves higher data efficiency than unweighted baselines, and produces calibrated uncertainty quantification for LLM rankings.

paragraphs: When open-ended responses have no reference answers, evaluators often ask language models to judge competing outputs. Those judges differ in reliability. Treating their decisions as equally informative can distort a leaderboard and its uncertainty estimates; collecting more comparisons can then increase confidence in an incorrect ranking.

This paper extends the Bradley-Terry-Luce model for pairwise comparisons with a separate discrimination parameter for each judge. The framework jointly estimates the underlying quality of evaluated models and the reliability of judges without reference labels. It establishes that these quantities are identifiable after natural normalizations, and proves consistency and asymptotic normality for its maximum-likelihood estimator.

Those statistical results support confidence intervals for quality differences and comparisons between ranks, making uncertainty part of the ranking procedure. Across public benchmarks and a newly collected dataset, the method agrees better with human preferences, uses comparison data more efficiently than unweighted baselines, and produces calibrated uncertainty estimates. The findings show why modeling who makes a judgment can matter alongside collecting the judgment itself.
summary.tldr: Jointly estimating judge reliability and model quality improves reference-free LLM rankings and their uncertainty estimates.

title: A Judge-Aware Ranking Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models without Ground Truth

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has gained popularity as a fine-tuning approach for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its low resource requirements and good performance. While numerous studies have investigated improving LoRA serving efficiency by serving multiple LoRAs concurrently, existing methods assume that a wide range of LoRA adapters are available for serving. In our work, we conduct extensive empirical studies to show that current LoRA training paradigms do not efficiently utilize hardware resources and incur high overhead to obtain a performant LoRA adapter. Leveraging these insights, we propose PLoRA, which automatically orchestrates concurrent LoRA fine-tuning jobs under given hardware and model constraints and develops performant kernels to improve training efficiency. Across a range of LLMs and LoRA configurations, PLoRA improves training throughput by up to 12.8x and reduces the overall fine-tuning makespan by up to 7.52x compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: LoRA offers a resource-efficient way to fine-tune language models, but producing many useful adapters still requires efficient training. This paper focuses on that production stage. The authors note that work on serving multiple adapters often assumes they already exist, leaving the cost of creating them insufficiently addressed.

Empirical studies identify poor hardware utilization and substantial overhead in current LoRA training paradigms. PLoRA responds by automatically coordinating concurrent fine-tuning jobs according to the available hardware and model constraints. It also introduces efficient kernels, addressing both how jobs are scheduled together and how their computations execute.

Across a range of language models and LoRA configurations, PLoRA improves training throughput by up to 12.8 times and reduces total fine-tuning makespan by up to 7.52 times relative to existing approaches. Throughput captures how much training work the system handles, while makespan captures how long the overall workload takes to finish. The reported maxima show the potential of coordinating adapter training, without implying identical gains for every model or workload.
summary.tldr: PLoRA coordinates concurrent adapter fine-tuning and efficient kernels, improving throughput by up to 12.8 times and shortening makespan by up to 7.52 times.

title: PLoRA: Efficient Concurrent LoRA Training for Large Language Models

abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning generates multiple candidate answers via repeated rollouts and performs online updates using pseudo-labels constructed by majority voting. To reduce overhead and improve exploration, prior work introduces tree-structured rollouts, which share reasoning prefixes and branch at key nodes to improve sampling efficiency. However, this paradigm still faces two challenges: (1) high-entropy branching can trigger rollout collapse, where the branching budget concentrates on a few trajectories with consecutive high-entropy segments, rapidly reducing the number of effective branches; (2) early pseudo-labels are noisy and biased, which can induce self-reinforcing overfitting, causing the policy to sharpen prematurely and suppress exploration. To address these issues, we propose Entropy–Confidence Hybrid Group Relative Policy Optimization (ECHO). During rollout, ECHO jointly leverages local entropy and group-level confidence to adaptively control branch width, and further introduces online confidence-based pruning to terminate persistently low-confidence branches, avoiding high-entropy traps and mitigating collapse. During policy updates, ECHO employs confidence-adaptive clipping and an entropy–confidence hybrid advantage shaping approach to enhance training robustness and mitigate early-stage bias. Experiments demonstrate that ECHO achieves consistent gains on multiple mathematical and visual reasoning benchmarks, and generalizes more effectively under a limited rollout budget.

paragraphs: Test-time reinforcement learning samples candidate answers and updates a model using provisional labels derived from majority votes. Tree-shaped sampling saves work by sharing reasoning prefixes, but uncertainty-driven branching can spend most of the budget on a few repeatedly uncertain paths. Early voting errors can also become self-reinforcing as the model updates toward unreliable answers.

ECHO addresses sampling and updating together. During sampling, it combines local entropy, a measure of uncertainty, with confidence assessed across a group to control how widely the tree branches. It also stops branches that remain low-confidence, reducing the chance that persistent uncertainty consumes the available exploration budget.

During updates, ECHO adjusts clipping according to confidence and combines entropy with confidence when shaping the learning signal. These mechanisms aim to reduce the influence of early biased labels while retaining exploration. Experiments report consistent improvements on mathematical and visual reasoning benchmarks and better generalization with limited rollout budgets. The findings support coordinating where a model explores with how strongly it learns from the resulting answers.
summary.tldr: ECHO combines uncertainty and confidence to allocate reasoning branches and stabilize test-time reinforcement learning under limited sampling budgets.

title: ECHO: Entropy-Confidence Hybrid Optimization for Test-Time Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This position paper argues for metacognition as a general design principle for creating more accurate, secure, and efficient AI. The metacognitive solution involves systems monitoring their own states and judiciously allocating resources depending on each problem instance’s difficulty or cost of mistakes. Drawing inspiration both from past work on resource-rational AI and from well-documented metacognitive strategies in psychology and cognitive science, we identify specific challenges in embedding these strategies into AI design and highlight open theoretical and implementation problems. We showcase these principles through a tangible example of improved learning efficiency, effectiveness, and security in a Federated Learning case study. We show how these principles can be translated into practice with a novel software framework developed specifically to allow the community to design, deploy, and experiment with metacognition-enabled AI applications.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes metacognition as a general principle for AI design. Here, metacognition means monitoring a system's own state and adjusting how it uses resources. The allocation should depend on the difficulty of the particular problem and the cost of making a mistake, connecting internal monitoring to practical decisions about computation.

The authors draw on resource-rational AI research and metacognitive strategies studied in psychology and cognitive science. They examine the challenges of turning those ideas into AI systems and identify unresolved theoretical and implementation questions. Their argument is that this approach can support accuracy, security, and efficiency together, rather than treating resource allocation as a separate design concern.

The paper makes the proposal concrete through a federated learning case study that reports improvements in learning efficiency, effectiveness, and security. It also introduces a software framework for building, deploying, and experimenting with applications that use metacognition. The case study illustrates the principles in one setting, while the framework gives the community a way to investigate their broader use.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates AI that monitors itself and allocates resources adaptively, illustrated through federated learning and a new software framework.

abstract: We consider the problem of eliminating redundant Boolean features for a givendata set, where a feature is redundant if it separates the classes less wellthan another feature or set of features. Lavrac et al. proposed the algorithmREDUCE that works by pairwise comparison of features, i.e., it eliminates afeature if it is redundant with respect to another feature. Their algorithmoperates in an ILP setting and is restricted to two-class problems. In thispaper we improve their method and extend it to multiple classes. Central toour approach is the notion of a neighbourhood of examples: a set of examplesof the same class where the number of different features between examples isrelatively small. Redundant features are eliminated by applying a revisedversion of the REDUCE method to each pair of neighbourhoods of differentclass. We analyse the performance of our method on a range of data sets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to remove redundant Boolean features, which record whether a property is present or absent. A feature is considered redundant when another feature or collection of features separates the classes better. The starting point is REDUCE, a method that compares features in pairs but was restricted to two-class problems in an inductive logic programming setting.

The authors improve that method and extend it to multiple classes through neighborhoods of examples. Each neighborhood contains examples from the same class that differ on relatively few features. A revised version of REDUCE is then applied to pairs of neighborhoods belonging to different classes.

This construction organizes the multiclass problem around comparisons between relatively similar groups within classes. Feature elimination is thereby tied to how those groups are distinguished across class boundaries. The authors analyze the method on a range of datasets. The central contribution is the neighborhood-based extension of redundancy elimination to multiclass data, together with an empirical examination of its performance.
summary.tldr: The paper extends redundant Boolean feature elimination to multiple classes by comparing neighborhoods from different classes.

title: Redundant feature elimination for multi-class problems

abstract: We consider support vector machines for binary classification. As opposed to most approaches we use the number of support vectors (the “L0 norm”) as a regularizing term instead of the L1 or L2 norms. In order to solve the optimization problem we use the cross entropy method to search over the possible sets of support vectors. The algorithm consists of solving a sequence of efficient linear programs. We report experiments where our method produces generalization errors that are similar to support vector machines, while using a considerably smaller number of support vectors.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary classification with support vector machines while directly penalizing the number of support vectors in the solution. It uses this count, described as an L0 regularization term, in place of the more usual L1 or L2 terms. The objective therefore explicitly favors solutions represented by fewer support vectors.

To solve the resulting optimization problem, the authors apply the cross entropy method to search over possible support-vector sets. The algorithm works through a sequence of efficient linear programs. This supplies a computational approach for selecting the set itself, bringing the desired reduction in representation size into the optimization process.

The reported experiments produce generalization errors similar to those of support vector machines while using considerably fewer support vectors. The significance is the observed balance between a smaller solution and retained predictive performance on new examples. The paper thus demonstrates that directly regularizing the support-vector count can yield compact classifiers in the evaluated cases, with the cross entropy search and linear programs providing the mechanism for obtaining them.
summary.tldr: Cross entropy search directly penalizes support-vector counts, producing smaller classifiers with similar generalization error in the reported experiments.

title: The cross entropy method for classification

abstract: We present an efficient “sparse sampling” technique for approximating Bayes optimal decision making in reinforcement learning, addressing the well known exploration versus exploitation tradeoff. Our approach combines sparse sampling with Bayesian exploration to achieve improved decision making while controlling computational cost. The idea is to grow a sparse lookahead tree, intelligently, by exploiting information in a Bayesian posterior—rather than enumerate action branches (standard sparse sampling) or compensate myopically (value of perfect information). The outcome is a flexible, practical technique for improving action selection in simple reinforcement learning scenarios.

The outcome is a flexible, practical technique for improving action selection in simple reinforcement learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Choosing an action in reinforcement learning involves both immediate reward and the possibility of learning something useful. Bayesian decision making addresses this tradeoff using uncertainty about the environment, but evaluating possible futures can require substantial computation. This paper proposes an efficient sparse-sampling technique for approximating Bayes-optimal decisions while keeping the computational cost under control.

The method builds a sparse lookahead tree, using information in a Bayesian posterior to guide its growth. The tree represents selected possible futures relevant to choosing an action. Posterior information helps determine how to expand that calculation intelligently, combining sparse sampling with Bayesian exploration. The abstract contrasts this strategy with enumerating action branches and with myopic compensation based on the value of perfect information.

The resulting technique is presented as a flexible, practical way to improve action selection in simple reinforcement learning scenarios. Its contribution is a computational approach to considering exploration within lookahead planning. The stated outcome is an approximation to Bayes-optimal behavior, with improved decision making balanced against the effort required to calculate decisions.
summary.tldr: Bayesian sparse sampling uses posterior information to guide lookahead planning and approximate Bayes-optimal action selection at controlled computational cost.

title: Bayesian sparse sampling for on-line reward optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of choosing, sequentially, a map which assigns elements of a set A to a few elements of a set B. On each round, the algorithm suffers some cost associated with the chosen assignment, and the goal is to minimize the cumulative loss of these choices relative to the best map on the entire sequence. Even though the offline problem of finding the best map is provably hard, we show that there is an equivalent online approximation algorithm, Randomized Map Prediction (RMP), that is efficient and performs nearly as well. While drawing upon results from the “Online Prediction with Expert Advice” setting, we show how RMP can be utilized as an online approach to several standard batch problems. We apply RMP to online clustering as well as online feature selection and, surprisingly, RMP often outperforms the standard batch algorithms on these problems.

Even though the offline problem of finding the best map is provably hard, we show that there is an equivalent online approximation algorithm, Randomized Map Prediction (RMP), that is efficient and performs nearly as well. paragraphs: The paper considers a sequential assignment problem: repeatedly choose a map that assigns elements of one set to a few elements of another. Each choice incurs a cost. The objective is to keep the accumulated loss close to that of the best single map chosen with knowledge of the entire sequence.

Finding that best map offline is provably hard. The authors introduce Randomized Map Prediction, or RMP, as an efficient online approximation that performs nearly as well. The method draws on prediction with expert advice, connecting sequential choices among mappings to a broader framework for learning from the performance of alternatives.

RMP also provides an online approach to problems usually treated as batch tasks, where all data are processed together. The authors apply it to online clustering and online feature selection. In their experiments, it often outperforms standard batch algorithms on those problems. This empirical result is separate from the approximation claim: the paper offers both a theoretically motivated sequential method and evidence that its online formulation can be practically competitive.
summary.tldr: Randomized Map Prediction efficiently learns sequential assignments and often outperforms standard batch methods in clustering and feature-selection experiments.

title: Online discovery of similarity mappings

abstract: Conditional random fields (CRFs) are graphical models for modeling the probability of labels given the observations. They have traditionally been trained with using a set of observation and label pairs. Underlying all CRFs is the assumption that, conditioned on the training data, the labels are independent and identically distributed (iid). In this paper we explore the use of CRFs in a class of temporal learning algorithms, namely policygradient reinforcement learning (RL). Now the labels are no longer iid. They are actions that update the environment and affect the next observation. From an RL point of view, CRFs provide a natural way to model joint actions in a decentralized Markov decision process. They define how agents can communicate with each other to choose the optimal joint action. Our experiments include a synthetic network alignment problem, a distributed sensor network, and road traffic control; clearly outperforming RL methods which do not model the proper joint policy.
