In this paper we explore the use of CRFs in a class of temporal learning algorithms, namely policygradient reinforcement learning (RL). Now the labels are no longer iid. They are actions that update the environment and affect the next observation. From an RL point of view, CRFs provide a natural way to model joint actions in a decentralized Markov decision process. Our experiments include a synthetic network alignment problem, a distributed sensor network, and road traffic control; clearly outperforming RL methods which do not model the proper joint policy.

paragraphs: This paper uses conditional random fields to coordinate agents in reinforcement learning. CRFs model label probabilities given observations, and their conventional training uses observation–label pairs. The authors examine a temporal setting in which the predicted labels are actions: choosing them changes the environment and therefore affects what the agents observe next.

The approach places CRFs inside policy-gradient reinforcement learning. In a decentralized Markov decision process, the CRF represents a joint policy, capturing how agents' action choices relate to one another. It also describes how agents can communicate when choosing a joint action. This makes coordination part of the policy representation rather than treating each action choice in isolation.

The experiments cover synthetic network alignment, a distributed sensor network, and road traffic control. The abstract reports clear improvements over reinforcement-learning methods that do not model the appropriate joint policy. These findings support the value of explicitly representing coordinated behavior in the tested settings. The objective of choosing an optimal joint action should be distinguished from a general guarantee that learning always finds one.
summary.tldr: CRFs represent coordinated multi-agent policies within policy-gradient learning, improving results over methods without the appropriate joint policy in the reported experiments.

title: Conditional random fields for multi-agent reinforcement learning

abstract: We study the problem of one-class classification, in which we seek a rule to separate a coherent subset of instances similar to a few positive examples from a large pool of instances. We find that the problem can be formulated naturally in terms of a rate-distortion tradeoff, which can be analyzed precisely and leads to an efficient algorithm that competes well with two previous one-class methods. We also show that our model can be extended naturally to clustering problems in which it is important to remove background clutter to improve cluster purity.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of one-class classification, in which we seek a rule to separate a coherent subset of instances similar to a few positive examples from a large pool of instances. We find that the problem can be formulated naturally in terms of a rate-distortion tradeoff, which can be analyzed precisely and leads to an efficient algorithm that competes well with two previous one-class methods. We also show that our model can be extended naturally to clustering problems in which it is important to remove background clutter to improve cluster purity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a coherent group when only a few examples of that group are available. The learner receives positive examples and a much larger pool of instances, then seeks a rule that separates similar instances from the rest. The challenge is to describe the intended group without requiring labeled examples of everything outside it.

The authors formulate this task as a rate-distortion tradeoff. This gives the problem a mathematical structure in which competing demands on the representation can be analyzed precisely. Their formulation also leads to an efficient algorithm, connecting the theoretical account to a practical method for selecting instances.

The algorithm compares favorably with two earlier one-class methods. The authors also extend the model to clustering situations where background clutter can weaken the coherence of the resulting groups. In that setting, removing clutter is part of obtaining purer clusters. The contribution therefore links learning from a few positive examples with clustering that explicitly accommodates unwanted background instances.
summary.tldr: A rate-distortion formulation yields an efficient one-class classifier and extends to clustering that removes background clutter.

title: A rate-distortion one-class model and its applications to clustering
